content.text:
The core answer: the Default Persona is one shared, read-only Egma persona. It is not copied for each customer. Its system prompt combines: 1. A fixed Egma instruction. 2. The Default Persona’s traits. 3. The current test’s scenario. 4. The full conversation history. This is exact for current `origin/main`, commit `e68cb90ce2f03bef95561718917d183e39e0aaa9`. I did not inspect the hosted deployment, so this does not prove which commit its containers run. ## The complete flow ```mermaid flowchart TD A["One shared Default Persona v1"] --> B["New project points to it"] B --> C{"Does the test name personas?"} C -- "No" --> D["Test version saves the project's default persona ID"] C -- "Yes" --> E["Test version saves the selected persona IDs"] D --> F["Run pins the current persona version"] E --> F F --> G["Claim API builds SimulationSpec v3:
traits + models + test scenario + current provider keys"] G --> H["Simulator builds the system prompt"] H --> I{"Has the customer agent spoken?"} I -- "Yes" --> J["Add agent words as role: user"] I -- "No" --> K["Add hidden opening nudge as role: user"] J --> L["OpenAI gpt-4o-mini
system prompt + full history"] K --> L L --> M["Persona reply"] M --> N{"Contains [CONCLUDED]?"} N -- "No" --> O{"Chat or voice?"} O -- "Chat" --> P["Send text to the customer agent"] O -- "Voice" --> Q["Cartesia turns text into audio"] P --> R["Customer agent answers"] Q --> S["OpenAI STT turns agent audio into text"] R --> T["Append both turns to history"] S --> T T --> L N -- "Yes" --> U["Remove marker and end"] U --> V["Store turns and timing spans"] V --> W["Finish simulation and create grading work"] ``` I refreshed Graphify for this checkout: 1,069 code files, 11,284 nodes, and 28,876 post-cluster edges. Its queries centered on `projectDefaultPersona`, `resolvePersonaVersions`, `assembledSpec`, `RunningSimulation`, `Persona`, and `messages_for`. The API-to-simulator step crosses a JSON contract, so I checked both ends directly in the source. [Open the fresh Graphify call-flow export](/Users/nischalj10/.codex/visualizations/2026/08/25/01a03642-a2bb-74d3-9510-3c7ae83c3f8c/egma-persona/egma-persona-callflow.html) ## The exact system prompt Only the marked test scenario changes: ```text You are playing a person in a live conversation with a customer service agent. You are the person; the agent is who you are talking to. Who you are, exactly as authored: { "accent": "Neutral American English.", "backgroundNoise": "None.", "language": "en-US", "manner": "Clear, natural, and conversational.", "patience": "Starts patient and gives the agent time to explain.", "personality": "Speaks clear, natural English. Starts patient and cooperative, answers one question at a time, and becomes firmer if the agent is confusing or repetitive without becoming rude.", "underFriction": "Becomes firmer if the agent is confusing or repetitive, without becoming rude." } Why you are here today: How to conduct yourself: - Stay in character as this person for the whole exchange. Never mention being simulated, tested, or an AI. - Speak one conversational turn at a time, in plain spoken words — no lists, no headings, no stage directions. - Pursue what you came for until it is concluded to your satisfaction, and let your persona decide how patiently. - When your goal is concluded and nothing further is needed, say a brief goodbye and end your reply with [CONCLUDED]. ``` The exact template and role mapping are in [persona.py](/Users/nischalj10/.codex/worktrees/8669/egma/apps/simulator/src/egma_simulator/persona.py:24). The exact Default Persona traits are in [catalog.ts](/Users/nischalj10/.codex/worktrees/8669/egma/packages/db/src/persona-library/catalog.ts:54). There is no single universal final prompt because every test supplies a different scenario. ## What is sent to the LLM If the customer agent has not spoken, the first request has this shape: ```json { "model": "gpt-4o-mini", "messages": [ { "role": "system", "content": "" }, { "role": "user", "content": "(The conversation is open and the agent is listening. Speak your first turn.)" } ] } ``` If the customer agent greets first, its greeting replaces that hidden nudge. On later calls: - Customer-agent turns use `role: "user"`. - Persona turns use `role: "assistant"`. - Egma sends the complete accumulated history each time. - The hidden opening nudge is not stored as a transcript turn. Egma sends `POST https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions`. The body contains only `model` and `messages`. Egma does not set temperature, token limits, tools, seed, `top_p`, or penalties. The timeout is 60 seconds. See [model.py](/Users/nischalj10/.codex/worktrees/8669/egma/apps/simulator/src/egma_simulator/model.py:179). ## Exact models for Default Persona v1 | Function | Exact selection | |---|---| | Persona LLM | OpenAI `gpt-4o-mini` | | Voice transcription | OpenAI `gpt-live-transcribe` | | Text-to-speech | Cartesia `sonic-3.5` | | Cartesia voice ID | `5ee9feff-1265-424a-9d7f-8e4d431a12c7` | | Speaking speed | `1` | | Voice activity detection | Silero in shipped Docker Compose; this is deployment configuration, not persona content | The repository has no human-readable name for that Cartesia voice ID. Chat simulations use only the LLM. Voice simulations use the same LLM plus OpenAI realtime transcription and Cartesia speech. The selections come from the immutable persona version; there is no simulator model or voice fallback. See [model catalog](/Users/nischalj10/.codex/worktrees/8669/egma/packages/db/src/models/catalog.ts:24) and [speech.py](/Users/nischalj10/.codex/worktrees/8669/egma/apps/simulator/src/egma_simulator/speech.py:413). Provider keys are separate from the persona. You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents. All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.

When you provide a response in the final channel, that content is immediately delivered back to your parent agent.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: NEW_TASK | MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
You may also see them addressed as to=/root/..., which indicates your identity is /root/...

- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.

description: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
---

<!-- path-routing:start -->

# Diagnosing Bugs

A discipline for hard bugs. Skip phases only when explicitly justified.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) to get a clear mental model of the relevant modules, and check ADRs in the area you're touching.

## Phase 1 — Build a feedback loop

**This is the skill.** Everything else is mechanical. If you have a **tight** pass/fail signal for the bug — one that goes red on _this_ bug — you will find the cause; bisection, hypothesis-testing, and instrumentation all just consume it. If you don't have one, no amount of staring at code will save you.

Spend disproportionate effort here. **Be aggressive. Be creative. Refuse to give up.**

### Ways to construct one — try them in roughly this order

1. **Failing test** at whatever seam reaches the bug — unit, integration, e2e.
2. **Curl / HTTP script** against a running dev server.
3. **CLI invocation** with a fixture input, diffing stdout against a known-good snapshot.
4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright / Puppeteer) — drives the UI, asserts on DOM/console/network.
5. **Replay a captured trace.** Save a real network request / payload / event log to disk; replay it through the code path in isolation.
6. **Throwaway harness.** Spin up a minimal subset of the system (one service, mocked deps) that exercises the bug code path with a single function call.
7. **Property / fuzz loop.** If the bug is "sometimes wrong output", run 1000 random inputs and look for the failure mode.
8. **Bisection harness.** If the bug appeared between two known states (commit, dataset, version), automate "boot at state X, check, repeat" so you can `git bisect run` it.
9. **Differential loop.** Run the same input through old-version vs new-version (or two configs) and diff outputs.
10. **HITL bash script.** Last resort. If a human must click, drive _them_ with `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh` so the loop is still structured. Captured output feeds back to you.

Build the right feedback loop, and the bug is 90% fixed.

### Tighten the loop

Treat the loop as a product. Once you have _a_ loop, **tighten** it:

- Can I make it faster? (Cache setup, skip unrelated init, narrow the test scope.)
- Can I make the signal sharper? (Assert on the specific symptom, not "didn't crash".)
- Can I make it more deterministic? (Pin time, seed RNG, isolate filesystem, freeze network.)

A 30-second flaky loop is barely better than no loop; a 2-second deterministic one is tight — a debugging superpower.

### Non-deterministic bugs

The goal is not a clean repro but a **higher reproduction rate**. Loop the trigger 100×, parallelise, add stress, narrow timing windows, inject sleeps. A 50%-flake bug is debuggable; 1% is not — keep raising the rate until it's debuggable.

### When you genuinely cannot build a loop

Stop and say so explicitly. List what you tried. Ask the user for: (a) access to whatever environment reproduces it, (b) a captured artifact (HAR file, log dump, core dump, screen recording with timestamps), or (c) permission to add temporary production instrumentation. Do **not** proceed to hypothesise without a loop.

### Completion criterion — a tight loop that goes red

Phase 1 is done when the loop is **tight** and **red-capable**: you can name **one command** — a script path, a test invocation, a curl — that you have **already run at least once** (paste the invocation and its output), and that is:

- [ ] **Red-capable** — it drives the actual bug code path and asserts the **user's exact symptom**, so it can go red on this bug and green once fixed. Not "runs without erroring" — it must be able to _catch this specific bug_.
- [ ] **Deterministic** — same verdict every run (flaky bugs: a pinned, high reproduction rate, per above).
- [ ] **Fast** — seconds, not minutes.
- [ ] **Agent-runnable** — you can run it unattended; a human in the loop only via `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh`.

If you catch yourself reading code to build a theory before this command exists, **stop — jumping straight to a hypothesis is the exact failure this skill prevents.** No red-capable command, no Phase 2.

## Phase 2 — Reproduce + minimise

Run the loop. Watch it go red — the bug appears.

Confirm:

- [ ] The loop produces the failure mode the **user** described — not a different failure that happens to be nearby. Wrong bug = wrong fix.
- [ ] The failure is reproducible across multiple runs (or, for non-deterministic bugs, reproducible at a high enough rate to debug against).
- [ ] You have captured the exact symptom (error message, wrong output, slow timing) so later phases can verify the fix actually addresses it.

### Minimise

Once it's red, shrink the repro to the **smallest scenario that still goes red**. Cut inputs, callers, config, data, and steps **one at a time**, re-running the loop after each cut — keep only what's load-bearing for the failure.

Why bother: a minimal repro shrinks the hypothesis space in Phase 3 (fewer moving parts left to suspect) and becomes the clean regression test in Phase 5.

Done when **every remaining element is load-bearing** — removing any one of them makes the loop go green.

Do not proceed until you have reproduced **and** minimised.

## Phase 3 — Hypothesise

Generate **3–5 ranked hypotheses** before testing any of them. Single-hypothesis generation anchors on the first plausible idea.

Each hypothesis must be **falsifiable**: state the prediction it makes.

> Format: "If <X> is the cause, then <changing Y> will make the bug disappear / <changing Z> will make it worse."

If you cannot state the prediction, the hypothesis is a vibe — discard or sharpen it.

**Show the ranked list to the user before testing.** They often have domain knowledge that re-ranks instantly ("we just deployed a change to #3"), or know hypotheses they've already ruled out. Cheap checkpoint, big time saver. Don't block on it — proceed with your ranking if the user is AFK.

## Phase 4 — Instrument

Each probe must map to a specific prediction from Phase 3. **Change one variable at a time.**

Tool preference:

1. **Debugger / REPL inspection** if the env supports it. One breakpoint beats ten logs.
2. **Targeted logs** at the boundaries that distinguish hypotheses.
3. Never "log everything and grep".

**Tag every debug log** with a unique prefix, e.g. `[DEBUG-a4f2]`. Cleanup at the end becomes a single grep. Untagged logs survive; tagged logs die.

**Perf branch.** For performance regressions, logs are usually wrong. Instead: establish a baseline measurement (timing harness, `performance.now()`, profiler, query plan), then bisect. Measure first, fix second.

## Phase 5 — Fix + regression test

Write the regression test **before the fix** — but only if there is a **correct seam** for it.

A correct seam is one where the test exercises the **real bug pattern** as it occurs at the call site. If the only available seam is too shallow (single-caller test when the bug needs multiple callers, unit test that can't replicate the chain that triggered the bug), a regression test there gives false confidence.

**If no correct seam exists, that itself is the finding.** Note it. The codebase architecture is preventing the bug from being locked down. Flag this for the next phase.

If a correct seam exists:

1. Turn the minimised repro into a failing test at that seam.
2. Watch it fail.
3. Apply the fix.
4. Watch it pass.
5. Re-run the Phase 1 feedback loop against the original (un-minimised) scenario.

## Phase 6 — Cleanup + post-mortem

Required before declaring done:

- [ ] Original repro no longer reproduces (re-run the Phase 1 loop)
- [ ] Regression test passes (or absence of seam is documented)
- [ ] All `[DEBUG-...]` instrumentation removed (`grep` the prefix)
- [ ] Throwaway prototypes deleted (or moved to a clearly-marked debug location)
- [ ] The hypothesis that turned out correct is stated in the commit / PR message — so the next debugger learns

**Then ask: what would have prevented this bug?** If the answer involves architectural change (no good test seam, tangled callers, hidden coupling) hand off to the `/improve-codebase-architecture` skill with the specifics. Make the recommendation **after** the fix is in, not before — you have more information now than when you started.

4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright / Puppeteer) — drives the UI, asserts on DOM/console/network.
5. **Replay a captured trace.** Save a real network request / payload / event log to disk; replay it through the code path in isolation.
6. **Throwaway harness.** Spin up a minimal subset of the system (one service, mocked deps) that exercises the bug code path with a single function call.
7. **Property / fuzz loop.** If the bug is "sometimes wrong output", run 1000 random inputs and look for the failure mode.
8. **Bisection harness.** If the bug appeared between two known states (commit, dataset, version), automate "boot at state X, check, repeat" so you can `git bisect run` it.
9. **Differential loop.** Run the same input through old-version vs new-version (or two configs) and diff outputs.

# egma — internal agent instructions

This private repository is the planning half of the public Egma code repository. Read this file whenever it is present.

## Repository roots

- **Planning root:** the Git repository containing this file. From the Egma code root, its path is `egma-planning/`.
- **Code root:** the parent Egma Git repository when this checkout is nested in its standard internal location.

All internal plans, tickets, research, domain terms, architecture decisions, and specifications live in the Planning root. Source code, tests, builds, and public documentation live in the Code root.

These are separate Git repositories. Commit planning changes in the Planning root and code changes in the Code root. A request to commit changes can require one commit in each repository.

## Agent skills

### Planning root

Repository configuration overrides the default planning paths in installed Matt skills.

Resolve these paths from the Planning root:

- `CONTEXT.md`
- `docs/adr/`
- `docs/agents/`
- `.scratch/`
- `.out-of-scope/`

Resolve every other repository path from the Code root unless the task says otherwise. Skill-local paths, such as a template beside a `SKILL.md`, remain relative to that skill.

### Issue tracker

Use the local Markdown tracker under `.scratch/<effort>/`. See `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.

The Planning root is private and separately version-controlled. All internal documentation stays here. This positional rule removes the need to decide which parts of a planning document are safe to publish.

### Triage labels

Use the five canonical triage roles and write their values to the issue file's `Status:` line. See `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`.

### Domain docs

This project uses one domain context. Use `CONTEXT.md` as the glossary and `docs/adr/` for architecture decisions. See `docs/agents/domain.md`.

The settled vocabulary is `test` → `test suite` → `run` → `simulation`, with `grader` for judgment logic, `persona` for the synthetic caller, and `agent` only for the customer's agent under test. `eval` names nothing.

## Matt skill maintenance

When the developer invokes `/update-matt-skills`, read and follow `.agents/skills/update-matt-skills/SKILL.md`. The skill updates the public copies, restores their generic path-routing block, and verifies every tracked Matt skill.

## Pull-request reviews

Greptile reviews every public pull request automatically and can comment in several waves. Keep fixes in the same branch. Answer a review thread when its recommendation is not applied. A pull request is ready to hand off when every Greptile thread is fixed or answered.

## Keep the public repository quiet

The public `AGENTS.md` carries one conditional pointer to this file. Other public files must stand on their own and must not explain the private planning repository. Write public documentation for external readers instead of copying internal material.

# Diagnosing Bugs

A discipline for hard bugs. Skip phases only when explicitly justified.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) to get a clear mental model of the relevant modules, and check ADRs in the area you're touching.

## Phase 1 — Build a feedback loop

**This is the skill.** Everything else is mechanical. If you have a **tight** pass/fail signal for the bug — one that goes red on _this_ bug — you will find the cause; bisection, hypothesis-testing, and instrumentation all just consume it. If you don't have one, no amount of staring at code will save you.

Spend disproportionate effort here. **Be aggressive. Be creative. Refuse to give up.**

### Ways to construct one — try them in roughly this order

1. **Failing test** at whatever seam reaches the bug — unit, integration, e2e.
2. **Curl / HTTP script** against a running dev server.
3. **CLI invocation** with a fixture input, diffing stdout against a known-good snapshot.
4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright / Puppeteer) — drives the UI, asserts on DOM/console/network.
5. **Replay a captured trace.** Save a real network request / payload / event log to disk; replay it through the code path in isolation.
6. **Throwaway harness.** Spin up a minimal subset of the system (one service, mocked deps) that exercises the bug code path with a single function call.
7. **Property / fuzz loop.** If the bug is "sometimes wrong output", run 1000 random inputs and look for the failure mode.
8. **Bisection harness.** If the bug appeared between two known states (commit, dataset, version), automate "boot at state X, check, repeat" so you can `git bisect run` it.
9. **Differential loop.** Run the same input through old-version vs new-version (or two configs) and diff outputs.
10. **HITL bash script.** Last resort. If a human must click, drive _them_ with `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh` so the loop is still structured. Captured output feeds back to you.

Build the right feedback loop, and the bug is 90% fixed.

### Tighten the loop

Treat the loop as a product. Once you have _a_ loop, **tighten** it:

- Can I make it faster? (Cache setup, skip unrelated init, narrow the test scope.)
- Can I make the signal sharper? (Assert on the specific symptom, not "didn't crash".)
- Can I make it more deterministic? (Pin time, seed RNG, isolate filesystem, freeze network.)

A 30-second flaky loop is barely better than no loop; a 2-second deterministic one is tight — a debugging superpower.

### Non-deterministic bugs

The goal is not a clean repro but a **higher reproduction rate**. Loop the trigger 100×, parallelise, add stress, narrow timing windows, inject sleeps. A 50%-flake bug is debuggable; 1% is not — keep raising the rate until it's debuggable.

### When you genuinely cannot build a loop

Stop and say so explicitly. List what you tried. Ask the user for: (a) access to whatever environment reproduces it, (b) a captured artifact (HAR file, log dump, core dump, screen recording with timestamps), or (c) permission to add temporary production instrumentation. Do **not** proceed to hypothesise without a loop.

### Completion criterion — a tight loop that goes red

Phase 1 is done when the loop is **tight** and **red-capable**: you can name **one command** — a script path, a test invocation, a curl — that you have **already run at least once** (paste the invocation and its output), and that is:

- [ ] **Red-capable** — it drives the actual bug code path and asserts the **user's exact symptom**, so it can go red on this bug and green once fixed. Not "runs without erroring" — it must be able to _catch this specific bug_.
- [ ] **Deterministic** — same verdict every run (flaky bugs: a pinned, high reproduction rate, per above).
- [ ] **Fast** — seconds, not minutes.
- [ ] **Agent-runnable** — you can run it unattended; a human in the loop only via `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh`.

If you catch yourself reading code to build a theory before this command exists, **stop — jumping straight to a hypothesis is the exact failure this skill prevents.** No red-capable command, no Phase 2.

## Phase 2 — Reproduce + minimise

Run the loop. Watch it go red — the bug appears.

Confirm:

- [ ] The loop produces the failure mode the **user** described — not a different failure that happens to be nearby. Wrong bug = wrong fix.
- [ ] The failure is reproducible across multiple runs (or, for non-deterministic bugs, reproducible at a high enough rate to debug against).
- [ ] You have captured the exact symptom (error message, wrong output, slow timing) so later phases can verify the fix actually addresses it.

### Minimise

Once it's red, shrink the repro to the **smallest scenario that still goes red**. Cut inputs, callers, config, data, and steps **one at a time**, re-running the loop after each cut — keep only what's load-bearing for the failure.

Why bother: a minimal repro shrinks the hypothesis space in Phase 3 (fewer moving parts left to suspect) and becomes the clean regression test in Phase 5.

Done when **every remaining element is load-bearing** — removing any one of them makes the loop go green.

Do not proceed until you have reproduced **and** minimised.

## Phase 3 — Hypothesise

Generate **3–5 ranked hypotheses** before testing any of them. Single-hypothesis generation anchors on the first plausible idea.

Each hypothesis must be **falsifiable**: state the prediction it makes.

> Format: "If <X> is the cause, then <changing Y> will make the bug disappear / <changing Z> will make it worse."

If you cannot state the prediction, the hypothesis is a vibe — discard or sharpen it.

**Show the ranked list to the user before testing.** They often have domain knowledge that re-ranks instantly ("we just deployed a change to #3"), or know hypotheses they've already ruled out. Cheap checkpoint, big time saver. Don't block on it — proceed with your ranking if the user is AFK.

## Phase 4 — Instrument

Each probe must map to a specific prediction from Phase 3. **Change one variable at a time.**

Tool preference:

1. **Debugger / REPL inspection** if the env supports it. One breakpoint beats ten logs.
2. **Targeted logs** at the boundaries that distinguish hypotheses.
3. Never "log everything and grep".

**Tag every debug log** with a unique prefix, e.g. `[DEBUG-a4f2]`. Cleanup at the end becomes a single grep. Untagged logs survive; tagged logs die.

**Perf branch.** For performance regressions, logs are usually wrong. Instead: establish a baseline measurement (timing harness, `performance.now()`, profiler, query plan), then bisect. Measure first, fix second.

## Phase 5 — Fix + regression test

Write the regression test **before the fix** — but only if there is a **correct seam** for it.

A correct seam is one where the test exercises the **real bug pattern** as it occurs at the call site. If the only available seam is too shallow (single-caller test when the bug needs multiple callers, unit test that can't replicate the chain that triggered the bug), a regression test there gives false confidence.

**If no correct seam exists, that itself is the finding.** Note it. The codebase architecture is preventing the bug from being locked down. Flag this for the next phase.

If a correct seam exists:

1. Turn the minimised repro into a failing test at that seam.
2. Watch it fail.
3. Apply the fix.
4. Watch it pass.
5. Re-run the Phase 1 feedback loop against the original (un-minimised) scenario.

## Phase 6 — Cleanup + post-mortem

Required before declaring done:

- [ ] Original repro no longer reproduces (re-run the Phase 1 loop)
- [ ] Regression test passes (or absence of seam is documented)
- [ ] All `[DEBUG-...]` instrumentation removed (`grep` the prefix)
- [ ] Throwaway prototypes deleted (or moved to a clearly-marked debug location)
- [ ] The hypothesis that turned out correct is stated in the commit / PR message — so the next debugger learns

**Then ask: what would have prevented this bug?** If the answer involves architectural change (no good test seam, tangled callers, hidden coupling) hand off to the `/improve-codebase-architecture` skill with the specifics. Make the recommendation **after** the fix is in, not before — you have more information now than when you started.

# egma — internal agent instructions

This private repository is the planning half of the public Egma code repository. Read this file whenever it is present.

## Repository roots

- **Planning root:** the Git repository containing this file. From the Egma code root, its path is `egma-planning/`.
- **Code root:** the parent Egma Git repository when this checkout is nested in its standard internal location.

All internal plans, tickets, research, domain terms, architecture decisions, and specifications live in the Planning root. Source code, tests, builds, and public documentation live in the Code root.

These are separate Git repositories. Commit planning changes in the Planning root and code changes in the Code root. A request to commit changes can require one commit in each repository.

## Agent skills

### Planning root

Repository configuration overrides the default planning paths in installed Matt skills.

Resolve these paths from the Planning root:

- `CONTEXT.md`
- `docs/adr/`
- `docs/agents/`
- `.scratch/`
- `.out-of-scope/`

Resolve every other repository path from the Code root unless the task says otherwise. Skill-local paths, such as a template beside a `SKILL.md`, remain relative to that skill.

### Issue tracker

Use the local Markdown tracker under `.scratch/<effort>/`. See `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.

The Planning root is private and separately version-controlled. All internal documentation stays here. This positional rule removes the need to decide which parts of a planning document are safe to publish.

### Triage labels

Use the five canonical triage roles and write their values to the issue file's `Status:` line. See `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`.

### Domain docs

This project uses one domain context. Use `CONTEXT.md` as the glossary and `docs/adr/` for architecture decisions. See `docs/agents/domain.md`.

The settled vocabulary is `test` → `test suite` → `run` → `simulation`, with `grader` for judgment logic, `persona` for the synthetic caller, and `agent` only for the customer's agent under test. `eval` names nothing.

## Matt skill maintenance

When the developer invokes `/update-matt-skills`, read and follow `.agents/skills/update-matt-skills/SKILL.md`. The skill updates the public copies, restores their generic path-routing block, and verifies every tracked Matt skill.

## Pull-request reviews

Greptile reviews every public pull request automatically and can comment in several waves. Keep fixes in the same branch. Answer a review thread when its recommendation is not applied. A pull request is ready to hand off when every Greptile thread is fixed or answered.

## Keep the public repository quiet

The public `AGENTS.md` carries one conditional pointer to this file. Other public files must stand on their own and must not explain the private planning repository. Write public documentation for external readers instead of copying internal material.

egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:1:# ADR-0010: Egma's own telemetry — one flag, OpenTelemetry out, PostHog and CloudWatch behind it
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:8:Hosted egma is one box running three containers behind a Cloudflare tunnel, and until this decision the only way to see inside it was an SSM session and `docker logs`, one container at a time. The runbook exists because failures cost evenings; every one of them was diagnosed blind. Separately, the product had no analytics at all — nobody could say what a user does in the pages.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:10:The confusable thing is that egma already *is* a tracing product: the OTLP door, ClickHouse, the span vocabulary. Those are **customers' conversations** — tenancy-scoped product data with a transcript-shaped reading surface. Debugging our own deployment is a different job with a different owner, retention, and reader, and the vocabulary (`trace`, `span` as conversation words) was settled before this effort existed.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:12:Tool facts, checked against primary sources on the day of the decision (PostHog's docs, its official Claude plugin v1.1.57, and its own feature matrix): PostHog is OTLP-native for logs (beta, priced, 10 GB/month free) and distributed tracing (alpha — full query surface shipped, instrumentation contract still settling); error tracking and product analytics are mature; it has no infrastructure-metrics product at all, no profiling, no cron monitoring. Datadog/New Relic buy those at a third vendor's price and weight; SigNoz and ClickStack (on the ClickHouse Cloud we already pay) are the OTel-native alternatives.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:18:**The instrumentation is OpenTelemetry; the backend is an address; the flag is the only switch.** The api and grader carry the OTel SDK behind `EGMA_TELEMETRY` — off by default, anything but `on` means off — loaded before the entry module so it can see `pg` and `fastify` arrive. `on` means everything reports at once: there are no smaller switches inside it, and a deployment that says `on` without the endpoint and the key is **refused at boot by name**, because an absent setting must never be a quiet no — the 2026-08-15 lesson, applied to telemetry itself. Past that check, a backend that fails stays loud-but-alive: telemetry must never take the platform down. The public repository promises: a default deployment imports nothing, sends nothing, phones nothing home. The flag reaches the browser the same way: next.config maps `EGMA_TELEMETRY` into the client bundle at build, refuses an `on` build with no key, and the pages initialize on the flag alone — a key left set in a build environment cannot turn reporting on by itself, and no self-host build does either. (Greptile's review of this ADR caught the first draft gating the browser on the key; the dev then collapsed the whole design to the single switch — the endpoint-configured and key-configured branches were deleted, along with the `EGMA_TELEMETRY_OTLP_HEADERS` knob, since a collector beside the apps makes per-app credentials unnecessary and OTel's own variables still serve anyone pointing straight at a vendor.)
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:20:**PostHog is the backend for everything that reads like software, CloudWatch for everything that reads like hardware.** One PostHog project takes the pages' analytics, replays and errors, the containers' logs, and the api's and grader's spans — one vendor, roughly free at our volume, and the tracing-alpha risk is priced at one environment variable because everything speaks OTLP. Container and host vitals (CPU, memory, disk, restarts — an allowlist, since CloudWatch charges per series) go to CloudWatch, where four alarms email through SNS; PostHog has no infra-metrics product, and the box is already on AWS. SigNoz or ClickStack is the named fallback if the alpha disappoints: same instrumentation, different address.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:28:- A hosted failure is now a PostHog search and a CloudWatch alarm instead of an evening over `docker logs`; a log line carries the trace id of the request it happened inside.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:30:- The egma change must merge before the egma-cloud change, or `drift-check` goes red asking about settings main does not yet have.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:6:Egma's web app, CLI, and outside clients all act on the same organizations, projects, agents, connections, tests, runs, simulations, personas, graders, and verdicts. They use one customer-facing platform API under `/v1`, rather than separate first-party `/api/*` routes and public routes. One executable definition of each operation owns its method, path, request, response, refusals, and authentication choices; it drives server validation and serialization, the OpenAPI document, and one generated TypeScript client.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:8:The platform API covers customer-managed Egma resources, including members, invitation management, API keys, monitoring sources, monitoring import failures, trace reads, and recording access. Identity flows, deployment-wide settings, simulator work traffic, OTLP ingestion, and health checks remain separate protocols. Platform resource paths are organization-wide: a project is a write field and an optional read filter, never a path parent. This cutover changes the contract seam, not the product model: existing resource addresses and operation behavior remain intact after the `/api` prefix becomes `/v1`.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:20:The existing TypeScript-to-Python simulation JSON Schemas and private worker routes do not change. A phone run checks for a complete carrier route inside run start or simulation rerun and returns a documented refusal when it is missing; clients do not read a public phone-readiness status first. The current self-host settings door remains a narrow protocol: on a single-organization deployment, an organization administrator uses it to set the carrier route. Egma does not add a new operator identity or operator API. A run becomes complete only after execution and grading finish; execution completion remains a separate progress fact.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:16:Ticket 08 makes the coupling tighter rather than looser. The repository file format now records a behavior's priority, a persona's stable identifier, a test's description, its graders, its required capabilities, and the identity revision of its live half. A CLI that cannot read those cannot write a correct file, and a platform that cannot answer them cannot be written to correctly.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:25:- The number is bumped whenever a shape a repository client reads or writes changes. Contract **2** was: behaviors carry a priority, personas carry a stable identifier beside their display name, a test carries a description, graders, required capabilities and an identity revision, and a repository write names both the version and the revision it was written against.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:26:- **Contract 3 is the current one, and it is the first bump this decision was written to absorb.** The grader redesign ([ADR-0009 on graders](0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md), 2026-08-14) retired the two fields contract 2 was mostly defined by: an expected behavior is a plain sentence again, because under binary scoring every behavior must hold and a priority had nothing left to say; and a test names no graders, because the project's running copies judge every test and the junction is dropped. Contract 3 is contract 2 without those two — a persona's stable identifier, a test's description, its required capabilities, its identity revision, and a write naming both the version and the revision. On read, a contract-2 file is tolerated rather than refused: the `[P0]` markers and the `graders:` key are passed over and the file is rewritten as contract 3. That tolerance is deliberate and it is the one place this decision bends, because refusing would strand a folder somebody committed months ago over fields the platform has stopped having an opinion about.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:13:Three facts of egma's own posture bear on the choice. The simulator is already a participant in the room for every LiveKit simulation. The deployment rule is every-arrow-points-out — self-hosters must not grow a new inbound surface to adopt a feature. And dispatch metadata already tells the agent it is in a simulation (simulation id, modality — deliberately small, never the test's content).
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:27:- No new network surface anywhere. Not for egma cloud, not for self-hosters: the mock exchange rides the room that already exists, signalling outbound as ever. The HTTP-endpoint alternative would have added a mock service reachable from wherever customers run workers, plus its auth story, to every deployment.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md:14:**Two identities, with immutable versions on both sides.** A `grader_library` table holds stable definition identities; immutable library-definition versions hold the executable prompt, output definition, parameter schema, or code. The `grader` table holds running copies that point at library entries by a non-nullable `library_id`; immutable `grader_version` rows carry each copy's deployment values and point at one exact library-definition version. Null tenancy means Egma owns the library entry, which is the schema's one deliberate exception to hard-required tenancy. Deleting a referenced entry is refused, and predefined entries are undeletable.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0002-roles-and-how-a-permission-is-decided.md:12:**Project-scoped RBAC ships in core, not behind the licence.** [The OSS/cloud boundary](../../.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/05-oss-cloud-boundary-and-license.md) rules it *tenancy, not governance* — a self-hoster with two teams needs it to use the product at all. Only **custom roles and fine-grained grants** sit above the commercial line. So the fixed form has to be genuinely usable, or the commercial layer would be restoring basic function rather than adding flexibility.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:23:A run keeps the stable ID of the suite that started it. It does not copy the suite name, copy its membership, mint a suite version, or store a membership revision or fingerprint. A later rename is visible on old run pages because the ID still names the same suite. Run creation resolves the suite and creates every simulation with the exact test and persona versions it will execute in one transaction. Those simulation records are the execution plan and the evidence; the run row carries no second list of pinned test versions. This is not a version or snapshot of the suite.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:8:Egma Cloud and self-hosted Egma use the same CLI. A developer can use both from one machine. Agent, connection, test, and run identifiers are valid only on the platform that created them.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:10:The current CLI stores one platform URL and one key. The most recent sign-in can therefore change the target of later commands in every repository. `egma/config.yaml` stores resource identifiers but not the platform that owns them. A command can send local-platform identifiers to Egma Cloud, or cloud identifiers to a local platform, before either side reports that they do not exist.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:20:- An unbound repository uses Egma Cloud by default.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:25:- Repository command resolution is: explicit `--url`, then `EGMA_URL`, then the repository binding, then Egma Cloud for an unbound repository.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:27:- If a bound platform is unavailable or reports a different instance identifier, the command stops. It never falls back to Egma Cloud.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:35:- Bare onboarding stays simple for cloud users: a new repository targets Egma Cloud.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:37:- Cloud and several self-hosted credentials can coexist on one machine.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:42:- Tests must cover cloud default, first self-host binding, multi-platform credentials, unavailable bound platforms, instance mismatch, and no silent fallback.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:47:- **Egma Cloud always wins unless every command has `--url`:** safe default, but poor self-host experience.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:53:## Amendment — 2026-08-10: there is no Egma Cloud yet
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:55:**Superseded 2026-08-15.** Hosted egma answers at `https://app.egma.ai`, so the fourth step is back exactly as the decision above states it: an unbound repository uses the hosted platform. The amendment is kept rather than deleted because it is the record of why the tree carried a refusal in that step's place for five days. egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:57:This decision was written as though a hosted Egma existed, and it does not. `app.egma.ai` hosts a different product. Every sentence below that treats "Egma Cloud" as a running platform describes an intended future, not a system a developer can reach today.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:61:**What changed in the code:** the fourth step of that order was "then Egma Cloud for an unbound repository". There is nothing to fall back *to*, so an unbound repository that names no platform is now **refused before any address is asked anything** — with a sentence naming the one move that is the developer's, which is to name their own. egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:1:# ADR-0010: Persona versions own model execution
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:7:Production assembled one simulation from unrelated live settings. Postgres held STT provider `openai` from an older deployment and later inserted model `gpt-live-transcribe` into an empty row. Readiness checked that values existed, not that they formed a valid selection. The simulator therefore sent a realtime-only model to the completed-audio endpoint and failed before turn one.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:9:The same design also gave technical voice two owners: persona traits and platform speech settings. A run pinned the persona version but claim assembly read model and speech settings again later. An old result therefore did not have one immutable meaning.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:13:One persona version owns one complete execution selection:
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:25:Provider credentials are operational data and never belong to a persona,
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:26:grader, run, or platform-setting row. For Egma Cloud, the credential owner is
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:35:The first release has no gateway, no Cloud BYOK mode, no organization model-access switch, and no fallback. A selected provider without a current credential fails before execution with one direct error.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:37:The run pins the persona and grader version IDs. It does not own credentials or network routes.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:41:- Provider, model, voice, and speed cannot drift within a pinned persona version.

egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:51:- A later gateway adds one transport for self-hosted use of Egma credentials. It does not change persona, grader, or credential ownership.

egma-planning/docs/adr/0014-object-storage-is-the-trace-ingestion-boundary.md:12:Customer input that cannot be authenticated, decoded, validated, or normalized is refused before the local log and object store, and Egma does not return success. An accepted segment can become unprocessable only because Egma later encounters an internal defect such as corrupt bytes, an unsupported envelope version, a bad deployment order, or a ClickHouse schema mismatch. That exceptional path must retain the segment for repair without treating invalid customer input as queued work.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0014-object-storage-is-the-trace-ingestion-boundary.md:38:Egma keeps one deployable image with three runtime roles: `all` runs acceptance, upload, and draining; `ingest` runs acceptance and upload; `drain` moves durable segments into ClickHouse. Current hosted and self-hosted deployments run `all` and add no container. The role boundary exists now so hosted Egma can scale ingestion and draining separately later without changing the public route, segment format, or durability contract.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0014-object-storage-is-the-trace-ingestion-boundary.md:40:The first release runs exactly one active drainer per deployment. It adds no Postgres segment-claim rows, SQS, BullMQ, or other work queue. Object keys are passed directly to that drainer and recovered by the pending-prefix scan. Several active drainers require a later ownership design and are not part of this release.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:3:The simulation runtime — the service that plays the persona and conducts simulations — is built on Pipecat and is therefore Python, inside an otherwise all-TypeScript monorepo. Ticket 10 already said "most likely Pipecat"; this record firms it up and adds the reasoning that survived a fresh comparison (2026-08-05).
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:5:egma's runtime is a *caller into other people's infrastructure*: it must join a Retell session, speak a telephony provider's media protocol, or attach to whatever transport a future connection type demands. Pipecat is a transport-agnostic pipeline whose exposed frame/processor model makes testing instrumentation — per-turn latency stamps, dual-channel recording, scripted interruptions, injected noise, the measured audio band ticket 10 made irreversible — ordinary middleware rather than a fork. The alternatives: LiveKit Agents assumes it owns the media (agents live in LiveKit rooms, adding a LiveKit server + SIP service to every self-hosted deployment) — the right shape for *hosting* agents, not *visiting* them — and its Node SDK, the one TypeScript path anywhere, officially trails its Python SDK. Pipecat has no server-side TypeScript at all, so choosing it is choosing Python.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:7:The language cost is contained by a boundary that exists for its own reasons: the runtime receives fully-resolved simulation specs and reports over a language-neutral HTTP contract, never touches Postgres, never imports monorepo code. The contract is the language firewall.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:26:- Grading capacity scales independently of both conversation capacity and API capacity, by running more copies against the same claim mechanics — burst absorption is the deployment's dial, not a queue's prayer.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:9:`architecture.md` locks BetterAuth for authentication, and one codebase must serve both self-hosters and an egma-run cloud service. A standing constraint from [The auth and tenancy model](../../.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/06-auth-and-tenancy-model.md) adds a third requirement: auth must sit behind an interface narrow enough that WorkOS could replace BetterAuth for the cloud service later without touching the rest of the codebase.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:17:**No hosted vendor can own tenancy for an open-source product.** Auth0 and Clerk both ship "Organizations" and both are cloud-only. A self-hoster could not run egma if its org model lived there. The same reasoning already ruled out WorkOS FGA, which is hosted-only.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:120:**The second half is worse than the refusal, and only shows up once the door is open.** With single-organization mode off — the cloud service — `admitIdentity` lets everyone through, and then `onIdentityCreated` provisions a person with no intent by calling `provision()`, which **creates a brand-new organization for them**. Every employee arriving through their employer's IdP would land in an organization of their own rather than in their employer's. `onSsoLogin` is the hook that exists to prevent exactly this, and it has no implementation and is not even registered: `IdentityOptions.hooks` in `apps/api/src/auth/better-auth.ts` is typed `Pick<IdentityHooks, "admitIdentity" | "onIdentityCreated">`, and `apps/api/src/server.ts` passes those two.

egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:9:A **test** describes a situation to put an agent in, and names the **personas** who should call about it. Every test has one home inside its **project**: a **test suite**, the named container for tests normally run and reviewed together. Executing one complete suite is a **run**; each test executed once inside it is a **simulation**, which produces a **transcript**, an **outcome**, and **metrics**. **Graders** read those and return verdicts.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:16:- **project** — a product area inside it: *Outbound*, *Support*. **A permission scope and a query filter — never a wall.** A project isolates nothing; it labels rows so a permission can name a subset and a query can filter to one. Two projects in the same organization are always queryable together. **Tests, personas and graders all belong to a project**, not to an agent. A test has no agent assignment or applicability list, so the same complete suite can run against any selected agent and the results stay comparable. That comparison is the whole point of testing prompt variants, and it is impossible if each agent owns its own copy. Because the project owns nothing, an asset is never *trapped* in one — the failure that forced Humanloop to rebuild its datasets and graders as new object types. See [What is scoped to a project, and what stays at the organization](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/17-project-versus-organization-scoping.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:58:**persona** — the synthetic person who calls the agent. Who they are: manner, patience, accent, background noise, and how they behave under friction. A first-class, reusable, versioned entity. A persona is either **Egma-provided** and shared read-only, or **Custom** and owned by one project.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:60:**persona version** — one immutable, executable form of a persona. It owns the caller's traits and the complete model selection used to bring that caller to life: LLM provider and model, STT provider and model, and TTS provider, model, voice ID, and speed. The technical voice has no second home in traits or platform settings. Editing any of these facts creates a new persona version.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:62:A persona says nothing about *what* the caller wants — that's the test's scenario. The same persona calls about many different things.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:64:Every project carries one active **default persona** — a project choice, not a persona type. A new project points at Egma's shared default persona. A project may point at any active Egma-provided or Custom persona available to it instead. A default cannot be archived until the project pointer moves. A test created naming no callers receives this pointer, so authoring a first test never waits on authoring a caller.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:68:> Renamed from `digital human` on 2026-08-05 (public issue #8). `digital human` was originally chosen over `persona` for saying plainly that the caller is synthetic — accepting that users arriving from other tools would say "persona" and need correcting. They did say it, and the correcting bought nothing: `persona` is the voice industry's near-unanimous term, and now it is egma's. Also considered and still not chosen: `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `phantom`, `surrogate`.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:75:- **personas** — an array. One to start; several when a scenario should be checked against several kinds of caller. Three personas on a test means running it produces three simulations.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:85:**mock tool** — a project-owned stand-in for one of the agent's tools: the tool's name, and the answer egma serves when the agent calls it during a simulation. The answer may be an error — that is how a test forces the failure branch — and may carry a delay, so a mocked backend takes as long as the real one would. **Matching is by tool name, strictly: one answer per tool.** A mock tool never reads a call's arguments; wrong arguments are caught by grading, not matching, because the arguments are on the record either way. Chosen over `tool mock` because it is the word users arrive with (Cekura, Vapi) — the persona lesson, applied the cheap way this time. Added 2026-08-09, mock-tools grilling.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:97:**A run pins the versions it executed against** through its evidence records, not through a versioned suite. Each simulation pins its exact test and persona versions, and the run's grading plan pins its exact grader versions. Editing any of them cannot rewrite what last week's result meant. **Authored things are never overwritten**: an edit creates a new version and the old one remains. Mock tools are the single exception — unversioned by decision, and held to one world per run by snapshot rather than by version, for the reasons the Mock tools section gives. The run row itself keeps the stable suite ID and no second pinned-test list. See [ADR-0013](docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md) and [The Postgres control-plane schema](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/08-postgres-control-plane-schema.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:101:A run produces one simulation per test per persona. Running the same test twice produces two simulations — there is no separate word for a repeat.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:105:**simulator** — the component that executes a simulation: it brings the persona to life, holds the conversation with the agent over a connection, and emits the transcript, outcome, metrics and spans. It runs inside egma's own deployment, hosted or self-hosted — never anywhere else. Earlier records call it *the runtime* or *the simulation runtime*; `simulator` is the canonical name, adopted 2026-08-03 when the simulator effort began.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:131:**telemetry** — what egma reports about *itself*: the containers' logs and request spans, the pages' analytics and errors, the box's vitals. Never a customer's data and never in ClickHouse — `trace` and `span` stay conversation words, and egma's own telemetry never shares the trace store's pipe. Behind one flag, `EGMA_TELEMETRY`, off by default everywhere; hosted egma turns it on and points it at PostHog and CloudWatch. Added 2026-08-17, observability effort; see [ADR-0010](docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:149:**predefined grader** — a library entry egma owns and ships. v0 ships two: **expected_behaviors** (`llm_as_judge`) and **latency** (`code`). egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:1:# ADR-0010: Egma's own telemetry — one flag, OpenTelemetry out, PostHog and CloudWatch behind it
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:8:Hosted egma is one box running three containers behind a Cloudflare tunnel, and until this decision the only way to see inside it was an SSM session and `docker logs`, one container at a time. The runbook exists because failures cost evenings; every one of them was diagnosed blind. Separately, the product had no analytics at all — nobody could say what a user does in the pages.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:10:The confusable thing is that egma already *is* a tracing product: the OTLP door, ClickHouse, the span vocabulary. Those are **customers' conversations** — tenancy-scoped product data with a transcript-shaped reading surface. Debugging our own deployment is a different job with a different owner, retention, and reader, and the vocabulary (`trace`, `span` as conversation words) was settled before this effort existed.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:12:Tool facts, checked against primary sources on the day of the decision (PostHog's docs, its official Claude plugin v1.1.57, and its own feature matrix): PostHog is OTLP-native for logs (beta, priced, 10 GB/month free) and distributed tracing (alpha — full query surface shipped, instrumentation contract still settling); error tracking and product analytics are mature; it has no infrastructure-metrics product at all, no profiling, no cron monitoring. Datadog/New Relic buy those at a third vendor's price and weight; SigNoz and ClickStack (on the ClickHouse Cloud we already pay) are the OTel-native alternatives.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:18:**The instrumentation is OpenTelemetry; the backend is an address; the flag is the only switch.** The api and grader carry the OTel SDK behind `EGMA_TELEMETRY` — off by default, anything but `on` means off — loaded before the entry module so it can see `pg` and `fastify` arrive. `on` means everything reports at once: there are no smaller switches inside it, and a deployment that says `on` without the endpoint and the key is **refused at boot by name**, because an absent setting must never be a quiet no — the 2026-08-15 lesson, applied to telemetry itself. Past that check, a backend that fails stays loud-but-alive: telemetry must never take the platform down. The public repository promises: a default deployment imports nothing, sends nothing, phones nothing home. The flag reaches the browser the same way: next.config maps `EGMA_TELEMETRY` into the client bundle at build, refuses an `on` build with no key, and the pages initialize on the flag alone — a key left set in a build environment cannot turn reporting on by itself, and no self-host build does either. (Greptile's review of this ADR caught the first draft gating the browser on the key; the dev then collapsed the whole design to the single switch — the endpoint-configured and key-configured branches were deleted, along with the `EGMA_TELEMETRY_OTLP_HEADERS` knob, since a collector beside the apps makes per-app credentials unnecessary and OTel's own variables still serve anyone pointing straight at a vendor.)
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:20:**PostHog is the backend for everything that reads like software, CloudWatch for everything that reads like hardware.** One PostHog project takes the pages' analytics, replays and errors, the containers' logs, and the api's and grader's spans — one vendor, roughly free at our volume, and the tracing-alpha risk is priced at one environment variable because everything speaks OTLP. Container and host vitals (CPU, memory, disk, restarts — an allowlist, since CloudWatch charges per series) go to CloudWatch, where four alarms email through SNS; PostHog has no infra-metrics product, and the box is already on AWS. SigNoz or ClickStack is the named fallback if the alpha disappoints: same instrumentation, different address.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:28:- A hosted failure is now a PostHog search and a CloudWatch alarm instead of an evening over `docker logs`; a log line carries the trace id of the request it happened inside.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:30:- The egma change must merge before the egma-cloud change, or `drift-check` goes red asking about settings main does not yet have.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:6:Egma's web app, CLI, and outside clients all act on the same organizations, projects, agents, connections, tests, runs, simulations, personas, graders, and verdicts. They use one customer-facing platform API under `/v1`, rather than separate first-party `/api/*` routes and public routes. One executable definition of each operation owns its method, path, request, response, refusals, and authentication choices; it drives server validation and serialization, the OpenAPI document, and one generated TypeScript client.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:8:The platform API covers customer-managed Egma resources, including members, invitation management, API keys, monitoring sources, monitoring import failures, trace reads, and recording access. Identity flows, deployment-wide settings, simulator work traffic, OTLP ingestion, and health checks remain separate protocols. Platform resource paths are organization-wide: a project is a write field and an optional read filter, never a path parent. This cutover changes the contract seam, not the product model: existing resource addresses and operation behavior remain intact after the `/api` prefix becomes `/v1`.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:20:The existing TypeScript-to-Python simulation JSON Schemas and private worker routes do not change. A phone run checks for a complete carrier route inside run start or simulation rerun and returns a documented refusal when it is missing; clients do not read a public phone-readiness status first. The current self-host settings door remains a narrow protocol: on a single-organization deployment, an organization administrator uses it to set the carrier route. Egma does not add a new operator identity or operator API. A run becomes complete only after execution and grading finish; execution completion remains a separate progress fact.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:16:Ticket 08 makes the coupling tighter rather than looser. The repository file format now records a behavior's priority, a persona's stable identifier, a test's description, its graders, its required capabilities, and the identity revision of its live half. A CLI that cannot read those cannot write a correct file, and a platform that cannot answer them cannot be written to correctly.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:25:- The number is bumped whenever a shape a repository client reads or writes changes. Contract **2** was: behaviors carry a priority, personas carry a stable identifier beside their display name, a test carries a description, graders, required capabilities and an identity revision, and a repository write names both the version and the revision it was written against.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:26:- **Contract 3 is the current one, and it is the first bump this decision was written to absorb.** The grader redesign ([ADR-0009 on graders](0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md), 2026-08-14) retired the two fields contract 2 was mostly defined by: an expected behavior is a plain sentence again, because under binary scoring every behavior must hold and a priority had nothing left to say; and a test names no graders, because the project's running copies judge every test and the junction is dropped. Contract 3 is contract 2 without those two — a persona's stable identifier, a test's description, its required capabilities, its identity revision, and a write naming both the version and the revision. On read, a contract-2 file is tolerated rather than refused: the `[P0]` markers and the `graders:` key are passed over and the file is rewritten as contract 3. That tolerance is deliberate and it is the one place this decision bends, because refusing would strand a folder somebody committed months ago over fields the platform has stopped having an opinion about.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:13:Three facts of egma's own posture bear on the choice. The simulator is already a participant in the room for every LiveKit simulation. The deployment rule is every-arrow-points-out — self-hosters must not grow a new inbound surface to adopt a feature. And dispatch metadata already tells the agent it is in a simulation (simulation id, modality — deliberately small, never the test's content).
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:27:- No new network surface anywhere. Not for egma cloud, not for self-hosters: the mock exchange rides the room that already exists, signalling outbound as ever. The HTTP-endpoint alternative would have added a mock service reachable from wherever customers run workers, plus its auth story, to every deployment.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md:14:**Two identities, with immutable versions on both sides.** A `grader_library` table holds stable definition identities; immutable library-definition versions hold the executable prompt, output definition, parameter schema, or code. The `grader` table holds running copies that point at library entries by a non-nullable `library_id`; immutable `grader_version` rows carry each copy's deployment values and point at one exact library-definition version. Null tenancy means Egma owns the library entry, which is the schema's one deliberate exception to hard-required tenancy. Deleting a referenced entry is refused, and predefined entries are undeletable.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0002-roles-and-how-a-permission-is-decided.md:12:**Project-scoped RBAC ships in core, not behind the licence.** [The OSS/cloud boundary](../../.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/05-oss-cloud-boundary-and-license.md) rules it *tenancy, not governance* — a self-hoster with two teams needs it to use the product at all. Only **custom roles and fine-grained grants** sit above the commercial line. So the fixed form has to be genuinely usable, or the commercial layer would be restoring basic function rather than adding flexibility.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:23:A run keeps the stable ID of the suite that started it. It does not copy the suite name, copy its membership, mint a suite version, or store a membership revision or fingerprint. A later rename is visible on old run pages because the ID still names the same suite. Run creation resolves the suite and creates every simulation with the exact test and persona versions it will execute in one transaction. Those simulation records are the execution plan and the evidence; the run row carries no second list of pinned test versions. This is not a version or snapshot of the suite.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:8:Egma Cloud and self-hosted Egma use the same CLI. A developer can use both from one machine. Agent, connection, test, and run identifiers are valid only on the platform that created them.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:10:The current CLI stores one platform URL and one key. The most recent sign-in can therefore change the target of later commands in every repository. `egma/config.yaml` stores resource identifiers but not the platform that owns them. A command can send local-platform identifiers to Egma Cloud, or cloud identifiers to a local platform, before either side reports that they do not exist.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:20:- An unbound repository uses Egma Cloud by default.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:25:- Repository command resolution is: explicit `--url`, then `EGMA_URL`, then the repository binding, then Egma Cloud for an unbound repository.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:27:- If a bound platform is unavailable or reports a different instance identifier, the command stops. It never falls back to Egma Cloud.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:35:- Bare onboarding stays simple for cloud users: a new repository targets Egma Cloud.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:37:- Cloud and several self-hosted credentials can coexist on one machine.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:42:- Tests must cover cloud default, first self-host binding, multi-platform credentials, unavailable bound platforms, instance mismatch, and no silent fallback.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:47:- **Egma Cloud always wins unless every command has `--url`:** safe default, but poor self-host experience.

egma-planning/docs/adr/0014-object-storage-is-the-trace-ingestion-boundary.md:12:Customer input that cannot be authenticated, decoded, validated, or normalized is refused before the local log and object store, and Egma does not return success. An accepted segment can become unprocessable only because Egma later encounters an internal defect such as corrupt bytes, an unsupported envelope version, a bad deployment order, or a ClickHouse schema mismatch. That exceptional path must retain the segment for repair without treating invalid customer input as queued work.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0014-object-storage-is-the-trace-ingestion-boundary.md:38:Egma keeps one deployable image with three runtime roles: `all` runs acceptance, upload, and draining; `ingest` runs acceptance and upload; `drain` moves durable segments into ClickHouse. Current hosted and self-hosted deployments run `all` and add no container. The role boundary exists now so hosted Egma can scale ingestion and draining separately later without changing the public route, segment format, or durability contract.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0014-object-storage-is-the-trace-ingestion-boundary.md:40:The first release runs exactly one active drainer per deployment. It adds no Postgres segment-claim rows, SQS, BullMQ, or other work queue. Object keys are passed directly to that drainer and recovered by the pending-prefix scan. Several active drainers require a later ownership design and are not part of this release.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:3:The simulation runtime — the service that plays the persona and conducts simulations — is built on Pipecat and is therefore Python, inside an otherwise all-TypeScript monorepo. Ticket 10 already said "most likely Pipecat"; this record firms it up and adds the reasoning that survived a fresh comparison (2026-08-05).
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:5:egma's runtime is a *caller into other people's infrastructure*: it must join a Retell session, speak a telephony provider's media protocol, or attach to whatever transport a future connection type demands. Pipecat is a transport-agnostic pipeline whose exposed frame/processor model makes testing instrumentation — per-turn latency stamps, dual-channel recording, scripted interruptions, injected noise, the measured audio band ticket 10 made irreversible — ordinary middleware rather than a fork. The alternatives: LiveKit Agents assumes it owns the media (agents live in LiveKit rooms, adding a LiveKit server + SIP service to every self-hosted deployment) — the right shape for *hosting* agents, not *visiting* them — and its Node SDK, the one TypeScript path anywhere, officially trails its Python SDK. Pipecat has no server-side TypeScript at all, so choosing it is choosing Python.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:7:The language cost is contained by a boundary that exists for its own reasons: the runtime receives fully-resolved simulation specs and reports over a language-neutral HTTP contract, never touches Postgres, never imports monorepo code. The contract is the language firewall.

egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:9:A **test** describes a situation to put an agent in, and names the **personas** who should call about it. Every test has one home inside its **project**: a **test suite**, the named container for tests normally run and reviewed together. Executing one complete suite is a **run**; each test executed once inside it is a **simulation**, which produces a **transcript**, an **outcome**, and **metrics**. **Graders** read those and return verdicts.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:16:- **project** — a product area inside it: *Outbound*, *Support*. **A permission scope and a query filter — never a wall.** A project isolates nothing; it labels rows so a permission can name a subset and a query can filter to one. Two projects in the same organization are always queryable together. **Tests, personas and graders all belong to a project**, not to an agent. A test has no agent assignment or applicability list, so the same complete suite can run against any selected agent and the results stay comparable. That comparison is the whole point of testing prompt variants, and it is impossible if each agent owns its own copy. Because the project owns nothing, an asset is never *trapped* in one — the failure that forced Humanloop to rebuild its datasets and graders as new object types. See [What is scoped to a project, and what stays at the organization](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/17-project-versus-organization-scoping.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:58:**persona** — the synthetic person who calls the agent. Who they are: manner, patience, accent, background noise, and how they behave under friction. A first-class, reusable, versioned entity. A persona is either **Egma-provided** and shared read-only, or **Custom** and owned by one project.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:60:**persona version** — one immutable, executable form of a persona. It owns the caller's traits and the complete model selection used to bring that caller to life: LLM provider and model, STT provider and model, and TTS provider, model, voice ID, and speed. The technical voice has no second home in traits or platform settings. Editing any of these facts creates a new persona version.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:62:A persona says nothing about *what* the caller wants — that's the test's scenario. The same persona calls about many different things.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:64:Every project carries one active **default persona** — a project choice, not a persona type. A new project points at Egma's shared default persona. A project may point at any active Egma-provided or Custom persona available to it instead. A default cannot be archived until the project pointer moves. A test created naming no callers receives this pointer, so authoring a first test never waits on authoring a caller.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:68:> Renamed from `digital human` on 2026-08-05 (public issue #8). `digital human` was originally chosen over `persona` for saying plainly that the caller is synthetic — accepting that users arriving from other tools would say "persona" and need correcting. They did say it, and the correcting bought nothing: `persona` is the voice industry's near-unanimous term, and now it is egma's. egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:75:- **personas** — an array. One to start; several when a scenario should be checked against several kinds of caller. Three personas on a test means running it produces three simulations.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:85:**mock tool** — a project-owned stand-in for one of the agent's tools: the tool's name, and the answer egma serves when the agent calls it during a simulation. The answer may be an error — that is how a test forces the failure branch — and may carry a delay, so a mocked backend takes as long as the real one would. **Matching is by tool name, strictly: one answer per tool.** A mock tool never reads a call's arguments; wrong arguments are caught by grading, not matching, because the arguments are on the record either way. egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:97:**A run pins the versions it executed against** through its evidence records, not through a versioned suite. Each simulation pins its exact test and persona versions, and the run's grading plan pins its exact grader versions. Editing any of them cannot rewrite what last week's result meant. **Authored things are never overwritten**: an edit creates a new version and the old one remains. It runs inside egma's own deployment, hosted or self-hosted — never anywhere else. Earlier records call it *the runtime* or *the simulation runtime*; `simulator` is the canonical name, adopted 2026-08-03 when the simulator effort began.
