egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:1:# ADR-0010: Egma's own telemetry — one flag, OpenTelemetry out, PostHog and CloudWatch behind it
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:8:Hosted egma is one box running three containers behind a Cloudflare tunnel, and until this decision the only way to see inside it was an SSM session and `docker logs`, one container at a time. The runbook exists because failures cost evenings; every one of them was diagnosed blind. Separately, the product had no analytics at all — nobody could say what a user does in the pages.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:10:The confusable thing is that egma already *is* a tracing product: the OTLP door, ClickHouse, the span vocabulary. Those are **customers' conversations** — tenancy-scoped product data with a transcript-shaped reading surface. Debugging our own deployment is a different job with a different owner, retention, and reader, and the vocabulary (`trace`, `span` as conversation words) was settled before this effort existed.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:12:Tool facts, checked against primary sources on the day of the decision (PostHog's docs, its official Claude plugin v1.1.57, and its own feature matrix): PostHog is OTLP-native for logs (beta, priced, 10 GB/month free) and distributed tracing (alpha — full query surface shipped, instrumentation contract still settling); error tracking and product analytics are mature; it has no infrastructure-metrics product at all, no profiling, no cron monitoring. Datadog/New Relic buy those at a third vendor's price and weight; SigNoz and ClickStack (on the ClickHouse Cloud we already pay) are the OTel-native alternatives.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:18:**The instrumentation is OpenTelemetry; the backend is an address; the flag is the only switch.** The api and grader carry the OTel SDK behind `EGMA_TELEMETRY` — off by default, anything but `on` means off — loaded before the entry module so it can see `pg` and `fastify` arrive. `on` means everything reports at once: there are no smaller switches inside it, and a deployment that says `on` without the endpoint and the key is **refused at boot by name**, because an absent setting must never be a quiet no — the 2026-08-15 lesson, applied to telemetry itself. Past that check, a backend that fails stays loud-but-alive: telemetry must never take the platform down. The public repository promises: a default deployment imports nothing, sends nothing, phones nothing home. The flag reaches the browser the same way: next.config maps `EGMA_TELEMETRY` into the client bundle at build, refuses an `on` build with no key, and the pages initialize on the flag alone — a key left set in a build environment cannot turn reporting on by itself, and no self-host build does either. (Greptile's review of this ADR caught the first draft gating the browser on the key; the dev then collapsed the whole design to the single switch — the endpoint-configured and key-configured branches were deleted, along with the `EGMA_TELEMETRY_OTLP_HEADERS` knob, since a collector beside the apps makes per-app credentials unnecessary and OTel's own variables still serve anyone pointing straight at a vendor.)
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:20:**PostHog is the backend for everything that reads like software, CloudWatch for everything that reads like hardware.** One PostHog project takes the pages' analytics, replays and errors, the containers' logs, and the api's and grader's spans — one vendor, roughly free at our volume, and the tracing-alpha risk is priced at one environment variable because everything speaks OTLP. Container and host vitals (CPU, memory, disk, restarts — an allowlist, since CloudWatch charges per series) go to CloudWatch, where four alarms email through SNS; PostHog has no infra-metrics product, and the box is already on AWS. SigNoz or ClickStack is the named fallback if the alpha disappoints: same instrumentation, different address.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:28:- A hosted failure is now a PostHog search and a CloudWatch alarm instead of an evening over `docker logs`; a log line carries the trace id of the request it happened inside.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:30:- The egma change must merge before the egma-cloud change, or `drift-check` goes red asking about settings main does not yet have.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:6:Egma's web app, CLI, and outside clients all act on the same organizations, projects, agents, connections, tests, runs, simulations, personas, graders, and verdicts. They use one customer-facing platform API under `/v1`, rather than separate first-party `/api/*` routes and public routes. One executable definition of each operation owns its method, path, request, response, refusals, and authentication choices; it drives server validation and serialization, the OpenAPI document, and one generated TypeScript client.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:8:The platform API covers customer-managed Egma resources, including members, invitation management, API keys, monitoring sources, monitoring import failures, trace reads, and recording access. Identity flows, deployment-wide settings, simulator work traffic, OTLP ingestion, and health checks remain separate protocols. Platform resource paths are organization-wide: a project is a write field and an optional read filter, never a path parent. This cutover changes the contract seam, not the product model: existing resource addresses and operation behavior remain intact after the `/api` prefix becomes `/v1`.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:20:The existing TypeScript-to-Python simulation JSON Schemas and private worker routes do not change. A phone run checks for a complete carrier route inside run start or simulation rerun and returns a documented refusal when it is missing; clients do not read a public phone-readiness status first. The current self-host settings door remains a narrow protocol: on a single-organization deployment, an organization administrator uses it to set the carrier route. Egma does not add a new operator identity or operator API. A run becomes complete only after execution and grading finish; execution completion remains a separate progress fact.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:16:Ticket 08 makes the coupling tighter rather than looser. The repository file format now records a behavior's priority, a persona's stable identifier, a test's description, its graders, its required capabilities, and the identity revision of its live half. A CLI that cannot read those cannot write a correct file, and a platform that cannot answer them cannot be written to correctly.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:25:- The number is bumped whenever a shape a repository client reads or writes changes. Contract **2** was: behaviors carry a priority, personas carry a stable identifier beside their display name, a test carries a description, graders, required capabilities and an identity revision, and a repository write names both the version and the revision it was written against.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:26:- **Contract 3 is the current one, and it is the first bump this decision was written to absorb.** The grader redesign ([ADR-0009 on graders](0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md), 2026-08-14) retired the two fields contract 2 was mostly defined by: an expected behavior is a plain sentence again, because under binary scoring every behavior must hold and a priority had nothing left to say; and a test names no graders, because the project's running copies judge every test and the junction is dropped. Contract 3 is contract 2 without those two — a persona's stable identifier, a test's description, its required capabilities, its identity revision, and a write naming both the version and the revision. On read, a contract-2 file is tolerated rather than refused: the `[P0]` markers and the `graders:` key are passed over and the file is rewritten as contract 3. egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:13:Three facts of egma's own posture bear on the choice. egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md:14:**Two identities, with immutable versions on both sides.** A `grader_library` table holds stable definition identities; immutable library-definition versions hold the executable prompt, output definition, parameter schema, or code. Null tenancy means Egma owns the library entry, which is the schema's one deliberate exception to hard-required tenancy. egma-planning/docs/adr/0002-roles-and-how-a-permission-is-decided.md:12:**Project-scoped RBAC ships in core, not behind the licence.** [The OSS/cloud boundary](../../.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/05-oss-cloud-boundary-and-license.md) rules it *tenancy, not governance* — a self-hoster with two teams needs it to use the product at all. egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:23:A run keeps the stable ID of the suite that started it. egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:3:The simulation runtime — the service that plays the persona and conducts simulations — is built on Pipecat and is therefore Python, inside an otherwise all-TypeScript monorepo. Ticket 10 already said "most likely Pipecat"; this record firms it up and adds the reasoning that survived a fresh comparison (2026-08-05).
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:5:egma's runtime is a *caller into other people's infrastructure*: it must join a Retell session, speak a telephony provider's media protocol, or attach to whatever transport a future connection type demands. Pipecat is a transport-agnostic pipeline whose exposed frame/processor model makes testing instrumentation — per-turn latency stamps, dual-channel recording, scripted interruptions, injected noise, the measured audio band ticket 10 made irreversible — ordinary middleware rather than a fork. The alternatives: LiveKit Agents assumes it owns the media (agents live in LiveKit rooms, adding a LiveKit server + SIP service to every self-hosted deployment) — the right shape for *hosting* agents, not *visiting* them — and its Node SDK, the one TypeScript path anywhere, officially trails its Python SDK. Pipecat has no server-side TypeScript at all, so choosing it is choosing Python.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:7:The language cost is contained by a boundary that exists for its own reasons: the runtime receives fully-resolved simulation specs and reports over a language-neutral HTTP contract, never touches Postgres, never imports monorepo code. The contract is the language firewall.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:26:- Grading capacity scales independently of both conversation capacity and API capacity, by running more copies against the same claim mechanics — burst absorption is the deployment's dial, not a queue's prayer.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:9:`architecture.md` locks BetterAuth for authentication, and one codebase must serve both self-hosters and an egma-run cloud service. A standing constraint from [The auth and tenancy model](../../.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/06-auth-and-tenancy-model.md) adds a third requirement: auth must sit behind an interface narrow enough that WorkOS could replace BetterAuth for the cloud service later without touching the rest of the codebase.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:17:**No hosted vendor can own tenancy for an open-source product.** Auth0 and Clerk both ship "Organizations" and both are cloud-only. A self-hoster could not run egma if its org model lived there. The same reasoning already ruled out WorkOS FGA, which is hosted-only.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:120:**The second half is worse than the refusal, and only shows up once the door is open.** With single-organization mode off — the cloud service — `admitIdentity` lets everyone through, and then `onIdentityCreated` provisions a person with no intent by calling `provision()`, which **creates a brand-new organization for them**. Every employee arriving through their employer's IdP would land in an organization of their own rather than in their employer's. `onSsoLogin` is the hook that exists to prevent exactly this, and it has no implementation and is not even registered: `IdentityOptions.hooks` in `apps/api/src/auth/better-auth.ts` is typed `Pick<IdentityHooks, "admitIdentity" | "onIdentityCreated">`, and `apps/api/src/server.ts` passes those two.

egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:9:A **test** describes a situation to put an agent in, and names the **personas** who should call about it. Every test has one home inside its **project**: a **test suite**, the named container for tests normally run and reviewed together. Executing one complete suite is a **run**; each test executed once inside it is a **simulation**, which produces a **transcript**, an **outcome**, and **metrics**. **Graders** read those and return verdicts.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:16:- **project** — a product area inside it: *Outbound*, *Support*. **A permission scope and a query filter — never a wall.** A project isolates nothing; it labels rows so a permission can name a subset and a query can filter to one. Two projects in the same organization are always queryable together. **Tests, personas and graders all belong to a project**, not to an agent. A test has no agent assignment or applicability list, so the same complete suite can run against any selected agent and the results stay comparable. That comparison is the whole point of testing prompt variants, and it is impossible if each agent owns its own copy. Because the project owns nothing, an asset is never *trapped* in one — the failure that forced Humanloop to rebuild its datasets and graders as new object types. See [What is scoped to a project, and what stays at the organization](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/17-project-versus-organization-scoping.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:58:**persona** — the synthetic person who calls the agent. Who they are: manner, patience, accent, background noise, and how they behave under friction. A first-class, reusable, versioned entity. A persona is either **Egma-provided** and shared read-only, or **Custom** and owned by one project.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:60:**persona version** — one immutable, executable form of a persona. It owns the caller's traits and the complete model selection used to bring that caller to life: LLM provider and model, STT provider and model, and TTS provider, model, voice ID, and speed. The technical voice has no second home in traits or platform settings. Editing any of these facts creates a new persona version.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:62:A persona says nothing about *what* the caller wants — that's the test's scenario. The same persona calls about many different things.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:64:Every project carries one active **default persona** — a project choice, not a persona type. A new project points at Egma's shared default persona. A project may point at any active Egma-provided or Custom persona available to it instead. A default cannot be archived until the project pointer moves. A test created naming no callers receives this pointer, so authoring a first test never waits on authoring a caller.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:68:> Renamed from `digital human` on 2026-08-05 (public issue #8). `digital human` was originally chosen over `persona` for saying plainly that the caller is synthetic — accepting that users arriving from other tools would say "persona" and need correcting. They did say it, and the correcting bought nothing: `persona` is the voice industry's near-unanimous term, and now it is egma's. Also considered and still not chosen: `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `phantom`, `surrogate`.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:75:- **personas** — an array. One to start; several when a scenario should be checked against several kinds of caller. Three personas on a test means running it produces three simulations.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:85:**mock tool** — a project-owned stand-in for one of the agent's tools: the tool's name, and the answer egma serves when the agent calls it during a simulation. The answer may be an error — that is how a test forces the failure branch — and may carry a delay, so a mocked backend takes as long as the real one would. **Matching is by tool name, strictly: one answer per tool.** A mock tool never reads a call's arguments; wrong arguments are caught by grading, not matching, because the arguments are on the record either way. egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:97:**A run pins the versions it executed against** through its evidence records, not through a versioned suite. egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:105:**simulator** — the component that executes a simulation: it brings the persona to life, holds the conversation with the agent over a connection, and emits the transcript, outcome, metrics and spans. It runs inside egma's own deployment, hosted or self-hosted — never anywhere else. egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:1:# ADR-0010: Egma's own telemetry — one flag, OpenTelemetry out, PostHog and CloudWatch behind it
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:8:Hosted egma is one box running three containers behind a Cloudflare tunnel, and until this decision the only way to see inside it was an SSM session and `docker logs`, one container at a time. The runbook exists because failures cost evenings; every one of them was diagnosed blind. Separately, the product had no analytics at all — nobody could say what a user does in the pages.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:10:The confusable thing is that egma already *is* a tracing product: the OTLP door, ClickHouse, the span vocabulary. Those are **customers' conversations** — tenancy-scoped product data with a transcript-shaped reading surface. Debugging our own deployment is a different job with a different owner, retention, and reader, and the vocabulary (`trace`, `span` as conversation words) was settled before this effort existed.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:12:Tool facts, checked against primary sources on the day of the decision (PostHog's docs, its official Claude plugin v1.1.57, and its own feature matrix): PostHog is OTLP-native for logs (beta, priced, 10 GB/month free) and distributed tracing (alpha — full query surface shipped, instrumentation contract still settling); error tracking and product analytics are mature; it has no infrastructure-metrics product at all, no profiling, no cron monitoring. Datadog/New Relic buy those at a third vendor's price and weight; SigNoz and ClickStack (on the ClickHouse Cloud we already pay) are the OTel-native alternatives.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:18:**The instrumentation is OpenTelemetry; the backend is an address; the flag is the only switch.** The api and grader carry the OTel SDK behind `EGMA_TELEMETRY` — off by default, anything but `on` means off — loaded before the entry module so it can see `pg` and `fastify` arrive. `on` means everything reports at once: there are no smaller switches inside it, and a deployment that says `on` without the endpoint and the key is **refused at boot by name**, because an absent setting must never be a quiet no — the 2026-08-15 lesson, applied to telemetry itself. Past that check, a backend that fails stays loud-but-alive: telemetry must never take the platform down. The public repository promises: a default deployment imports nothing, sends nothing, phones nothing home. The flag reaches the browser the same way: next.config maps `EGMA_TELEMETRY` into the client bundle at build, refuses an `on` build with no key, and the pages initialize on the flag alone — a key left set in a build environment cannot turn reporting on by itself, and no self-host build does either. (Greptile's review of this ADR caught the first draft gating the browser on the key; the dev then collapsed the whole design to the single switch — the endpoint-configured and key-configured branches were deleted, along with the `EGMA_TELEMETRY_OTLP_HEADERS` knob, since a collector beside the apps makes per-app credentials unnecessary and OTel's own variables still serve anyone pointing straight at a vendor.)
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:20:**PostHog is the backend for everything that reads like software, CloudWatch for everything that reads like hardware.** One PostHog project takes the pages' analytics, replays and errors, the containers' logs, and the api's and grader's spans — one vendor, roughly free at our volume, and the tracing-alpha risk is priced at one environment variable because everything speaks OTLP. Container and host vitals (CPU, memory, disk, restarts — an allowlist, since CloudWatch charges per series) go to CloudWatch, where four alarms email through SNS; PostHog has no infra-metrics product, and the box is already on AWS. SigNoz or ClickStack is the named fallback if the alpha disappoints: same instrumentation, different address.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:28:- A hosted failure is now a PostHog search and a CloudWatch alarm instead of an evening over `docker logs`; a log line carries the trace id of the request it happened inside.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:30:- The egma change must merge before the egma-cloud change, or `drift-check` goes red asking about settings main does not yet have.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:6:Egma's web app, CLI, and outside clients all act on the same organizations, projects, agents, connections, tests, runs, simulations, personas, graders, and verdicts. They use one customer-facing platform API under `/v1`, rather than separate first-party `/api/*` routes and public routes. One executable definition of each operation owns its method, path, request, response, refusals, and authentication choices; it drives server validation and serialization, the OpenAPI document, and one generated TypeScript client.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:8:The platform API covers customer-managed Egma resources, including members, invitation management, API keys, monitoring sources, monitoring import failures, trace reads, and recording access. Identity flows, deployment-wide settings, simulator work traffic, OTLP ingestion, and health checks remain separate protocols. Platform resource paths are organization-wide: a project is a write field and an optional read filter, never a path parent. This cutover changes the contract seam, not the product model: existing resource addresses and operation behavior remain intact after the `/api` prefix becomes `/v1`.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:20:The existing TypeScript-to-Python simulation JSON Schemas and private worker routes do not change. A phone run checks for a complete carrier route inside run start or simulation rerun and returns a documented refusal when it is missing; clients do not read a public phone-readiness status first. The current self-host settings door remains a narrow protocol: on a single-organization deployment, an organization administrator uses it to set the carrier route. Egma does not add a new operator identity or operator API. A run becomes complete only after execution and grading finish; execution completion remains a separate progress fact.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:16:Ticket 08 makes the coupling tighter rather than looser. The repository file format now records a behavior's priority, a persona's stable identifier, a test's description, its graders, its required capabilities, and the identity revision of its live half. A CLI that cannot read those cannot write a correct file, and a platform that cannot answer them cannot be written to correctly.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:25:- The number is bumped whenever a shape a repository client reads or writes changes. Contract **2** was: behaviors carry a priority, personas carry a stable identifier beside their display name, a test carries a description, graders, required capabilities and an identity revision, and a repository write names both the version and the revision it was written against.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:26:- **Contract 3 is the current one, and it is the first bump this decision was written to absorb.** The grader redesign ([ADR-0009 on graders](0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md), 2026-08-14) retired the two fields contract 2 was mostly defined by: an expected behavior is a plain sentence again, because under binary scoring every behavior must hold and a priority had nothing left to say; and a test names no graders, because the project's running copies judge every test and the junction is dropped. Contract 3 is contract 2 without those two — a persona's stable identifier, a test's description, its required capabilities, its identity revision, and a write naming both the version and the revision. On read, a contract-2 file is tolerated rather than refused: the `[P0]` markers and the `graders:` key are passed over and the file is rewritten as contract 3. That tolerance is deliberate and it is the one place this decision bends, because refusing would strand a folder somebody committed months ago over fields the platform has stopped having an opinion about.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:13:Three facts of egma's own posture bear on the choice. The simulator is already a participant in the room for every LiveKit simulation. The deployment rule is every-arrow-points-out — self-hosters must not grow a new inbound surface to adopt a feature. And dispatch metadata already tells the agent it is in a simulation (simulation id, modality — deliberately small, never the test's content).
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:27:- No new network surface anywhere. Not for egma cloud, not for self-hosters: the mock exchange rides the room that already exists, signalling outbound as ever. The HTTP-endpoint alternative would have added a mock service reachable from wherever customers run workers, plus its auth story, to every deployment.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md:14:**Two identities, with immutable versions on both sides.** A `grader_library` table holds stable definition identities; immutable library-definition versions hold the executable prompt, output definition, parameter schema, or code. The `grader` table holds running copies that point at library entries by a non-nullable `library_id`; immutable `grader_version` rows carry each copy's deployment values and point at one exact library-definition version. Null tenancy means Egma owns the library entry, which is the schema's one deliberate exception to hard-required tenancy. Deleting a referenced entry is refused, and predefined entries are undeletable.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0002-roles-and-how-a-permission-is-decided.md:12:**Project-scoped RBAC ships in core, not behind the licence.** [The OSS/cloud boundary](../../.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/05-oss-cloud-boundary-and-license.md) rules it *tenancy, not governance* — a self-hoster with two teams needs it to use the product at all. Only **custom roles and fine-grained grants** sit above the commercial line. So the fixed form has to be genuinely usable, or the commercial layer would be restoring basic function rather than adding flexibility.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:23:A run keeps the stable ID of the suite that started it. It does not copy the suite name, copy its membership, mint a suite version, or store a membership revision or fingerprint. A later rename is visible on old run pages because the ID still names the same suite. Run creation resolves the suite and creates every simulation with the exact test and persona versions it will execute in one transaction. Those simulation records are the execution plan and the evidence; the run row carries no second list of pinned test versions. This is not a version or snapshot of the suite.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:8:Egma Cloud and self-hosted Egma use the same CLI. A developer can use both from one machine. Agent, connection, test, and run identifiers are valid only on the platform that created them.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:10:The current CLI stores one platform URL and one key. The most recent sign-in can therefore change the target of later commands in every repository. `egma/config.yaml` stores resource identifiers but not the platform that owns them. A command can send local-platform identifiers to Egma Cloud, or cloud identifiers to a local platform, before either side reports that they do not exist.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:20:- An unbound repository uses Egma Cloud by default.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:25:- Repository command resolution is: explicit `--url`, then `EGMA_URL`, then the repository binding, then Egma Cloud for an unbound repository.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:27:- If a bound platform is unavailable or reports a different instance identifier, the command stops. It never falls back to Egma Cloud.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:35:- Bare onboarding stays simple for cloud users: a new repository targets Egma Cloud.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:37:- Cloud and several self-hosted credentials can coexist on one machine.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:42:- Tests must cover cloud default, first self-host binding, multi-platform credentials, unavailable bound platforms, instance mismatch, and no silent fallback.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:47:- **Egma Cloud always wins unless every command has `--url`:** safe default, but poor self-host experience.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:53:## Amendment — 2026-08-10: there is no Egma Cloud yet
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:55:**Superseded 2026-08-15.** Hosted egma answers at `https://app.egma.ai`, so the fourth step is back exactly as the decision above states it: an unbound repository uses the hosted platform. The amendment is kept rather than deleted because it is the record of why the tree carried a refusal in that step's place for five days. Two things it settled outlive it — the refusal it describes is gone, but nothing else in the decision moved, and the hosted platform is named `hosted egma` throughout; `Egma Cloud` names nothing and is not a product. See `.scratch/hosted-egma/spec.md`.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:57:This decision was written as though a hosted Egma existed, and it does not. `app.egma.ai` hosts a different product. Every sentence below that treats "Egma Cloud" as a running platform describes an intended future, not a system a developer can reach today.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-agent-repositories-bind-to-one-platform.md:61:**What changed in the code:** the fourth step of that order was "then Egma Cloud for an unbound repository". There is nothing to fall back *to*, so an unbound repository that names no platform is now **refused before any address is asked anything** — with a sentence naming the one move that is the developer's, which is to name their own. A built-in default pointing at a host egma does not run would send a developer to inspect somebody else's website and report it as a broken egma.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:1:# ADR-0010: Persona versions own model execution
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:7:Production assembled one simulation from unrelated live settings. Postgres held STT provider `openai` from an older deployment and later inserted model `gpt-live-transcribe` into an empty row. Readiness checked that values existed, not that they formed a valid selection. The simulator therefore sent a realtime-only model to the completed-audio endpoint and failed before turn one.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:9:The same design also gave technical voice two owners: persona traits and platform speech settings. A run pinned the persona version but claim assembly read model and speech settings again later. An old result therefore did not have one immutable meaning.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:13:One persona version owns one complete execution selection:
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:25:Provider credentials are operational data and never belong to a persona,
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:26:grader, run, or platform-setting row. For Egma Cloud, the credential owner is
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:35:The first release has no gateway, no Cloud BYOK mode, no organization model-access switch, and no fallback. A selected provider without a current credential fails before execution with one direct error.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:37:The run pins the persona and grader version IDs. It does not own credentials or network routes.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:41:- Provider, model, voice, and speed cannot drift within a pinned persona version.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:42:- On Egma Cloud, credential rotation affects the next simulation claim and the
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-persona-versions-own-model-execution.md:43:  next model-judged grading job without minting a persona version or restarting

egma-planning/docs/adr/0014-object-storage-is-the-trace-ingestion-boundary.md:12:Customer input that cannot be authenticated, decoded, validated, or normalized is refused before the local log and object store, and Egma does not return success. An accepted segment can become unprocessable only because Egma later encounters an internal defect such as corrupt bytes, an unsupported envelope version, a bad deployment order, or a ClickHouse schema mismatch. That exceptional path must retain the segment for repair without treating invalid customer input as queued work.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0014-object-storage-is-the-trace-ingestion-boundary.md:38:Egma keeps one deployable image with three runtime roles: `all` runs acceptance, upload, and draining; `ingest` runs acceptance and upload; `drain` moves durable segments into ClickHouse. Current hosted and self-hosted deployments run `all` and add no container. The role boundary exists now so hosted Egma can scale ingestion and draining separately later without changing the public route, segment format, or durability contract.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0014-object-storage-is-the-trace-ingestion-boundary.md:40:The first release runs exactly one active drainer per deployment. It adds no Postgres segment-claim rows, SQS, BullMQ, or other work queue. Object keys are passed directly to that drainer and recovered by the pending-prefix scan. Several active drainers require a later ownership design and are not part of this release.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:3:The simulation runtime — the service that plays the persona and conducts simulations — is built on Pipecat and is therefore Python, inside an otherwise all-TypeScript monorepo. Ticket 10 already said "most likely Pipecat"; this record firms it up and adds the reasoning that survived a fresh comparison (2026-08-05).
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:5:egma's runtime is a *caller into other people's infrastructure*: it must join a Retell session, speak a telephony provider's media protocol, or attach to whatever transport a future connection type demands. Pipecat is a transport-agnostic pipeline whose exposed frame/processor model makes testing instrumentation — per-turn latency stamps, dual-channel recording, scripted interruptions, injected noise, the measured audio band ticket 10 made irreversible — ordinary middleware rather than a fork. The alternatives: LiveKit Agents assumes it owns the media (agents live in LiveKit rooms, adding a LiveKit server + SIP service to every self-hosted deployment) — the right shape for *hosting* agents, not *visiting* them — and its Node SDK, the one TypeScript path anywhere, officially trails its Python SDK. Pipecat has no server-side TypeScript at all, so choosing it is choosing Python.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:7:The language cost is contained by a boundary that exists for its own reasons: the runtime receives fully-resolved simulation specs and reports over a language-neutral HTTP contract, never touches Postgres, never imports monorepo code. The contract is the language firewall.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:26:- Grading capacity scales independently of both conversation capacity and API capacity, by running more copies against the same claim mechanics — burst absorption is the deployment's dial, not a queue's prayer.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:9:`architecture.md` locks BetterAuth for authentication, and one codebase must serve both self-hosters and an egma-run cloud service. A standing constraint from [The auth and tenancy model](../../.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/06-auth-and-tenancy-model.md) adds a third requirement: auth must sit behind an interface narrow enough that WorkOS could replace BetterAuth for the cloud service later without touching the rest of the codebase.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:17:**No hosted vendor can own tenancy for an open-source product.** Auth0 and Clerk both ship "Organizations" and both are cloud-only. A self-hoster could not run egma if its org model lived there. The same reasoning already ruled out WorkOS FGA, which is hosted-only.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:120:**The second half is worse than the refusal, and only shows up once the door is open.** With single-organization mode off — the cloud service — `admitIdentity` lets everyone through, and then `onIdentityCreated` provisions a person with no intent by calling `provision()`, which **creates a brand-new organization for them**. Every employee arriving through their employer's IdP would land in an organization of their own rather than in their employer's. `onSsoLogin` is the hook that exists to prevent exactly this, and it has no implementation and is not even registered: `IdentityOptions.hooks` in `apps/api/src/auth/better-auth.ts` is typed `Pick<IdentityHooks, "admitIdentity" | "onIdentityCreated">`, and `apps/api/src/server.ts` passes those two.

item.stdout:
# egma-cloud

How hosted egma is deployed. Private, and allowed to be specific: unlike the
public repository, files here may name our account, our bucket, our addresses.

**The rule this repository exists to enforce: nothing about the deployment is
ever authored on a machine.** The box runs egma's own compose files at the
deployed commit, plus the overlay in `deployment/`, and holds nothing that
this repository and the public one cannot rebuild.

## What lives here

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `deployment/local.yml` | The whole difference between our cloud and stock egma: the tunnel, the collector, the Supabase root, four image pins, no published port |
| `deployment/otel-collector.yaml` | What leaves the box and where it goes: spans and logs to PostHog, vitals to CloudWatch. The token is a secret; this file only names it |
| `deployment/setup-cloudwatch.sh` | One-time AWS wiring for the container runtime and telemetry: the metadata hop limit needed by AWS-backed workloads, the box role's log permissions, the alarms, and who they email. Run from an operator's machine, never the box |
| `deployment/setup-cloudtrail.sh` | One-time AWS account audit setup: one multi-Region management-event trail and its dedicated S3 bucket. It is always separate from app telemetry and runs from an operator's machine |
| `deployment/setup-ingestion-bucket.sh` | One-time AWS wiring for the pending-evidence spool: the ingestion bucket, the IAM user confined to its `pending/` prefix, and the secret that credential is fetched from. Run from an operator's machine, never the box |
| `deployment/settings.map` | One line per setting egma asks for, saying where the answer comes from. Never a secret value |
| `deployment/check-settings.sh` | Proves the map answers everything egma's compose files ask, both directions. No AWS, no secrets |
| `deployment/assemble-env.sh` | Turns the map into `/opt/egma/.env`, fetching values from Secrets Manager. Refuses if the check fails |
| `deployment/deploy.sh` | The sequence the box runs: fetch code at the ref, fetch the CA, check, assemble, pull, up |
| `runbook.md` | What AWS cannot tell you: the failures that name the wrong cause, the things not to change |
| `where-the-settings-live.md` | Which of the five holders (AWS, Vercel, Cloudflare, GitHub, Secrets Manager) keeps what |

## How a deploy happens

```
merge to main on the public repo, touching platform paths
  → the full test suite, on main's own tree
  → the three images → ECR
  → one SSM command to the box:
      aws s3 sync  s3://egma-deploy-599151709955/deployment → /opt/egma/deployment
      bash /opt/egma/deployment/deploy.sh <sha>
  → the workflow reads the identity contract back
  → the workflow tells Vercel to ship the web application
```

The tag is retired. `platform-v*` was the deploy button while a deploy could
drop a mid-call **simulation**; the simulator drains now — first stop signal
ends claiming, in-flight simulations finish, ten minutes at most — so every
green merge deploys, and the web ships only after the API it calls.
`workflow_dispatch` on the public repository is the by-hand override.

Merging to main **here** still does not deploy. It publishes: the `publish`
workflow syncs `deployment/` to S3, and the next deploy — the next platform
merge — picks it up. Config changes ride deploys; they do not cause them.

## The guard

`drift-check` runs nightly and on every push: it clones the public repository
at main and runs `check-settings.sh` against it. The day egma gains, loses or
renames a setting, this repository goes red — before any tag exists, instead
of in production. That check is the direct product of 2026-08-15, when a
rename landed with every test green and took the persona's settings down
silently, because the deployment was maintained by hand where no test could
see it.

## What is deliberately not here

- **Secret values.** Every one lives in AWS Secrets Manager under `egma/*`.
  This repository holds only the names.
- **egma itself.** The box clones the public repository at deploy time, so the
  compose files and the images always come from one commit.
- **The Supabase root certificate.** A published file; `deploy.sh` fetches it
  from the address recorded in the `egma/db/supabase` secret.
# Where hosted egma's settings live

Five companies hold one deployment's answers. Nothing ties them together, which
is the only reason this page exists.

No secret value is here. This says which system owns each value. The private
deployment map also records non-secret facts that must be reviewed with code.

| Holder | What it holds | Why it cannot live anywhere else |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **AWS Secrets Manager** | Passwords, keys and tokens only, under `egma/*` | Deployment assembly reads service secrets. The API reads `egma/providers` for simulation claims; the grader reads it only for model-judged work. Non-secret choices do not belong here |
| **AWS** | The box, the recordings and ingestion buckets, the image repositories, the two deploy roles | The deployment runs here |
| **Vercel** | `EGMA_API_ORIGIN`, and the project that serves `app.egma.ai` | **A build argument, not a runtime setting.** Next resolves rewrites into the build, so no compose file and no secret store can ever hold it |
| **Cloudflare** | DNS for both addresses, and the tunnel's route to the API | The tunnel is a Cloudflare object. It survives the box being replaced |
| **GitHub** | Three repository variables the deploy workflow reads, and one secret: the Vercel deploy hook URL | Actions cannot read a value it has not been given, and OIDC replaces a stored key. The hook is a secret because anyone holding it can trigger a production web deploy |
| **PostHog** | The project that receives egma's own telemetry: the web application's analytics and errors, the containers' logs and spans | The sixth holder, and a read-side one: nothing of ours is configured there beyond the project itself. Its project token lives in Secrets Manager (`egma/posthog`) for the box, and in Vercel for the pages |

## The two addresses, and why they differ

**`app.egma.ai` is the platform's address.** `EGMA_BASE_URL` is exactly this. The
Next application rewrites `/api/*` and `/v1/traces/*` through to the API, so
pages and API answer on one origin — which is what makes the session cookie valid
for both, and what the CLI's origin check depends on.

**`api.egma.ai` is a service door, not an address.** Its identity contract
correctly names `app.egma.ai`, so a CLI pointed at it refuses. That is the design
working.

In Cloudflare, `app.egma.ai` must stay **DNS-only (grey cloud)**. Vercel issues
its own certificate, and orange-clouding it would let Bot Fight Mode challenge
the CLI — which is a script, not a browser, and would get an HTML challenge page
where it expects JSON.

## Settings that are easy to get wrong

**Three small secret objects hold this path.** Their current JSON shapes are
exact. A note or a non-secret setting in one of them is a second owner and must
be removed.

| Secret | Exact fields |
| --- | --- |
| `egma/providers` | `openai_api_key`, `deepgram_api_key`, `cartesia_api_key` |
| `egma/mail` | `smtp_url` |
| `egma/phone` | `sip_password` |

Persona and grader versions hold provider and model choices in Postgres. The
cloud API reads the current `egma/providers` value for each simulation claim.
The grader reads it only when a claimed job includes a model-judged grader.
They do not copy those keys into Postgres or into the assembled `.env`.
Rotating a provider key therefore changes the next model-using work without a
deploy or container restart.

The carrier trunk address, source number, and SIP username are non-secret
deployment facts. They live as reviewed literals in `deployment/settings.map`.
API startup combines those three facts with the password and writes one sealed
carrier route to the Postgres platform store. The password has no second copy
in this repository.

**The pages' telemetry settings are Vercel's to hold, like `EGMA_API_ORIGIN`.**
Three build arguments — Next resolves them into the built pages — set in the
Vercel project's environment variables and nowhere else: `EGMA_TELEMETRY=on`
(the same one flag everything else reads; next.config maps it into the
bundle, so a key left set cannot turn reporting on by itself),
`NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY`, and `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST`. The key is the
same PostHog project token the box holds in `egma/posthog`; it is write-only
by design, which is what makes shipping it inside a public page sane at all.
Without the flag and the key both, the pages initialize nothing and send
nothing — which is every build that is not ours.

**Mail sends from `updates.egma.ai`, not `egma.ai`.** That is the domain verified
in Resend. A from address on the apex would be rejected. If mail should come from
`egma.ai`, verify the apex domain first.

**The deploy workflow needs three GitHub repository variables** — the deploy
role's ARN, the ECR registry, and the platform instance id — under Settings →
Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables on the public repository. Without
them the workflow fails at its first step and names which one is missing.
**And one repository secret:** `VERCEL_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL`, the Deploy Hook
minted in the Vercel project (Settings → Git → Deploy Hooks, branch `main`,
created 2026-08-17). The pipeline posts it after the platform proves healthy;
without it the web job fails and says so, because `apps/web/vercel.json`
stops Vercel shipping main on its own.

## The two halves of the deployment machinery

| File | Where | Why that side |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `docker-compose.yml`, `docker-compose.managed.yml`, `.env.example` | **public** repo | They describe what egma is. Any deployment uses them unchanged |
| `deployment/deploy.sh`, `deployment/settings.map` | **here** | This deployment's AWS, registry, SSM and Secrets Manager wiring |

`deploy.sh` was published for about an hour and then withdrawn. The commit that
added it called it generic; it is not. A self-hoster on an ordinary virtual
server would write something quite different, and **a published interface is a
promise to keep it working** — made, in that case, to nobody, since egma has no
self-hosters yet. What a self-hoster genuinely needs is the compose files and
`.env.example`, and those were always public.

The published deployment files live on the box under `/opt/egma/deployment/`.
The assembled Compose and environment files live under `/opt/egma/`. These
copies exist so that losing the box loses nothing — which was the whole reason
for writing any of this down.

**It carries no secret value.** It does carry reviewed non-secret deployment
facts, including the carrier address, source number, and SIP username. A
`secret` line writes only the secret object's name and field name. Most secret
values are fetched when a deployment runs. Model-provider keys are fetched by
the API and grader only when work starts.

## What is deliberately *not* here

**The compose files and the deploy workflow are in the public repository.** They
describe what egma is rather than what this deployment answered, and keeping
them public puts them under the same `deployment.test.ts` guard that once caught
a feature that was silently off — written, documented, tested, and still not
working, because a compose entry never passed three variables through.

Two settings were unlocked to make that possible. `DATABASE_URL` and
`CLICKHOUSE_URL` were the only values in `docker-compose.yml` that named a
compose service and could not be overridden, which is exactly why the object
store and the media bridge moved to managed services for one variable each and
the two databases could not move at all. `docker-compose.managed.yml` is the
other half: it profiles the containers a managed deployment does not run.

**The deploy script is the exception, and it is here rather than there.** It
assumes AWS, a container registry and a machine reachable over SSM — one worked
example, not a facility.

See `.scratch/hosted-egma/research/where-the-deployment-lives.md` for the
evidence behind both calls.
# Runbook — hosted egma

What AWS cannot tell you.

This page deliberately holds **no inventory**. Which account, which instance,
which secrets exist — the console answers all of that, and a written copy only
goes stale. What is here is the knowledge that exists nowhere else: why things
are the way they are, what breaks if you change them, and which failures name
something other than their cause.

No secret value is on this page and none ever should be. Every password, key and
token is in AWS Secrets Manager, `us-east-1`, under names beginning `egma/`.

## Reaching the box

There is **no SSH port**. The box publishes nothing at all — not 22, not 80, not
443. Administration goes through SSM, which the box dials outward; traffic goes
through a Cloudflare tunnel, which it also dials outward.

```sh
aws ssm start-session --target <instance-id> --region us-east-1
```

If SSM does not answer, the box is down or has lost its outbound route. Check
that before assuming anything else.

## Deploying

Merge to main on the public repository. A merge that touches platform paths
runs the full suite on main's own tree, builds the three images, replaces
what the box runs, reads the identity contract back to prove it answered, and
then — only then — tells Vercel to ship the web application. A web-only merge
ships the web at once; a docs-only merge deploys nothing. By hand, when a
merge is not the shape of the change: `workflow_dispatch` on the public
repository, or `/opt/egma/deployment/deploy.sh <sha>` on the box. An older SHA
is usable only when its schema contract is still compatible. The model-
execution cutover described below is forward-only after migration 0037 starts.

`deploy.sh` reassembles deployment settings every time, so those changes reach
the containers on the next deploy with no rebuild. The Postgres platform store
contains only the phone-carrier route. This deployment explicitly sets
`EGMA_CARRIER_SETTINGS_SOURCE=environment`. API startup therefore reconciles
the complete four-value carrier bundle from the deployment environment into
the platform store. Tenancy does not select this behavior.

Model and voice choices are versioned persona or grader content, not deployment
settings. `egma/providers` holds exactly `openai_api_key`,
`deepgram_api_key`, and `cartesia_api_key`. The API reads that object for each
simulation claim. The grader reads it only when a claimed job includes a
model-judged grader. A provider-key rotation affects the next model-using work
and does not require a deploy or restart. Mail has its own `egma/mail` object
with only `smtp_url`. The phone object, `egma/phone`, holds only `sip_password`.

When a public-code change first depends on a deployment setting, publish the
deployment setting first. Normally, merge the egma-cloud change and wait for
**Publish deployment config** before merging the public Egma change. The public
merge deploys immediately and reads the published files from S3. During the
first model-execution cutover, the cloud Drift check is expected to be red only
for the short interval before public `main` lands. Its exact order is below.

### First cutover to the clean secret shapes

Do this once, in this order. Each early step is additive, so the running
deployment keeps working until the new code is ready.

1. Get an Egma-owned Deepgram key. Do not reuse a key from another project.
2. Create `egma/mail` with the current `smtp_url` from `egma/providers`.
3. Add `deepgram_api_key` to `egma/providers`. Keep every old field for now.
4. Merge this cloud branch and wait for **Publish deployment config** to pass.
   This changes the files in S3 but does not restart the running deployment.
   The separate cloud **Drift check** is expected to report the new and removed
   settings while it still compares with the old public `main`; do not treat
   that one transitional result as a publish failure.
5. Merge the public model-execution change. Its normal main workflow builds the
   images, reads the published deployment files, and replaces the containers.
6. Run one real production phone simulation. It must complete at least one turn
   and receive grades. A healthy API or a readiness response is not proof.
7. Rerun the cloud **Drift check** against the new public `main` and require it
   to pass. The repositories now agree on the full settings contract.
8. Replace the current `egma/providers` value with exactly its three model keys.
   Replace `egma/phone` with exactly `sip_password`. Update both descriptions.
9. Run another work item that uses the current provider bundle. This proves the
   next claim read the cleaned `AWSCURRENT` value without a restart.

If step 5 fails, leave the running containers alone, fix the public or private
change, and deploy a corrected new SHA. Do not deploy an image older than
migration 0037 after that migration has started. Do not clean the old fields in
step 8 until step 6 has passed. The old fields are a bridge for the still-
running old deployment, not a permanent compatibility path.

### One trigger now, ordered — and why the order exists

Until 2026-08-17 the halves deployed on different triggers: merging shipped
the **web application** only, while the API, the grader and the simulator
waited for a `platform-v*` tag. The tag protected simulations — a deploy
could replace a simulator mid-call — and the memory rule holding the halves
together failed within a day of hosted egma existing. On 2026-08-15 password
reset merged, worked in every test, and went live as a page with no route:

```
app.egma.ai/forgot-password        200   the new page, live
POST app.egma.ai/api/password-reset 404   Route POST:/api/password-reset not found
```

Both halves were correct. Only one had been deployed.

Two changes retired the tag rather than the lesson. The simulator now drains
— the first stop signal ends claiming, in-flight **simulations** finish and
report, ten minutes at the most, and Docker's kill at the ceiling is the
backstop — so a deploy at any hour drops nobody's call. And the web deploys
through the pipeline (a Vercel deploy hook fired after the smoke check;
`apps/web/vercel.json` stops Vercel shipping main on its own), so a page can
no longer go live before the route it calls. A deploy landing mid-simulation
can legitimately hold for the drain: a quiet extra ten minutes on the SSM
step is the drain working, not a hang.

### Two facts about ordering

**The API goes first, and only one of the two stores is a hard gate.** The
Postgres migrations apply in the API's own process before it serves anything: a
file that fails stops the boot, so there is no migration step and there is no
missing one. The trace store's migrations do not work that way any more. They
run beside the server, started once it is listening, and a failure is logged
and retried by the next start rather than thrown — while they are running, the
draining process reports `drain` as `migrating`, and ClickHouse reachability is
reported as its own component that never decides the status code. **That is why
`/health` no longer answers 503 for ClickHouse.** An API whose trace store is
slow or down still accepts evidence into the ingestion bucket and drains it
later, where the old arrangement took the whole address down with the trace
store. The grader still reads a schema somebody else applied, so starting it
against an unmigrated schema is the one ordering mistake this deployment can
make. Compose enforces it through `depends_on: api: service_healthy`.

**A rollback does not undo a migration.** Redeploying an older image leaves the
newer schema in place. Most migrations are additive, and ClickHouse migrations
must be. Migration 0037 is a deliberate pre-launch cutover: it removes old
model-setting paths and does not support an older API afterward. Once it starts,
repair forward with a corrected new image. Never assume an image rollback
restores a schema.

## Restarting

Restarting the **api** container also restarts the **tunnel**, because the tunnel
shares the API's network namespace. So an API restart is a brief outage of the
whole address, not just of the API. That is deliberate — see below.

## Accepted evidence, and the one process that drains it

The API answers a customer as soon as their conversation is durable in the
ingestion bucket. Turning those objects into ClickHouse rows happens
afterwards, in a drainer. Everything in this section follows from that gap:
what has been accepted is a promise already made, and what has been retained is
a promise not yet kept.

**Exactly one process drains.** The drainer takes a session-scoped Postgres
advisory lock — namespace `0x65676d61`, id `2` — on a connection of its own. A
second `all` or `drain` instance starts its drainer, does not get the lock,
stands by harmlessly, and takes over by itself when the holder stops or dies,
because Postgres drops the lock with the connection. There is no hand-over to
perform and no lock to clear.

`/health` reports `drain` as one of `draining`, `standby`, `migrating` or
`not_running`. One `draining` and any number of `standby` is the intended
shape. Two instances both reporting `draining` is a bug worth paging about.

### A pending object that did not become rows

`/health` also reports `retainedDefects`, a map of reason class to count. A
non-zero count means egma accepted a segment it then could not turn into rows,
and has kept the object rather than deleting it. **Nothing deletes a retained
object automatically, ever.**

The reason classes are the eleven `apps/api/src/ingestion/defects.ts` names:
eight ways an object cannot be read at all, and three ways it reads perfectly
and still cannot become rows. Two of those three are disagreements rather than
damage — `identity_conflict`, where the store already holds one of those spans
with different content and the stored evidence stays authoritative, and
`impossible_tenant_binding`, where the sealed header names a project that is
not its organization's.

To deal with one:

1. The structured event `ingestion.segment.retained` names the object key.
2. Read that key out of the ingestion bucket's `pending/` prefix with the
   `egma/s3/ingest` credential. It is gzip NDJSON with a header line.
3. Repair it, then **restart the API**. A retained object is reported once and
   then skipped for the life of the process, so a repaired object is only
   looked at again after a restart.

**Never delete a retained object to clear the count.** The count is the only
record that evidence a customer was told was safe has not become visible.

## Restoring

**There is no *data* on the box to restore.** Every store is outside it: the
database is Supabase, the traces are ClickHouse Cloud, the recordings are S3, the
secrets are Secrets Manager. A dead box loses no **run**, no **simulation** and
no **verdict**.

**One exception, and it is the reason `-v` matters.** `docker compose down -v`
destroys the named volumes. `api-ingestion` is the API's write-ahead log:
evidence staged on its way to the ingestion bucket, plus the identity of any
sealed segment whose upload was not confirmed. The bucket is where a customer's
conversation was promised to be safe, so this is not that promise being
broken — it is what a restarted API would have come back to and recovered.
Destroying it loses the staged records outright and lets a repeated upload
invent a second object rather than reach for the first.
(`otel-collector-storage` goes the same way, at the cost of queued telemetry.)
`deploy.sh`'s `docker image prune -af` never touches a named volume; `down -v`
does. Use `down` without `-v`.

Pending objects are a separate question with a reassuring answer: they are in
the ingestion bucket, not on the box, and no compose command reaches them.

**The deployment is a different question, and this page used to get it wrong.**
It said there was nothing on the box at all. Until 2026-08-15 two things lived
only on the machine, and rebuilding from what was written down produced an API
that could not reach Postgres:

- `/opt/egma/docker-compose.yml` — bespoke, in neither repository. It is now
  assembled from the public Compose files by `deployment/deploy.sh`.
- `/opt/egma/certs/supabase-ca.crt` — the Supabase root. Still not in any
  repository, deliberately: it is a published file, and the address to fetch it
  from is in the `egma/db/supabase` secret under `ca_url`.

Without both, the API dies at boot with `SELF_SIGNED_CERT_IN_CHAIN` — the
failure this page already had a section about, reached by a route it did not
mention.

To replace a box: launch an Amazon Linux 2023 instance with the `egma-box`
instance profile, install Docker and the Compose plugin, put the deployment
files in `/opt/egma/`, run `setup-cloudwatch.sh` from an operator machine so
IMDSv2 has a hop limit of 2, **fetch the CA into `/opt/egma/certs/`**, run
`deploy.sh`, and point the Cloudflare tunnel at it. The hop limit is required by
the API and grader when they read provider credentials from AWS. The tunnel is
a Cloudflare object, so it survives the box.

The fetch, which is the step that was missing:

```sh
mkdir -p /opt/egma/certs && curl -fsSL \
  https://supabase-downloads.s3-ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/prod/ssl/prod-ca-2021.crt \
  -o /opt/egma/certs/supabase-ca.crt
```

**Known gap: the recordings bucket has no versioning.** A deleted or overwritten
recording is gone. Accepted while there are few customers; the first thing to
change when there are more.

## AWS account audit

PostHog and OpenTelemetry show what the application did. CloudWatch shows
whether the deployment is healthy. CloudTrail answers a different question:
who changed AWS, what API call they made, and when they made it.

The account uses one multi-Region trail named `egma-account-audit`. It records
all read and write management events, including global service events, in a
dedicated versioned S3 bucket. Log-file validation is on. Data events are not
included because they are high-volume resource activity, not the account-level
change history this trail exists to keep. There is no automatic expiry. Set a
lifecycle only after Egma has a written audit-retention rule.

This is not controlled by `EGMA_TELEMETRY`. It stays on when platform telemetry
is off, and no EC2 role, future ECS task role, deploy role, or collector needs
access to it. A move from EC2 to ECS or Fargate does not change the trail. The
trail will record ECS management API calls, but it never carries container
logs.

Set it up from an operator's machine with an opaque, globally unique bucket
name. Do not put the AWS account id in that name:

```sh
AWS_REGION=us-east-1 deployment/setup-cloudtrail.sh <opaque-audit-bucket-name>
```

The script refuses to create a second trail when another one already exists.
It also refuses to replace the policy of a bucket that it did not create. A
repeat run can omit the bucket name because the existing trail records it.

The bucket uses S3-managed encryption and versioning. It does not yet use a
customer-managed KMS key. Add that key and its policy when Egma adopts a formal
Security Hub or compliance baseline; a bad key policy can stop log delivery.

After setup, wait for delivery and inspect `LatestDeliveryError`. The first
digest normally follows later than the first log file. Validate it from a time
before setup:

```sh
trail_arn=$(aws cloudtrail get-trail --region us-east-1 \
  --name egma-account-audit --query Trail.TrailARN --output text)
aws cloudtrail validate-logs --region us-east-1 --trail-arn "$trail_arn" \
  --start-time '<ISO-8601 time before setup>'
```

## Watching it

When `EGMA_TELEMETRY=on`, three streams leave the box through the
`otel-collector` container. With any other value, `deploy.sh` removes the
collector and these three streams stop. None of them is the trace store —
customers' traces are ClickHouse's and never touch this pipe.

- **Logs and spans → PostHog.** The api, grader, simulator, and tunnel logs,
  plus the api's and grader's own request spans, in one PostHog project. A
  deliberate log event from the api carries the trace id of the request it
  happened inside, so the two find each other. Plain third-party text is kept
  as a fixed safe body rather than copied into PostHog. The web application
  reports there too, from the browser.
- **Vitals → CloudWatch, namespace `EgmaBox`.** CPU, memory, disk and
  restarts, an allowlist and deliberately nothing more — CloudWatch charges
  per series. The alarms live on these and on EC2's own metrics, and they
  email through the `egma-alarms` SNS topic.

What can break, and what it looks like:

- **The collector dying costs observations, never conversations.** The api
  and grader fire and forget; nothing waits on telemetry. A dead collector is
  a quiet PostHog and a stale `EgmaBox` namespace, not an outage.
- **`falling back to IMDSv1` or AWS credential errors in a container** read as
  an IAM problem. They can be the metadata hop limit: a process in a container
  sits one network hop deeper than the host, and the default limit of 1 refuses
  it. `setup-cloudwatch.sh` sets it to 2 on the instance. The collector, API,
  and grader all need that on a replacement box.
- **401s from PostHog in the collector's log** mean the `egma/posthog` secret
  holds a token PostHog did not accept. The collector keeps a bounded queue on
  disk and retries; correct the secret and deploy before that queue fills. An
  empty key is earlier and louder: the API and grader refuse to start.

## Five failures that name the wrong thing

Each of these cost an evening the first time. That is why this page exists.

### The deploy says `Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`

It reads as a permissions problem on the role. It is not. The role is fine and
the token is valid. **The subject in the token does not match the pattern in the
trust policy**, and AWS reports a mismatch and a genuine refusal with the same
sentence.

`egma-ai` has GitHub's **ID-qualified subject** turned on, so the claim carries
numeric organization and repository ids:

```
repo:egma-ai@304379583/egma@1319495166:ref:refs/heads/main
```

not the plain `repo:egma-ai/egma:ref:refs/heads/main` that most documentation
shows. The trust policy was written for the plain form and matched nothing.

**Do not guess at the subject — ask AWS what it saw.** CloudTrail records the
failed call with the exact claim:

```sh
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity \
  --region us-east-1 --max-results 3
```

The `Username` field on the event is the subject. Match the trust policy to it.

How hosted egma is deployed. Private, and allowed to be specific: unlike the
public repository, files here may name our account, our bucket, our addresses.

**The rule this repository exists to enforce: nothing about the deployment is
ever authored on a machine.** The box runs egma's own compose files at the
deployed commit, plus the overlay in `deployment/`, and holds nothing that
this repository and the public one cannot rebuild.

## What lives here

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `deployment/local.yml` | The whole difference between our cloud and stock egma: the tunnel, the collector, the Supabase root, four image pins, no published port |
| `deployment/otel-collector.yaml` | What leaves the box and where it goes: spans and logs to PostHog, vitals to CloudWatch. The token is a secret; this file only names it |
| `deployment/setup-cloudwatch.sh` | One-time AWS wiring for the container runtime and telemetry: the metadata hop limit needed by AWS-backed workloads, the box role's log permissions, the alarms, and who they email. Run from an operator's machine, never the box |

| `deployment/setup-ingestion-bucket.sh` | One-time AWS wiring for the pending-evidence spool: the ingestion bucket, the IAM user confined to its `pending/` prefix, and the secret that credential is fetched from. Run from an operator's machine, never the box |

| `deployment/check-settings.sh` | Proves the map answers everything egma's compose files ask, both directions. No AWS, no secrets |

| `runbook.md` | What AWS cannot tell you: the failures that name the wrong cause, the things not to change |
| `where-the-settings-live.md` | Which of the five holders (AWS, Vercel, Cloudflare, GitHub, Secrets Manager) keeps what |

## How a deploy happens

```

  → the full test suite, on main's own tree
  → the three images → ECR

# Where hosted egma's settings live

Five companies hold one deployment's answers. Nothing ties them together, which
is the only reason this page exists.

No secret value is here. This says which system owns each value. The private
deployment map also records non-secret facts that must be reviewed with code.

| Holder | What it holds | Why it cannot live anywhere else |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **AWS Secrets Manager** | Passwords, keys and tokens only, under `egma/*` | Deployment assembly reads service secrets. The API reads `egma/providers` for simulation claims; the grader reads it only for model-judged work. Non-secret choices do not belong here |
| **AWS** | The box, the recordings and ingestion buckets, the image repositories, the two deploy roles | The deployment runs here |
| **Vercel** | `EGMA_API_ORIGIN`, and the project that serves `app.egma.ai` | **A build argument, not a runtime setting.** Next resolves rewrites into the build, so no compose file and no secret store can ever hold it |
| **Cloudflare** | DNS for both addresses, and the tunnel's route to the API | The tunnel is a Cloudflare object. It survives the box being replaced |
| **GitHub** | Three repository variables the deploy workflow reads, and one secret: the Vercel deploy hook URL | Actions cannot read a value it has not been given, and OIDC replaces a stored key. The hook is a secret because anyone holding it can trigger a production web deploy |
| **PostHog** | The project that receives egma's own telemetry: the web application's analytics and errors, the containers' logs and spans | The sixth holder, and a read-side one: nothing of ours is configured there beyond the project itself. Its project token lives in Secrets Manager (`egma/posthog`) for the box, and in Vercel for the pages |

## The two addresses, and why they differ

**`app.egma.ai` is the platform's address.** `EGMA_BASE_URL` is exactly this. The
Next application rewrites `/api/*` and `/v1/traces/*` through to the API, so
pages and API answer on one origin — which is what makes the session cookie valid
for both, and what the CLI's origin check depends on.

**`api.egma.ai` is a service door, not an address.** Its identity contract
correctly names `app.egma.ai`, so a CLI pointed at it refuses. That is the design
working.

In Cloudflare, `app.egma.ai` must stay **DNS-only (grey cloud)**. Vercel issues
its own certificate, and orange-clouding it would let Bot Fight Mode challenge
the CLI — which is a script, not a browser, and would get an HTML challenge page
where it expects JSON.

## Settings that are easy to get wrong

**Three small secret objects hold this path.** Their current JSON shapes are
exact. A note or a non-secret setting in one of them is a second owner and must
be removed.

| Secret | Exact fields |
| --- | --- |
| `egma/providers` | `openai_api_key`, `deepgram_api_key`, `cartesia_api_key` |
| `egma/mail` | `smtp_url` |
| `egma/phone` | `sip_password` |

Persona and grader versions hold provider and model choices in Postgres. The
cloud API reads the current `egma/providers` value for each simulation claim.
The grader reads it only when a claimed job includes a model-judged grader.
They do not copy those keys into Postgres or into the assembled `.env`.
Rotating a provider key therefore changes the next model-using work without a
deploy or container restart.

The carrier trunk address, source number, and SIP username are non-secret
deployment facts. They live as reviewed literals in `deployment/settings.map`.
API startup combines those three facts with the password and writes one sealed
carrier route to the Postgres platform store. The password has no second copy
in this repository.

**The pages' telemetry settings are Vercel's to hold, like `EGMA_API_ORIGIN`.**
Three build arguments — Next resolves them into the built pages — set in the
Vercel project's environment variables and nowhere else: `EGMA_TELEMETRY=on`
(the same one flag everything else reads; next.config maps it into the
bundle, so a key left set cannot turn reporting on by itself),
`NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY`, and `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST`. The key is the
same PostHog project token the box holds in `egma/posthog`; it is write-only
by design, which is what makes shipping it inside a public page sane at all.
Without the flag and the key both, the pages initialize nothing and send
nothing — which is every build that is not ours.

**Mail sends from `updates.egma.ai`, not `egma.ai`.** That is the domain verified
in Resend. A from address on the apex would be rejected. If mail should come from
`egma.ai`, verify the apex domain first.

**The deploy workflow needs three GitHub repository variables** — the deploy
role's ARN, the ECR registry, and the platform instance id — under Settings →
Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables on the public repository. Without
them the workflow fails at its first step and names which one is missing.
**And one repository secret:** `VERCEL_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL`, the Deploy Hook
minted in the Vercel project (Settings → Git → Deploy Hooks, branch `main`,
created 2026-08-17). The pipeline posts it after the platform proves healthy;
without it the web job fails and says so, because `apps/web/vercel.json`
stops Vercel shipping main on its own.

| File | Where | Why that side |

| `deployment/deploy.sh`, `deployment/settings.map` | **here** | This deployment's AWS, registry, SSM and Secrets Manager wiring |
