#!/bin/bash
# Turn settings.map into the .env the platform runs on.
#
#   ./assemble-env.sh [output-path] [path-to-egma-checkout]
#
# Replaces the hand-written fetch-env.sh that used to live on the box. That file
# was maintained separately from the code, drifted behind a rename, and took the
# platform's persona down with it. Nothing here is maintained separately: the
# list of settings comes from egma's own compose files and the answers come from
# settings.map, which check-settings.sh proves covers them.
#
# **It refuses to write anything if the check fails.** A half-answered .env is
# the failure this whole arrangement exists to prevent, so a gap stops the
# deployment rather than reaching it.
#
# **No secret value is written anywhere but the output file**, which is created
# with mode 600. Nothing is echoed, and a secret is fetched once however many
# settings read from it.
set -euo pipefail

HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
OUT="${1:-/opt/egma/.env}"
CODE="${2:-$(cd "$HERE/../../.." && pwd)}"
REGION="${AWS_REGION:-us-east-1}"

bash "$HERE/check-settings.sh" "$CODE" || {
  echo >&2
  echo "Refusing to assemble a .env that does not answer every setting." >&2
  exit 1
}

umask 077
tmp="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT

declare -A cache

fetch() {
  local id="$1"
  [ -n "${cache[$id]+set}" ] || cache[$id]="$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value \
    --secret-id "$id" --region "$REGION" --query SecretString --output text)"
  printf '%s' "${cache[$id]}"
}

field() {
  python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.loads(sys.argv[1])[sys.argv[2]])' "$1" "$2"
}

written=0
while read -r name how a b _rest; do
  case "$how" in
    secret)
      value="$(field "$(fetch "$a")" "$b")"
      printf '%s=%s\n' "$name" "$value" >> "$tmp"
      written=$((written + 1))
      ;;
    literal|inert)
      # inert writes exactly like literal — the difference is what it tells a
      # reader of the map: this value feeds a profiled-out container that never
      # starts, and exists only because compose checks `:?` markers for every
      # service at file load, switched-off ones included.
      printf '%s=%s\n' "$name" "$a" >> "$tmp"
      written=$((written + 1))
      ;;
    deploy-time)
      # deploy.sh appends these after this script runs, because they describe
      # the deployment being made rather than the platform being deployed.
      ;;
    compose-default|unset)
      # Deliberately absent, so egma's own default applies. Writing an empty
      # value here would not be the same thing: compose passes an unset
      # optional through as an empty string, and the API treats "" and "never
      # set" alike only because it filters blanks out again on the way in.
      ;;
    *)
      echo "settings.map: $name has an unknown disposition '$how'" >&2
      exit 1
      ;;
  esac
done < <(grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' "$HERE/settings.map")

install -m 600 "$tmp" "$OUT"
echo "assembled $written settings into $OUT"
# THIS DEPLOYMENT'S ANSWERS — one line per setting egma asks for.
#
# `check-settings.sh` beside this file proves the two lists agree, without AWS
# and without reading a secret. If egma gains a setting and this file does not
# answer it, that check fails. That is the whole point of the file.
#
# **No secret value is here, and none ever should be.** A `secret` line names a
# secret and a field inside it. The value is fetched at deployment time.
#
#   <VARIABLE>  secret <secret-id> <field>   fetched from AWS Secrets Manager
#   <VARIABLE>  literal <value>              a fixed value, no secret involved
#   <VARIABLE>  compose-default              egma's own default is right for us
#   <VARIABLE>  unset                        deliberately not set — reason given
#   <VARIABLE>  inert <value>                written, and never read by anything
#
# `compose-default` and `unset` both mean "not written to .env". They differ in
# what they tell a reader: one says egma already chose well, the other says this
# deployment does not use the thing at all.
#
# `inert` exists for one compose behaviour: `${VAR:?}` markers are checked when
# the file is *loaded*, for every service in it — including the seven this
# deployment profiles out. A switched-off service's required credential still
# has to exist to satisfy the load step, so it gets a value that is visibly not
# a credential, feeding a container that is never started. The first deploy
# over this road failed exactly here, before touching anything.

# ── The two stores ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Whole URLs. These are the only two settings in docker-compose.yml that named a
# compose service and could not be overridden until this effort unlocked them.
DATABASE_URL                            secret egma/db/supabase url
CLICKHOUSE_URL                          secret egma/clickhouse url

# The bundled stores' own credentials. This deployment runs neither container,
# and the URLs above are whole, so nothing here is read.
POSTGRES_DB                             unset   no bundled Postgres — Supabase
POSTGRES_USER                           unset   no bundled Postgres — Supabase
POSTGRES_PASSWORD                       unset   no bundled Postgres — Supabase
CLICKHOUSE_DB                           unset   no bundled trace store — ClickHouse Cloud
CLICKHOUSE_USER                         unset   no bundled trace store — ClickHouse Cloud
CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD                     unset   no bundled trace store — ClickHouse Cloud

# ── The platform's own identity ──────────────────────────────────────────────
EGMA_AUTH_SECRET                        secret egma/platform/secrets EGMA_AUTH_SECRET
EGMA_ENCRYPTION_KEY                     secret egma/platform/secrets EGMA_ENCRYPTION_KEY
EGMA_SIMULATOR_SERVICE_TOKEN            secret egma/platform/secrets EGMA_SIMULATOR_SERVICE_TOKEN
EGMA_BASE_URL                           literal https://app.egma.ai
EGMA_SINGLE_ORGANIZATION                literal false
EGMA_TRUST_PROXY                        literal true
EGMA_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE              compose-default

# ── Recordings ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Two halves, two credentials, on purpose: the simulator writes a recording and
# the API signs the link a browser plays it back from. A leaked playback key
# reads a recording rather than replacing one.
EGMA_BLOB_BUCKET                        literal egma-simulation-recordings
EGMA_BLOB_REGION                        literal us-east-1
# **The store's origin, not the bucket's.** The API signs path-style and writes
# the bucket itself as the first path segment — signed-link.ts: "The path starts
# at the root, with nothing in front of the bucket." Give it the bucket's
# virtual host and the bucket appears twice, the signature is still valid
# because the host matches, and S3 answers 404 to every playback link. Proved on
# the live bucket: sim_…/dual-channel.wav is 1566764 bytes, and
# egma-simulation-recordings/sim_…/dual-channel.wav does not exist.
EGMA_BLOB_PUBLIC_URL                    literal https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
EGMA_BLOB_ACCESS_KEY_ID                 secret egma/s3/reader access_key_id
EGMA_BLOB_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY             secret egma/s3/reader secret_access_key
EGMA_SIMULATOR_S3_ENDPOINT              literal https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
EGMA_SIMULATOR_S3_BUCKET                literal egma-simulation-recordings
EGMA_SIMULATOR_S3_REGION                literal us-east-1
EGMA_SIMULATOR_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID         secret egma/s3/writer access_key_id
EGMA_SIMULATOR_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY     secret egma/s3/writer secret_access_key

# The bundled MinIO's settings, and the short names the compose file falls back
# to. Every one above is set explicitly, so no fallback is ever reached.
EGMA_S3_BUCKET                          unset   no bundled object store — S3
EGMA_S3_REGION                          unset   no bundled object store — S3
EGMA_S3_PORT                            unset   no bundled object store — S3
EGMA_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID                   inert not-a-credential-bundled-minio-is-off
EGMA_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY               inert not-a-credential-bundled-minio-is-off
EGMA_S3_READ_ACCESS_KEY_ID              inert not-a-credential-bundled-minio-is-off
EGMA_S3_READ_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY          inert not-a-credential-bundled-minio-is-off

# ── Ingestion ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Where accepted evidence becomes durable, which is the point after which egma
# has promised a customer their conversation is safe. A separate bucket and a
# separate credential from recordings on purpose: one workload must not be able
# to read, delete or expire the other's objects, and this is the half that can
# write. `setup-ingestion-bucket.sh` beside this file makes all three.
#
# **No lifecycle expiry on `pending/`.** A pending object is the work record for
# a conversation ClickHouse has not taken yet, so a rule that aged one out would
# delete evidence egma already told a customer it was keeping. The setup script
# says the same thing where the bucket is made.
EGMA_ROLE                               literal all
EGMA_INGEST_ENDPOINT                    literal https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
EGMA_INGEST_BUCKET                      literal egma-production-ingestion
EGMA_INGEST_REGION                      literal us-east-1
EGMA_INGEST_ACCESS_KEY_ID               secret egma/s3/ingest access_key_id
EGMA_INGEST_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY           secret egma/s3/ingest secret_access_key
# The bundled MinIO's own ingestion credential. This deployment runs no MinIO,
# so the bucket job that reads these never starts.
EGMA_S3_INGEST_ACCESS_KEY_ID            inert not-a-credential-bundled-minio-is-off
EGMA_S3_INGEST_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY        inert not-a-credential-bundled-minio-is-off

# Where the local write-ahead log lives, and the bounds it lives inside. The
# directory is a named volume on the api service in local.yml; it shares the
# t3.large root disk with the egma-box-disk alarm at 85%, so the byte bound
# stays at egma's own half-gigabyte default rather than being raised here.
EGMA_INGESTION_LOG_DIR                  compose-default
EGMA_INGESTION_LOG_MAX_BYTES            compose-default
EGMA_INGESTION_LOG_MAX_RECORDS          compose-default
EGMA_INGESTION_FLUSH_MILLISECONDS       compose-default
EGMA_INGESTION_SEGMENT_MAX_BYTES        compose-default
EGMA_INGESTION_SEGMENT_MAX_RECORDS      compose-default
EGMA_INGESTION_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MILLISECONDS  compose-default
EGMA_INGESTION_SCAN_INTERVAL_MILLISECONDS    compose-default

# ── Media ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# LiveKit Cloud replaces the three bundled containers, and with them the only
# inbound UDP this deployment would otherwise have.
EGMA_SIMULATOR_LIVEKIT_URL              secret egma/livekit url
EGMA_SIMULATOR_LIVEKIT_API_KEY          secret egma/livekit api_key
EGMA_SIMULATOR_LIVEKIT_API_SECRET       secret egma/livekit api_secret
EGMA_LIVEKIT_API_KEY                    inert not-a-credential-bundled-livekit-is-off
EGMA_LIVEKIT_API_SECRET                 inert not-a-credential-bundled-livekit-is-off

# ── Mail ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# The verified sender domain is updates.egma.ai, not the apex. A from address on
# egma.ai would be rejected.
EGMA_SMTP_URL                           secret egma/mail smtp_url
EGMA_MAIL_FROM                          literal noreply@updates.egma.ai

# ── Model-provider credentials ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# Persona and grader versions own provider/model/voice choices in Postgres.
# This deployment owns only the current provider keys. The API reads this AWS
# object for each simulation claim. The grader reads it only for a job that
# includes a model-judged grader. The next model-using work therefore sees a
# rotated key without a container restart. Direct key variables stay empty:
# there is one credential source, not an environment copy beside AWS.
EGMA_PROVIDER_CREDENTIALS_SECRET_ID     literal egma/providers
EGMA_PROVIDER_CREDENTIALS_REGION        literal us-east-1
EGMA_OPENAI_API_KEY                     unset   cloud reads the AWS bundle for model work
EGMA_DEEPGRAM_API_KEY                   unset   cloud reads the AWS bundle for model work
EGMA_CARTESIA_API_KEY                   unset   cloud reads the AWS bundle for model work

# ── The carrier ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# This deployment owns its carrier route. The three non-secret route facts are
# reviewed here; only the SIP password comes from Secrets Manager. API startup
# copies the complete bundle into the platform store, even when an older
# complete route is there.
EGMA_CARRIER_SETTINGS_SOURCE            literal environment
# The variable names stay stable even though the ownership is now explicit.
EGMA_PHONE_TRUNK_ADDRESS                literal egma-simulator-106e37f8.pstn.twilio.com
EGMA_PHONE_SOURCE_NUMBER                literal +18884174625
EGMA_PHONE_TRUNK_USERNAME               literal egma-production
EGMA_PHONE_TRUNK_PASSWORD               secret egma/phone sip_password

# ── How hard the two workers work ────────────────────────────────────────────
# Every one of these is a tuning knob egma has already chosen a sane value for.
# This deployment has no reason yet to disagree with any of them, and saying so
# here is what stops the next reader wondering whether it was an oversight.
EGMA_GRADER_CAPACITY                    compose-default
EGMA_GRADER_CLAIMANT                    compose-default
EGMA_GRADER_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS           compose-default
EGMA_GRADER_LEASE_SECONDS               compose-default
EGMA_GRADER_LOG_LEVEL                   compose-default
EGMA_GRADER_SWEEP_SECONDS               compose-default
EGMA_SIMULATOR_CAPACITY                 compose-default
EGMA_SIMULATOR_CLAIMANT                 compose-default
EGMA_SIMULATOR_CLAIM_WAIT_SECONDS       compose-default
EGMA_SIMULATOR_CONTROL_PLANE_URL        compose-default
EGMA_SIMULATOR_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS        compose-default
EGMA_SIMULATOR_LOG_LEVEL                compose-default
EGMA_SIMULATOR_REPORT_DEADLINE_SECONDS  compose-default

# ── Egma platform telemetry ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# The one deployment where egma's telemetry flag is on. The api and grader
# send their own spans to the collector beside them; the collector tails this
# deployment's application logs and ships both to PostHog, and its vitals to
# CloudWatch. deploy.sh uses this same flag to start or remove the collector.
# Off everywhere else by default, which is the public repo's promise. This is
# **not** the trace store: customers' traces stay in ClickHouse and never
# touch this pipe.
EGMA_TELEMETRY                          literal on
EGMA_TELEMETRY_OTLP_ENDPOINT            literal http://otel-collector:4318
# Resource identity added to every platform span and log. This is public
# deployment metadata, not a credential.
EGMA_DEPLOYMENT_ENVIRONMENT             literal production
EGMA_POSTHOG_KEY                        secret egma/posthog project_key
EGMA_POSTHOG_HOST                       literal https://us.i.posthog.com

# ── The deployment's own plumbing ────────────────────────────────────────────
CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN                 secret egma/cloudflare/tunnel token
EGMA_REGISTRY                           deploy-time  deploy.sh derives it from the account and region
EGMA_IMAGE_TAG                          deploy-time  deploy.sh takes it from the tag being deployed
#!/bin/bash
# Replace what the platform box is running with a named build.
#
#   /opt/egma/deployment/deploy.sh <ref>
#
# The deploy workflow in the public repository invokes this over SSM, after
# syncing this whole directory fresh from S3. It is equally a script to run by
# hand on the box when nobody wants to drive a deployment through CI.
#
# ## The layout, and the rule behind it
#
#   /opt/egma/deployment/   this directory. Synced from S3 with --delete on
#                           every deploy, so nothing in it can drift — it IS
#                           the egma-cloud repository's deployment/ folder
#   /opt/egma/egma/         egma's own repository, checked out at the ref
#                           being deployed. Rebuilt whenever it is missing
#   /opt/egma/certs/        the Supabase root, fetched when missing
#   /opt/egma/.env          assembled fresh on every deploy, root-only
#
# Nothing under /opt/egma is authored on the box. Every file either arrives
# from a repository (via S3 or git) or is derived at deploy time. That rule is
# the fix for 2026-08-15, when hand-written files on this box drifted behind a
# rename in the code and took the persona's settings down silently.
set -euo pipefail

REF="${1:-latest}"
REGION="${AWS_REGION:-${AWS_DEFAULT_REGION:-us-east-1}}"
HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
WORK="$(cd "$HERE/.." && pwd)"
CODE="$WORK/egma"

# ── egma's own files, at the commit the images were built from ───────────────
# The compose files and the images must come from one commit. Deploying an
# image built from one tree with compose files from another is how a setting
# goes missing without anything failing.
if [ -d "$CODE/.git" ]; then
  git -C "$CODE" fetch --tags --quiet origin
else
  git clone --quiet https://github.com/egma-ai/egma.git "$CODE"
fi
if git -C "$CODE" rev-parse --verify --quiet "$REF^{commit}" >/dev/null; then
  git -C "$CODE" checkout --quiet --detach "$REF"
  echo "egma files at $REF ($(git -C "$CODE" rev-parse --short HEAD))"
else
  git -C "$CODE" checkout --quiet --detach origin/main
  echo "no ref '$REF' in the repository; using origin/main for the compose files"
fi

# ── The Supabase root ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Fetched rather than committed: it is a published file, and its address is in
# the egma/db/supabase secret under ca_url. Without it the API dies at boot
# reporting a self-signed chain.
if [ ! -s "$WORK/certs/supabase-ca.crt" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$WORK/certs"
  curl -fsSL \
    "$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id egma/db/supabase \
        --region "$REGION" --query SecretString --output text \
      | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["ca_url"])')" \
    -o "$WORK/certs/supabase-ca.crt"
  echo "fetched the Supabase root certificate"
fi

# ── The settings ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Assembled fresh every time, so changing a secret and deploying is enough.
# assemble-env.sh refuses to write anything if settings.map does not answer
# every setting egma's compose files ask for — a gap stops the deployment here
# rather than reaching production.
bash "$HERE/assemble-env.sh" "$WORK/.env" "$CODE"

ACCOUNT="$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)"
REGISTRY="${EGMA_REGISTRY:-${ACCOUNT}.dkr.ecr.${REGION}.amazonaws.com}"

# The registry and tag join the assembled settings rather than being exported,
# so a `docker compose` run by hand afterwards sees exactly what the deployment
# saw rather than resolving to something else.
printf 'EGMA_REGISTRY=%s\nEGMA_IMAGE_TAG=%s\n' "$REGISTRY" "$REF" >> "$WORK/.env"

# One flag controls every platform telemetry path. The api and grader read it
# themselves. The collector is a Compose profile, so this deployment maps the
# same value to that profile. Anything but `on`, including an absent value,
# also removes a collector left running by an earlier enabled deployment.
PLATFORM_TELEMETRY="$(awk -F= '
  $1 == "EGMA_TELEMETRY" {
    value = substr($0, index($0, "=") + 1)
    gsub(/^[[:space:]]+|[[:space:]]+$/, "", value)
    print tolower(value)
    exit
  }
' "$WORK/.env")"

COMPOSE_PROFILE_ARGS=()
if [ "$PLATFORM_TELEMETRY" = "on" ]; then
  COMPOSE_PROFILE_ARGS=(--profile platform-telemetry)
fi

# --project-directory anchors every relative path in the stack — ./certs, the
# env_file — to /opt/egma, whichever file names it.
compose() {
  docker compose \
    -f "$CODE/docker-compose.yml" \
    -f "$CODE/docker-compose.managed.yml" \
    -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
    --project-directory "$WORK" \
    --project-name egma "${COMPOSE_PROFILE_ARGS[@]}" "$@"
}

# Activate the collector profile only for this cleanup command. Stop and
# remove it before the rest of the deploy when the flag is off. A failed
# removal stops the deploy; it must not say telemetry is off while an old
# collector still sends data.
if [ "$PLATFORM_TELEMETRY" != "on" ]; then
  compose --profile platform-telemetry rm --stop --force otel-collector
  echo "platform telemetry: off"
fi

aws ecr get-login-password --region "$REGION" \
  | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin "$REGISTRY"

# `--no-build` matters: egma's compose file builds all three services from
# source, which is right for a self-hoster and wrong here. CI built these
# already, and this box holds a read-only pull credential on purpose.
compose pull
compose up -d --wait --wait-timeout 300 --no-build
compose ps
if [ "$PLATFORM_TELEMETRY" = "on" ]; then
  echo "platform telemetry: on"
fi

# ── The images nothing runs anymore ──────────────────────────────────────────
# Every deploy pulls three images tagged with their commit, and the box never
# needs an old set again: the registry keeps every tag, so a rollback re-pulls
# whatever it names. Left alone they only accumulate — 21 GB of them by
# 2026-08-17, 90% of everything docker held — and the only question about an
# unbounded pile is which day it fills the disk. Pruned only here, after the
# new containers are up and healthy, and prune
# never touches an image a container is using — so what is running, including
# everything a `deploy.sh <ref>` rollback would stop, is never the thing
# removed.
docker image prune -af
echo "pruned the images nothing runs"
#!/bin/bash
# Does this deployment have an answer for every setting egma asks for?
#
#   ./check-settings.sh [path-to-egma-checkout]
#
# **This is the file that stops a rename reaching production silently.** On
# 2026-08-15 a variable was renamed in the code on 14 August, every test passed,
# and the platform came up with its persona unconfigured — because the box's
# settings were maintained by hand, in a file no test could see.
#
# It needs no AWS credential and reads no secret. It compares two lists:
#
#   what egma asks for   the compose files in the code repository, resolved by
#                        `docker compose config --no-interpolate`, which needs
#                        no values at all
#   what we answer       settings.map beside this script
#
# A variable in the first list and not the second fails. So does a map entry for
# a variable egma no longer has — otherwise the map silently accumulates answers
# to questions nobody asks any more.
#
# Run it before a deployment, and run it after pulling the code repository.
set -euo pipefail

HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
MAP="$HERE/settings.map"

# The code repository. Defaults to the standard nesting — this planning
# repository lives inside the code one — so the common case needs no argument.
CODE="${1:-$(cd "$HERE/../../.." && pwd)}"
[ -f "$CODE/docker-compose.yml" ] || {
  echo "No docker-compose.yml under $CODE" >&2
  echo "Pass the egma checkout as the first argument." >&2
  exit 2
}

[ -f "$MAP" ] || { echo "No settings.map beside this script." >&2; exit 2; }

# The three services this deployment runs. The managed overlay switches off the
# seven bundled ones, so this is exactly what is left, derived rather than
# listed — a service added to the overlay is picked up here for free.
asks=$(cd "$CODE" && docker compose \
  -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.managed.yml -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
  config --no-interpolate --format json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "
# json rather than yaml on purpose: PyYAML is preinstalled on CI runners and
# absent on the box, and this check must give the same answer in both places.
import sys, json, re
d = json.load(sys.stdin)
found = set()
for name, svc in (d.get('services') or {}).items():
    # The managed overlay marks stock services with the bundled profile, so
    # their settings are not this deployment's to answer. Other profiles still
    # belong to this deployment: the platform-telemetry collector is
    # conditional, but every setting it reads must remain in the map for the
    # day it is enabled.
    if 'bundled' in set(svc.get('profiles') or []):
        continue
    # The whole service definition, not just its environment block. A variable
    # can arrive through image:, command: or volumes: as easily as through
    # environment: — the tunnel takes its token on the command line, and the
    # image pins take the registry — and a check that read one key would have
    # been blind to exactly the settings this file was written to catch.
    found |= set(re.findall(r'\\\$\{([A-Z_0-9]+)', json.dumps(svc)))
print('\n'.join(sorted(found)))
")

[ -n "$asks" ] || { echo "Could not read the compose files under $CODE" >&2; exit 2; }

answers=$(grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' "$MAP" | awk '{print $1}' | sort -u)

missing=$(comm -23 <(echo "$asks") <(echo "$answers"))
extra=$(comm -13 <(echo "$asks") <(echo "$answers"))

status=0

if [ -n "$missing" ]; then
  status=1
  echo "egma asks for settings this deployment does not answer:" >&2
  echo "$missing" | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
  echo >&2
  echo "Add each to settings.map with one of: secret, literal, compose-default, unset." >&2
  echo >&2
fi

if [ -n "$extra" ]; then
  status=1
  echo "settings.map answers settings egma no longer asks for:" >&2
  echo "$extra" | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
  echo >&2
  echo "Remove each, or check whether it was renamed rather than dropped." >&2
  echo >&2
fi

# ── Phase two: prove the stack actually loads ────────────────────────────────
# The list comparison above cannot see one compose behaviour: `${VAR:?}`
# markers are checked when the file is loaded, for every service in it —
# profiled-out ones included. The first deploy over this road passed the list
# check and then failed exactly there. So this phase synthesizes a placeholder
# value for every answered setting and asks compose to resolve the whole
# stack, which needs no secret and no AWS — only the same files.
if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then
  envfile="$(mktemp)"
  trap 'rm -f "$envfile"' EXIT
  grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' "$MAP" | while read -r n how a _rest; do
    case "$how" in
      literal|inert) printf '%s=%s\n' "$n" "$a" ;;
      secret)        printf '%s=placeholder\n' "$n" ;;
    esac
  done > "$envfile"
  if ! loaderr=$(cd "$CODE" && EGMA_REGISTRY=placeholder EGMA_IMAGE_TAG=placeholder \
      docker compose --env-file "$envfile" \
        -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.managed.yml -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
        config --services 2>&1 >/dev/null); then
    status=1
    echo "every setting is answered, and the stack still refuses to load:" >&2
    echo "$loaderr" | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
    echo >&2
    echo "Usually a \${VAR:?} marker on a profiled-out service — answer it with inert." >&2
  fi

  # The collector is the deployment half of the one telemetry flag. It must
  # be absent without its profile and present with it. deploy.sh maps
  # EGMA_TELEMETRY=on to this profile and removes an old collector when off.
  if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then
    off_services=$(cd "$CODE" && EGMA_REGISTRY=placeholder EGMA_IMAGE_TAG=placeholder \
      docker compose --env-file "$envfile" \
        -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.managed.yml -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
        config --services)
    on_services=$(cd "$CODE" && EGMA_REGISTRY=placeholder EGMA_IMAGE_TAG=placeholder \
      docker compose --env-file "$envfile" --profile platform-telemetry \
        -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.managed.yml -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
        config --services)
    if echo "$off_services" | grep -qx otel-collector; then
      status=1
      echo "otel-collector starts without the platform-telemetry profile" >&2
    fi
    if ! echo "$on_services" | grep -qx otel-collector; then
      status=1
      echo "otel-collector is absent with the platform-telemetry profile" >&2
    fi
  fi
fi

if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "settings.map answers all $(echo "$asks" | wc -l | tr -d ' ') settings egma asks for, the stack loads, and the telemetry profile is gated."
fi

exit "$status"

item.stdout:
# The only part of hosted egma that is not in the public repository.
#
# `deploy.sh` is the normal entry point. It enables the
# `platform-telemetry` profile only when EGMA_TELEMETRY is `on`.
#
# Everything egma is comes from the first two files, under review and under
# `deployment.test.ts`. This third file holds the two things that are ours
# alone, and nothing else. **If something can go in the public files, it goes
# there** — that is the rule that broke when the box ran a whole hand-written
# compose file and drifted a day behind a rename.

services:
  # **The certificate, and the one line that makes it count.**
  #
  # Supabase signs its pooler with its own private CA — `*.pooler.supabase.com`
  # → `Supabase Intermediate 2021 CA` → `Supabase Root 2021 CA` — and that root
  # is in no public trust store. `pg` 8.22 verifies the chain where older
  # versions shrugged, so without this the API dies at boot reporting a
  # self-signed chain rather than a missing certificate.
  #
  # The alternative is `sslmode=no-verify`, and it is not an alternative. It
  # turns a verified connection into a merely encrypted one, and what that
  # protects is `EGMA_ENCRYPTION_KEY`'s work: the sealed **connection**
  # credentials of every customer. An encrypted connection to an attacker is
  # still a connection to an attacker.
  #
  # `deploy.sh` fetches the certificate before this file is ever read. Its
  # address is in the `egma/db/supabase` secret under `ca_url`.
  # **`image:` is the second thing this file is for.** egma's own compose file
  # builds all three services from source, which is right for a self-hoster and
  # wrong here: CI already built these, pushed them to ECR, and the box has a
  # read-only pull credential on purpose. Naming the image makes `pull` fetch
  # what CI made instead of the box compiling it again on a t3.large.
  #
  # `deploy.sh` appends EGMA_REGISTRY and EGMA_IMAGE_TAG to .env, so a run by
  # hand afterwards resolves to exactly what the deployment resolved to.
  api:
    image: ${EGMA_REGISTRY}/egma/api:${EGMA_IMAGE_TAG:-latest}
    # **Every container's log carries its own name, and is kept from eating
    # the disk.** The json-file driver's `labels` option writes the named
    # labels into each line's `attrs`, and compose already labels every
    # container with its project and service — so the collector below can
    # reject another Compose stack even if it also has a service named `api`.
    # The size cap is the other
    # half: unbounded logs on a box with a fixed disk are a quiet outage on a
    # timer. One anchor, aliased onto every service in this file.
    logging: &egma-logging
      driver: json-file
      options:
        labels: com.docker.compose.project,com.docker.compose.service
        max-size: 50m
        max-file: "3"
    # **This box publishes nothing — not 22, not 80, not 443, not 3100.** The
    # public compose file publishes the API on the host, which is right for a
    # self-hoster who reaches it in a browser and wrong here: the tunnel dials
    # out and shares this container's network namespace, so it reaches the API
    # without any port being bound on the host at all.
    #
    # `!reset` is how a compose override clears a list. Plain `ports: []` would
    # merge and change nothing, which would leave 3100 bound and the security
    # group as the only thing between it and the subnet.
    ports: !reset []
    environment:
      NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS: /certs/supabase-ca.crt
    volumes:
      - ./certs:/certs:ro
      # **The write-ahead log, on a volume rather than in the container's own
      # writable layer.** Evidence is staged here on its way to the ingestion
      # bucket: records waiting to be grouped into a segment, and the identity
      # of a sealed segment whose upload was not confirmed. The bucket is the
      # acknowledgement boundary, so nothing in here has been promised to a
      # customer yet — but an API replaced without this line comes back with
      # nothing to recover, which loses the staged records and lets a repeated
      # upload invent a second object instead of reaching for the first.
      # `docker compose down` keeps this volume unless an operator also passes
      # -v.
      #
      # It shares the box's root disk with everything else, which the
      # egma-box-disk alarm watches at 85%. egma's own
      # EGMA_INGESTION_LOG_MAX_BYTES default is 512 MiB and sits far under
      # that; raising it here without moving the alarm turns a bounded log
      # into a full disk.
      - api-ingestion:/var/lib/egma/ingestion

  # The grader reaches the same database and needs the same root.
  grader:
    image: ${EGMA_REGISTRY}/egma/grader:${EGMA_IMAGE_TAG:-latest}
    logging: *egma-logging
    environment:
      NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS: /certs/supabase-ca.crt
    volumes:
      - ./certs:/certs:ro

  # It reaches the API and the media bridge, not the database, so it needs no
  # certificate — only the image pin.
  simulator:
    image: ${EGMA_REGISTRY}/egma/simulator:${EGMA_IMAGE_TAG:-latest}
    logging: *egma-logging

  # **The only thing that faces the internet, and it faces it by dialling out.**
  # No `ports:` line appears anywhere in this deployment, and the box publishes
  # nothing at all — not 22, not 80, not 443.
  #
  # It shares the API container's network namespace rather than sitting beside
  # it on the compose network. That is what makes `http://localhost:3100` — the
  # origin the Cloudflare dashboard writes unless told otherwise — actually
  # true. Beside the API, `localhost` would be the tunnel itself, every request
  # would 502, and the log would blame an origin that is perfectly healthy.
  #
  # The cost of that choice, which is worth knowing before restarting anything:
  # restarting the API restarts the tunnel too, so it is a brief outage of the
  # whole address rather than of the API alone.
  # **Pinned by digest, like every other third-party image egma runs.** It was
  # on `:latest` until 2026-08-15, which made the one internet-facing component
  # of this deployment the only one a `docker compose pull` could change under
  # us. egma pins postgres, clickhouse, livekit, livekit-sip and redis; this was
  # the exception, and it was the worst one to make.
  #
  # To move it: pull the new tag, read its digest, put the digest here, deploy.
  tunnel:
    image: cloudflare/cloudflared@sha256:0aa26e284f05e6c77ae375b8c9c11d9eb6a448fb7bcd8d40f31cb6176189eb38
    restart: unless-stopped
    network_mode: "service:api"
    command: ["tunnel", "--no-autoupdate", "run", "--token", "${CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN}"]
    env_file: [.env]
    logging: *egma-logging
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy

  # **The one reader of everything above, and the only path telemetry leaves
  # this box on.** The api and grader send their own spans here (that is what
  # `EGMA_TELEMETRY_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4318` in settings.map
  # points at), it tails this Compose project's application logs straight off
  # the Docker daemon's files — the tunnel's included, which no in-process
  # exporter could ever see — and it reads this project's container vitals and
  # the host vitals. Spans and logs go to
  # PostHog; the vitals go to CloudWatch, where the alarms live, over the
  # instance role like every other AWS call this box makes.
  #
  # It publishes nothing, like everything else here: port 4318 answers on the
  # compose network only, and everything outbound is the collector dialling
  # out. The egma containers keep working exactly as before if it dies —
  # telemetry is fire-and-forget from their side, and a broken collector costs
  # observations, never conversations.
  #
  # Root, and three sensitive mounts, knowingly: the daemon's log files and
  # the Docker socket are root's, and /hostfs is what lets it report the
  # box's own memory and disk rather than its container's. The socket is
  # root-equivalent on this machine — acceptable for a container whose config
  # is in this repository, whose image is pinned by digest below, and which
  # reaches nothing that was not already this box's to read.
  #
  # Pinned by digest, like the tunnel above and for the tunnel's reason. To
  # move it: pull the new tag, read its digest, put the digest here, deploy.
  otel-collector:
    # deploy.sh maps the same flag the api, grader, and pages read to this
    # profile. With the flag off, it also removes an older running collector,
    # so changing on to off stops logs and metrics leaving the box.
    profiles: [platform-telemetry]
    image: otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib@sha256:c5918f78992ee73b0d6f0e599423ac5ec52dd5d9726733114d6eca53d5a32ed5
    restart: unless-stopped
    user: "0"
    command: ["--config=/etc/egma/otel-collector.yaml"]
    environment:
      EGMA_POSTHOG_KEY: ${EGMA_POSTHOG_KEY:-}
      EGMA_POSTHOG_HOST: ${EGMA_POSTHOG_HOST:-}

  # turns a verified connection into a merely encrypted one, and what that
  # protects is `EGMA_ENCRYPTION_KEY`'s work: the sealed **connection**
  # credentials of every customer. An encrypted connection to an attacker is
  # still a connection to an attacker.

  # address is in the `egma/db/supabase` secret under `ca_url`.

  # wrong here: CI already built these, pushed them to ECR, and the box has a
  # read-only pull credential on purpose. Naming the image makes `pull` fetch
  # what CI made instead of the box compiling it again on a t3.large.

  # hand afterwards resolves to exactly what the deployment resolved to.

    # the disk.** The json-file driver's `labels` option writes the named
    # labels into each line's `attrs`, and compose already labels every
    # container with its project and service — so the collector below can
    # reject another Compose stack even if it also has a service named `api`.

    # timer. One anchor, aliased onto every service in this file.

    # self-hoster who reaches it in a browser and wrong here: the tunnel dials
    # out and shares this container's network namespace, so it reaches the API
    # without any port being bound on the host at all.

      # upload invent a second object instead of reaching for the first.

    user: "0"
    command: ["--config=/etc/egma/otel-collector.yaml"]
    environment:
      EGMA_POSTHOG_KEY: ${EGMA_POSTHOG_KEY:-}
      EGMA_POSTHOG_HOST: ${EGMA_POSTHOG_HOST:-}
      EGMA_DEPLOYMENT_ENVIRONMENT: ${EGMA_DEPLOYMENT_ENVIRONMENT:-production}
      EGMA_SERVICE_VERSION: ${EGMA_IMAGE_TAG:-latest}

      # competing with the product containers for the box's memory.

      - /:/hostfs:ro
      - otel-collector-storage:/var/lib/otelcol

  # To move it: pull the new tag, read its digest, put the digest here, deploy.

    image: cloudflare/cloudflared@sha256:0aa26e284f05e6c77ae375b8c9c11d9eb6a448fb7bcd8d40f31cb6176189eb38
    restart: unless-stopped
    network_mode: "service:api"
    command: ["tunnel", "--no-autoupdate", "run", "--token", "${CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN}"]
    env_file: [.env]
    logging: *egma-logging
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy

  # **The one reader of everything above, and the only path telemetry leaves
  # this box on.** The api and grader send their own spans here (that is what
  # `EGMA_TELEMETRY_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4318` in settings.map
  # points at), it tails this Compose project's application logs straight off
  # the Docker daemon's files — the tunnel's included, which no in-process
  # exporter could ever see — and it reads this project's container vitals and
  # the host vitals. Spans and logs go to
  # PostHog; the vitals go to CloudWatch, where the alarms live, over the
  # instance role like every other AWS call this box makes.
  #
  # It publishes nothing, like everything else here: port 4318 answers on the
  # compose network only, and everything outbound is the collector dialling
  # out. The egma containers keep working exactly as before if it dies —
  # telemetry is fire-and-forget from their side, and a broken collector costs
  # observations, never conversations.
  #
  # Root, and three sensitive mounts, knowingly: the daemon's log files and
  # the Docker socket are root's, and /hostfs is what lets it report the
  # box's own memory and disk rather than its container's. The socket is
  # root-equivalent on this machine — acceptable for a container whose config
  # is in this repository, whose image is pinned by digest below, and which
  # reaches nothing that was not already this box's to read.
  #
  # Pinned by digest, like the tunnel above and for the tunnel's reason. To
  # move it: pull the new tag, read its digest, put the digest here, deploy.

    # deploy.sh maps the same flag the api, grader, and pages read to this
    # profile. With the flag off, it also removes an older running collector,
    # so changing on to off stops logs and metrics leaving the box.
    profiles: [platform-telemetry]
    image: otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib@sha256:c5918f78992ee73b0d6f0e599423ac5ec52dd5d9726733114d6eca53d5a32ed5

      EGMA_POSTHOG_HOST: ${EGMA_POSTHOG_HOST:-}
      EGMA_DEPLOYMENT_ENVIRONMENT: ${EGMA_DEPLOYMENT_ENVIRONMENT:-production}
      EGMA_SERVICE_VERSION: ${EGMA_IMAGE_TAG:-latest}

      # otel-collector.yaml. The two limits prevent an outage queue from
      # competing with the product containers for the box's memory.
      GOMEMLIMIT: 400MiB

      # --project-directory, and this directory is synced from S3 on every
      # deploy, so the config can never drift from this repository.
      - ./deployment/otel-collector.yaml:/etc/egma/otel-collector.yaml:ro

      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
      - /:/hostfs:ro
      - otel-collector-storage:/var/lib/otelcol
    logging: *egma-logging

name: Publish deployment config

# Merging to main here does not deploy anything. It publishes: deployment/
# goes to S3, and the next public-platform deploy picks it up. Public `main`
# merges deploy platform changes; config changes here ride that deploy and do
# not cause one themselves.
#
# This repository is private and allowed to be specific, so the bucket and the
# role are written here plainly rather than arriving as variables.

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["deployment/**"]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write

jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      AWS_REGION: us-east-1
      DEPLOY_ROLE: arn:aws:iam::599151709955:role/egma-cloud-publish
      BUCKET: egma-deploy-599151709955

    steps:
      # The same commit release-cli.yml and deploy-platform.yml already trust.
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1

      - name: Take a short-lived AWS credential
        # The same plain-shell OIDC exchange deploy-platform.yml uses: GitHub
        # proves which repository and ref this is, AWS answers with an
        # hour-long credential, and no stored key exists anywhere.
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          token=$(curl -sSf -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN" \
            "$ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL&audience=sts.amazonaws.com" \
            | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["value"])')
          creds=$(aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity \
            --role-arn "$DEPLOY_ROLE" \
            --role-session-name "publish-${GITHUB_RUN_ID}" \
            --web-identity-token "$token" \
            --duration-seconds 900 \
            --query Credentials --output json)
          python3 - "$creds" >> "$GITHUB_ENV" <<'PY'
          import json, sys
          c = json.loads(sys.argv[1])
          print(f"AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID={c['AccessKeyId']}")
          print(f"AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY={c['SecretAccessKey']}")
          print(f"AWS_SESSION_TOKEN={c['SessionToken']}")
          PY
          echo "::add-mask::$(echo "$creds" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["SecretAccessKey"])')"
          echo "::add-mask::$(echo "$creds" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["SessionToken"])')"

      - name: Sync deployment/ to S3
        # --delete so a file removed from this repository is removed from the
        # bucket too — otherwise deletions never propagate and the bucket
        # accumulates config nobody can see in any repo.
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          aws s3 sync deployment "s3://${BUCKET}/deployment" --delete
          echo "published $(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"

        # No AWS credential and no secret anywhere in this job: the question

        run: bash deployment/check-settings.sh /tmp/egma

# egma-cloud

How hosted egma is deployed. Private, and allowed to be specific: unlike the
public repository, files here may name our account, our bucket, our addresses.

**The rule this repository exists to enforce: nothing about the deployment is
ever authored on a machine.** The box runs egma's own compose files at the
deployed commit, plus the overlay in `deployment/`, and holds nothing that
this repository and the public one cannot rebuild.

## What lives here

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `deployment/local.yml` | The whole difference between our cloud and stock egma: the tunnel, the collector, the Supabase root, four image pins, no published port |
| `deployment/otel-collector.yaml` | What leaves the box and where it goes: spans and logs to PostHog, vitals to CloudWatch. The token is a secret; this file only names it |
| `deployment/setup-cloudwatch.sh` | One-time AWS wiring for the container runtime and telemetry: the metadata hop limit needed by AWS-backed workloads, the box role's log permissions, the alarms, and who they email. Run from an operator's machine, never the box |
| `deployment/setup-cloudtrail.sh` | One-time AWS account audit setup: one multi-Region management-event trail and its dedicated S3 bucket. It is always separate from app telemetry and runs from an operator's machine |
| `deployment/setup-ingestion-bucket.sh` | One-time AWS wiring for the pending-evidence spool: the ingestion bucket, the IAM user confined to its `pending/` prefix, and the secret that credential is fetched from. Run from an operator's machine, never the box |
| `deployment/settings.map` | One line per setting egma asks for, saying where the answer comes from. Never a secret value |
| `deployment/check-settings.sh` | Proves the map answers everything egma's compose files ask, both directions. No AWS, no secrets |
| `deployment/assemble-env.sh` | Turns the map into `/opt/egma/.env`, fetching values from Secrets Manager. Refuses if the check fails |
| `deployment/deploy.sh` | The sequence the box runs: fetch code at the ref, fetch the CA, check, assemble, pull, up |
| `runbook.md` | What AWS cannot tell you: the failures that name the wrong cause, the things not to change |
| `where-the-settings-live.md` | Which of the five holders (AWS, Vercel, Cloudflare, GitHub, Secrets Manager) keeps what |

## How a deploy happens

```
merge to main on the public repo, touching platform paths
  → the full test suite, on main's own tree
  → the three images → ECR
  → one SSM command to the box:

      bash /opt/egma/deployment/deploy.sh <sha>
  → the workflow reads the identity contract back
  → the workflow tells Vercel to ship the web application
```

The tag is retired. `platform-v*` was the deploy button while a deploy could
drop a mid-call **simulation**; the simulator drains now — first stop signal
ends claiming, in-flight simulations finish, ten minutes at most — so every
green merge deploys, and the web ships only after the API it calls.
`workflow_dispatch` on the public repository is the by-hand override.

Merging to main **here** still does not deploy. It publishes: the `publish`
workflow syncs `deployment/` to S3, and the next deploy — the next platform
merge — picks it up. Config changes ride deploys; they do not cause them.

`drift-check` runs nightly and on every push: it clones the public repository

of in production. That check is the direct product of 2026-08-15, when a
rename landed with every test green and took the persona's settings down
silently, because the deployment was maintained by hand where no test could
see it.

# Where hosted egma's settings live

Five companies hold one deployment's answers. Nothing ties them together, which
is the only reason this page exists.

No secret value is here. This says which system owns each value. The private
deployment map also records non-secret facts that must be reviewed with code.

| Holder | What it holds | Why it cannot live anywhere else |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **AWS Secrets Manager** | Passwords, keys and tokens only, under `egma/*` | Deployment assembly reads service secrets. The API reads `egma/providers` for simulation claims; the grader reads it only for model-judged work. Non-secret choices do not belong here |
| **AWS** | The box, the recordings and ingestion buckets, the image repositories, the two deploy roles | The deployment runs here |
| **Vercel** | `EGMA_API_ORIGIN`, and the project that serves `app.egma.ai` | **A build argument, not a runtime setting.** Next resolves rewrites into the build, so no compose file and no secret store can ever hold it |
| **Cloudflare** | DNS for both addresses, and the tunnel's route to the API | The tunnel is a Cloudflare object. It survives the box being replaced |
| **GitHub** | Three repository variables the deploy workflow reads, and one secret: the Vercel deploy hook URL | Actions cannot read a value it has not been given, and OIDC replaces a stored key. The hook is a secret because anyone holding it can trigger a production web deploy |
| **PostHog** | The project that receives egma's own telemetry: the web application's analytics and errors, the containers' logs and spans | The sixth holder, and a read-side one: nothing of ours is configured there beyond the project itself. Its project token lives in Secrets Manager (`egma/posthog`) for the box, and in Vercel for the pages |

## The two addresses, and why they differ

**`app.egma.ai` is the platform's address.** `EGMA_BASE_URL` is exactly this. The
Next application rewrites `/api/*` and `/v1/traces/*` through to the API, so
pages and API answer on one origin — which is what makes the session cookie valid
for both, and what the CLI's origin check depends on.

**`api.egma.ai` is a service door, not an address.** Its identity contract
correctly names `app.egma.ai`, so a CLI pointed at it refuses. That is the design
working.

In Cloudflare, `app.egma.ai` must stay **DNS-only (grey cloud)**. Vercel issues
its own certificate, and orange-clouding it would let Bot Fight Mode challenge
the CLI — which is a script, not a browser, and would get an HTML challenge page
where it expects JSON.

## Settings that are easy to get wrong

**Three small secret objects hold this path.** Their current JSON shapes are
exact. A note or a non-secret setting in one of them is a second owner and must
be removed.

| Secret | Exact fields |
| --- | --- |
| `egma/providers` | `openai_api_key`, `deepgram_api_key`, `cartesia_api_key` |
| `egma/mail` | `smtp_url` |
| `egma/phone` | `sip_password` |

Persona and grader versions hold provider and model choices in Postgres. The
cloud API reads the current `egma/providers` value for each simulation claim.
The grader reads it only when a claimed job includes a model-judged grader.
They do not copy those keys into Postgres or into the assembled `.env`.
Rotating a provider key therefore changes the next model-using work without a
deploy or container restart.

The carrier trunk address, source number, and SIP username are non-secret
deployment facts. They live as reviewed literals in `deployment/settings.map`.
API startup combines those three facts with the password and writes one sealed
carrier route to the Postgres platform store. The password has no second copy
in this repository.

**The pages' telemetry settings are Vercel's to hold, like `EGMA_API_ORIGIN`.**

same PostHog project token the box holds in `egma/posthog`; it is write-only
by design, which is what makes shipping it inside a public page sane at all.

nothing — which is every build that is not ours.

**Mail sends from `updates.egma.ai`, not `egma.ai`.** That is the domain verified

`egma.ai`, verify the apex domain first.

**The deploy workflow needs three GitHub repository variables** — the deploy

# Runbook — hosted egma

What AWS cannot tell you.

This page deliberately holds **no inventory**. Which account, which instance,
which secrets exist — the console answers all of that, and a written copy only
goes stale. What is here is the knowledge that exists nowhere else: why things
are the way they are, what breaks if you change them, and which failures name
something other than their cause.

token is in AWS Secrets Manager, `us-east-1`, under names beginning `egma/`.

## Reaching the box

There is **no SSH port**. The box publishes nothing at all — not 22, not 80, not
443. Administration goes through SSM, which the box dials outward; traffic goes
through a Cloudflare tunnel, which it also dials outward.

```sh
aws ssm start-session --target <instance-id> --region us-east-1
```

If SSM does not answer, the box is down or has lost its outbound route. Check
that before assuming anything else.

    Point the persona at streaming legs, and stop it reasoning
    
    Matches the simulator change: the listening leg becomes the streaming
    transport, the speaking leg becomes Cartesia, and the model stops
    reasoning before it speaks. All three are about the same thing — a
    caller on a live phone line. A segmented listening leg cannot start
    transcribing until the agent stops talking, and reasoning adds more
    silence on top of that.
    
    The persona's model name moves from Secrets Manager to a literal here.
    A model name is not a secret, it is how the text-to-speech model was
    always carried, and it makes changing one a reviewable line in this
    file instead of a console edit nobody sees.
    
    The speaking key now comes from `egma/providers cartesia_api_key`,
    which has to exist in Secrets Manager before the next deploy.
    
    The two new simulator variables are answered `unset`: the platform
    holds the listening model and the reasoning effort, and hands the
    speaking key to each simulator on the work order it claims.

    Say what the model-selection upgrade does to this deployment, and what it does not
    
    It needs no step from an operator: the API runs it on boot beside the
    migrations. On a deployment serving several customers it copies nothing into
    anybody's rows, which is the rule rather than a setting — each organization
    gets a visible action on its own Model providers screen instead.
    
    The one thing the production flip also turns on is written beside the flip:
    with EGMA_HOSTED set, existing organizations start reading the same model
    access as the ones created after it. No key and no model choice moves.
    
    And the completion marker, with the four conditions it waits for and the two
    places to read it. It is what the later removal of the legacy paths reads —
    not a version number.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_016f1bq5Zyqjz2uK56wvr2w3

diff --git a/deployment/settings.map b/deployment/settings.map
index d24ce44..be2484e 100644
--- a/deployment/settings.map
+++ b/deployment/settings.map
@@ -74,6 +74,13 @@ EGMA_TRUST_PROXY                        literal true
 # deployables: the platform signs its own gateway credentials with it and the
 # gateway checks them with it, under this same name in `gateway/secrets.map`.
 # Rotating it means rotating both, platform first. See `where-the-settings-live.md`.
+# One more thing the flip turns on, written here because it is invisible until
+# it happens: with `EGMA_HOSTED` set, the boot upgrade writes `managed` model
+# access for every organization that has never chosen one. It copies no key and
+# no model choice — that is forbidden on a deployment serving several customers
+# and stays forbidden — it only makes existing organizations read the same
+# answer as the ones created after the flip. An organization that deliberately
+# chose customer-owned keeps its choice. See the runbook's upgrade section.
 EGMA_HOSTED                             unset  managed access is off until the human production-enablement decision
 EGMA_MODEL_GATEWAY_URL                  unset  managed access is off until the human production-enablement decision
 EGMA_GATEWAY_INTERNAL_KEY               unset  managed access is off until the human production-enablement decision
diff --git a/runbook.md b/runbook.md
index 18de4d4..a76a765 100644
--- a/runbook.md
+++ b/runbook.md
@@ -78,6 +78,81 @@ newer schema in place. Migrations are additive by convention — the ClickHouse
 ones are *required* to be, since ClickHouse has no transaction to wrap a file in
 — so this is a caution, not a wall. Never assume a rollback restores a schema.
 
+## The upgrade onto model selections
+
+The release that carries managed model access also moves every persona and
+grader that already exists onto an explicit model choice. It runs on the API's
+boot, in the same breath as the migrations, and it needs **no step from an
+operator at all**. What follows is what to expect and what to read.
+
+### What it does on this deployment
+
+This deployment serves several customers, so the upgrade **copies nothing** into
+anybody's rows: no provider key, no model choice. That is the rule, not a
+setting. Each organization has to use Managed by Egma or add its own provider
+credentials, and each one that still has work on the old path is given a visible
+action that says so on its Model providers screen.
+
+One thing it does do, and only while `EGMA_HOSTED` is set: it writes `managed`
+model access for every organization that has never chosen. **`EGMA_HOSTED` is
+unset today**, so today it does nothing at all — see `deployment/settings.map`.
+It becomes real on the same edit that turns managed access on, and the two
+belong together: without it, an organization created before the flip would read
+`customer-owned` while one created after reads `managed`, and the mandatory
+grading copy a hosted project is seeded with would then resolve a model choice
+against a credential nobody stored.
+
+An organization that has *deliberately* chosen customer-owned keeps that choice.
+
+### The deploy order, which has not changed
+
+The API first, then the grader, exactly as above: the API applies the schema and
+runs the upgrade in its own process. There is no upgrade step to run and none
+missing.
+
+### Old and new workers together
+
+Nothing has to be drained to deploy this. A simulator declares which contract
+versions it implements and the claim queue only offers it work it can conduct —
+so a worker built before model selections existed is never handed a document it
+cannot read, and a worker that can read both takes the rest. The grader works
+the same way through its claim capabilities.
+
+**So the choice is advertise or drain, and this deployment advertises.** A drain
+is still a legitimate way to roll out — bring the new workers up, let the old
+ones finish, then stop them — and it is what to do if a worker is ever deployed
+that cannot declare its versions. Neither is required here.
+
+### The completion marker, and what it gates
+
+Each installation stamps `platform_instance.model_upgrade_completed_at` the
+first time all four of these are true:
+
+- every current persona carries explicit model selections;
+- every current judged grader carries its own model selection;
+- no queued, claimed or running simulation is pinned to a persona version
+  without selections — that is a work order on the old contract;
+- no pending or claimed grading job belongs to a run whose frozen plan names a
+  judge credential — that is the old credential reference.
+
+The conditions are re-checked on every boot, so a deployment that finishes today
+is stamped at its next restart. **The stamp is what the later release that
+removes the legacy paths reads, and nothing else is.** Do not remove anything
+because a version number says so; read the marker.
+
+Two ways to read it:
+
+- the API's boot log says either "this installation has finished moving onto
+  model selections" or "this installation is still serving work that needs the
+  legacy model paths", and the second names which of the four conditions is
+  standing;
+- `GET /api/model-upgrade` with any credential of an organization on the
+  deployment answers `completed`, `completed_at` and `outstanding`.
+
+An installation that never finishes is normal and is not a fault: it means some
+customer still has a persona or grader nobody has given models to. Their Model
+providers screen says which, in a sentence written to be acted on.
+
 ## Restarting
 
 Restarting the **api** container also restarts the **tunnel**, because the tunnel

    47	cloud API reads the current `egma/providers` value for each simulation claim.

    49	      options:

     1	#!/bin/bash
     2	# Replace what the platform box is running with a named build.
     3	#
     4	#   /opt/egma/deployment/deploy.sh <ref>
     5	#
     6	# The deploy workflow in the public repository invokes this over SSM, after
     7	# syncing this whole directory fresh from S3. It is equally a script to run by
     8	# hand on the box when nobody wants to drive a deployment through CI.
     9	#
    10	# ## The layout, and the rule behind it
    11	#
    12	#   /opt/egma/deployment/   this directory. Synced from S3 with --delete on
    13	#                           every deploy, so nothing in it can drift — it IS
    14	#                           the egma-cloud repository's deployment/ folder
    15	#   /opt/egma/egma/         egma's own repository, checked out at the ref
    16	#                           being deployed. Rebuilt whenever it is missing
    17	#   /opt/egma/certs/        the Supabase root, fetched when missing
    18	#   /opt/egma/.env          assembled fresh on every deploy, root-only
    19	#
    20	# Nothing under /opt/egma is authored on the box. Every file either arrives
    21	# from a repository (via S3 or git) or is derived at deploy time. That rule is
    22	# the fix for 2026-08-15, when hand-written files on this box drifted behind a
    23	# rename in the code and took the persona's settings down silently.
    24	set -euo pipefail
    25	
    26	REF="${1:-latest}"
    27	REGION="${AWS_REGION:-${AWS_DEFAULT_REGION:-us-east-1}}"
    28	HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
    29	WORK="$(cd "$HERE/.." && pwd)"
    30	CODE="$WORK/egma"
    31	
    32	# ── egma's own files, at the commit the images were built from ───────────────
    33	# The compose files and the images must come from one commit. Deploying an
    34	# image built from one tree with compose files from another is how a setting
    35	# goes missing without anything failing.
    36	if [ -d "$CODE/.git" ]; then
    37	  git -C "$CODE" fetch --tags --quiet origin
    38	else
    39	  git clone --quiet https://github.com/egma-ai/egma.git "$CODE"
    40	fi
    41	if git -C "$CODE" rev-parse --verify --quiet "$REF^{commit}" >/dev/null; then
    42	  git -C "$CODE" checkout --quiet --detach "$REF"
    43	  echo "egma files at $REF ($(git -C "$CODE" rev-parse --short HEAD))"
    44	else
    45	  git -C "$CODE" checkout --quiet --detach origin/main
    46	  echo "no ref '$REF' in the repository; using origin/main for the compose files"
    47	fi
    48	
    49	# ── The Supabase root ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    50	# Fetched rather than committed: it is a published file, and its address is in
    51	# the egma/db/supabase secret under ca_url. Without it the API dies at boot
    52	# reporting a self-signed chain.
    53	if [ ! -s "$WORK/certs/supabase-ca.crt" ]; then
    54	  mkdir -p "$WORK/certs"
    55	  curl -fsSL \
    56	    "$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id egma/db/supabase \
    57	        --region "$REGION" --query SecretString --output text \
    58	      | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["ca_url"])')" \
    59	    -o "$WORK/certs/supabase-ca.crt"
    60	  echo "fetched the Supabase root certificate"
    61	fi
    62	
    63	# ── The settings ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    64	# Assembled fresh every time, so changing a secret and deploying is enough.
    65	# assemble-env.sh refuses to write anything if settings.map does not answer
    66	# every setting egma's compose files ask for — a gap stops the deployment here
    67	# rather than reaching production.
    68	bash "$HERE/assemble-env.sh" "$WORK/.env" "$CODE"

    70	ACCOUNT="$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)"
    71	REGISTRY="${EGMA_REGISTRY:-${ACCOUNT}.dkr.ecr.${REGION}.amazonaws.com}"
    72

    74	# so a `docker compose` run by hand afterwards sees exactly what the deployment
    75	# saw rather than resolving to something else.
    76	printf 'EGMA_REGISTRY=%s\nEGMA_IMAGE_TAG=%s\n' "$REGISTRY" "$REF" >> "$WORK/.env"

    81	# also removes a collector left running by an earlier enabled deployment.

    83	  $1 == "EGMA_TELEMETRY" {
    84	    value = substr($0, index($0, "=") + 1)

    87	    exit

    34	## Settings that are easy to get wrong
    35	
    36	**Three small secret objects hold this path.** Their current JSON shapes are

    46	Persona and grader versions hold provider and model choices in Postgres. The
    47	cloud API reads the current `egma/providers` value for each simulation claim.

    49	They do not copy those keys into Postgres or into the assembled `.env`.

     3	# `deploy.sh` is the normal entry point. It enables the
     4	# `platform-telemetry` profile only when EGMA_TELEMETRY is `on`.

     6	# Everything egma is comes from the first two files, under review and under
     7	# `deployment.test.ts`. This third file holds the two things that are ours
     8	# alone, and nothing else. **If something can go in the public files, it goes
     9	# there** — that is the rule that broke when the box ran a whole hand-written
    10	# compose file and drifted a day behind a rename.
    11	
    12	services:
    13	  # **The certificate, and the one line that makes it count.**
    14	  #
    15	  # Supabase signs its pooler with its own private CA — `*.pooler.supabase.com`
    16	  # → `Supabase Intermediate 2021 CA` → `Supabase Root 2021 CA` — and that root
    17	  # is in no public trust store. `pg` 8.22 verifies the chain where older
    18	  # versions shrugged, so without this the API dies at boot reporting a
    19	  # self-signed chain rather than a missing certificate.
    20	  #
    21	  # The alternative is `sslmode=no-verify`, and it is not an alternative. It
    22	  # turns a verified connection into a merely encrypted one, and what that
    23	  # protects is `EGMA_ENCRYPTION_KEY`'s work: the sealed **connection**
    24	  # credentials of every customer. An encrypted connection to an attacker is
    25	  # still a connection to an attacker.
    26	  #
    27	  # `deploy.sh` fetches the certificate before this file is ever read. Its
    28	  # address is in the `egma/db/supabase` secret under `ca_url`.
    29	  # **`image:` is the second thing this file is for.** egma's own compose file
    30	  # builds all three services from source, which is right for a self-hoster and
    31	  # wrong here: CI already built these, pushed them to ECR, and the box has a
    32	  # read-only pull credential on purpose. Naming the image makes `pull` fetch
    33	  # what CI made instead of the box compiling it again on a t3.large.
    34	  #
    35	  # `deploy.sh` appends EGMA_REGISTRY and EGMA_IMAGE_TAG to .env, so a run by
    36	  # hand afterwards resolves to exactly what the deployment resolved to.
    37	  api:
    38	    image: ${EGMA_REGISTRY}/egma/api:${EGMA_IMAGE_TAG:-latest}
    39	    # **Every container's log carries its own name, and is kept from eating
    40	    # the disk.** The json-file driver's `labels` option writes the named
    41	    # labels into each line's `attrs`, and compose already labels every
    42	    # container with its project and service — so the collector below can
    43	    # reject another Compose stack even if it also has a service named `api`.
    44	    # The size cap is the other
    45	    # half: unbounded logs on a box with a fixed disk are a quiet outage on a
    46	    # timer. One anchor, aliased onto every service in this file.
    47	    logging: &egma-logging
    48	      driver: json-file
    49	      options:
    50	        labels: com.docker.compose.project,com.docker.compose.service
    51	        max-size: 50m
    52	        max-file: "3"
    53	    # **This box publishes nothing — not 22, not 80, not 443, not 3100.** The
    54	    # public compose file publishes the API on the host, which is right for a
    55	    # self-hoster who reaches it in a browser and wrong here: the tunnel dials
    56	    # out and shares this container's network namespace, so it reaches the API
    57	    # without any port being bound on the host at all.
    58	    #
    59	    # `!reset` is how a compose override clears a list. Plain `ports: []` would
    60	    # merge and change nothing, which would leave 3100 bound and the security
    61	    # group as the only thing between it and the subnet.
    62	    ports: !reset []
    63	    environment:
    64	      NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS: /certs/supabase-ca.crt
    65	    volumes:
    66	      - ./certs:/certs:ro

    68	      # writable layer.** Evidence is staged here on its way to the ingestion
    69	      # bucket: records waiting to be grouped into a segment, and the identity
    70	      # of a sealed segment whose upload was not confirmed. The bucket is the
    71	      # acknowledgement boundary, so nothing in here has been promised to a
    72	      # customer yet — but an API replaced without this line comes back with

    74	      # upload invent a second object instead of reaching for the first.
    75	      # `docker compose down` keeps this volume unless an operator also passes
    76	      # -v.
    77	      #
    78	      # It shares the box's root disk with everything else, which the
    79	      # egma-box-disk alarm watches at 85%. egma's own
    80	      # EGMA_INGESTION_LOG_MAX_BYTES default is 512 MiB and sits far under

    82	      # into a full disk.

    87	    image: ${EGMA_REGISTRY}/egma/grader:${EGMA_IMAGE_TAG:-latest}
    88	    logging: *egma-logging
    89	    environment:
    90	      NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS: /certs/supabase-ca.crt
    91	    volumes:
    92	      - ./certs:/certs:ro
    93

    97	    image: ${EGMA_REGISTRY}/egma/simulator:${EGMA_IMAGE_TAG:-latest}
    98	    logging: *egma-logging
    99	
   100	  # **The only thing that faces the internet, and it faces it by dialling out.**
   101	  # No `ports:` line appears anywhere in this deployment, and the box publishes
   102	  # nothing at all — not 22, not 80, not 443.
   103	  #
   104	  # It shares the API container's network namespace rather than sitting beside
   105	  # it on the compose network. That is what makes `http://localhost:3100` — the
   106	  # origin the Cloudflare dashboard writes unless told otherwise — actually
   107	  # true. Beside the API, `localhost` would be the tunnel itself, every request
   108	  # would 502, and the log would blame an origin that is perfectly healthy.
   109	  #
   110	  # The cost of that choice, which is worth knowing before restarting anything:
   111	  # restarting the API restarts the tunnel too, so it is a brief outage of the
   112	  # whole address rather than of the API alone.
     1	#!/bin/bash
     2	# Replace what the platform box is running with a named build.
     3	#
     4	#   /opt/egma/deployment/deploy.sh <ref>
     5	#
     6	# The deploy workflow in the public repository invokes this over SSM, after
     7	# syncing this whole directory fresh from S3. It is equally a script to run by
     8	# hand on the box when nobody wants to drive a deployment through CI.
     9	#
    10	# ## The layout, and the rule behind it
    11	#
    12	#   /opt/egma/deployment/   this directory. Synced from S3 with --delete on
    13	#                           every deploy, so nothing in it can drift — it IS
    14	#                           the egma-cloud repository's deployment/ folder
    15	#   /opt/egma/egma/         egma's own repository, checked out at the ref
    16	#                           being deployed. Rebuilt whenever it is missing
    17	#   /opt/egma/certs/        the Supabase root, fetched when missing
    18	#   /opt/egma/.env          assembled fresh on every deploy, root-only
    19	#
    20	# Nothing under /opt/egma is authored on the box. Every file either arrives
    21	# from a repository (via S3 or git) or is derived at deploy time. That rule is
    22	# the fix for 2026-08-15, when hand-written files on this box drifted behind a
    23	# rename in the code and took the persona's settings down silently.
    24	set -euo pipefail
    25	
    26	REF="${1:-latest}"
    27	REGION="${AWS_REGION:-${AWS_DEFAULT_REGION:-us-east-1}}"
    28	HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
    29	WORK="$(cd "$HERE/.." && pwd)"
    30	CODE="$WORK/egma"
    31	
    32	# ── egma's own files, at the commit the images were built from ───────────────
    33	# The compose files and the images must come from one commit. Deploying an
    34	# image built from one tree with compose files from another is how a setting
    35	# goes missing without anything failing.
    36	if [ -d "$CODE/.git" ]; then
    37	  git -C "$CODE" fetch --tags --quiet origin
    38	else
    39	  git clone --quiet https://github.com/egma-ai/egma.git "$CODE"
    40	fi
    41	if git -C "$CODE" rev-parse --verify --quiet "$REF^{commit}" >/dev/null; then
    42	  git -C "$CODE" checkout --quiet --detach "$REF"
    43	  echo "egma files at $REF ($(git -C "$CODE" rev-parse --short HEAD))"
    44	else
    45	  git -C "$CODE" checkout --quiet --detach origin/main
    46	  echo "no ref '$REF' in the repository; using origin/main for the compose files"
    47	fi
    48	
    49	# ── The Supabase root ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    50	# Fetched rather than committed: it is a published file, and its address is in
    51	# the egma/db/supabase secret under ca_url. Without it the API dies at boot
    52	# reporting a self-signed chain.
    53	if [ ! -s "$WORK/certs/supabase-ca.crt" ]; then
    54	  mkdir -p "$WORK/certs"
    55	  curl -fsSL \
    56	    "$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id egma/db/supabase \
    57	        --region "$REGION" --query SecretString --output text \
    58	      | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["ca_url"])')" \
    59	    -o "$WORK/certs/supabase-ca.crt"
    60	  echo "fetched the Supabase root certificate"
    61	fi
    62	
    63	# ── The settings ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    64	# Assembled fresh every time, so changing a secret and deploying is enough.
    65	# assemble-env.sh refuses to write anything if settings.map does not answer
    66	# every setting egma's compose files ask for — a gap stops the deployment here
    67	# rather than reaching production.
    68	bash "$HERE/assemble-env.sh" "$WORK/.env" "$CODE"
    69	
    70	ACCOUNT="$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)"
    71	REGISTRY="${EGMA_REGISTRY:-${ACCOUNT}.dkr.ecr.${REGION}.amazonaws.com}"
    72	
    73	# The registry and tag join the assembled settings rather than being exported,
    74	# so a `docker compose` run by hand afterwards sees exactly what the deployment
    75	# saw rather than resolving to something else.
    76	printf 'EGMA_REGISTRY=%s\nEGMA_IMAGE_TAG=%s\n' "$REGISTRY" "$REF" >> "$WORK/.env"
    77	
    78	# One flag controls every platform telemetry path. The api and grader read it
    79	# themselves. The collector is a Compose profile, so this deployment maps the
    80	# same value to that profile. Anything but `on`, including an absent value,
    81	# also removes a collector left running by an earlier enabled deployment.
    82	PLATFORM_TELEMETRY="$(awk -F= '
    83	  $1 == "EGMA_TELEMETRY" {
    84	    value = substr($0, index($0, "=") + 1)
    85	    gsub(/^[[:space:]]+|[[:space:]]+$/, "", value)
    86	    print tolower(value)
    87	    exit
    88	  }
    89	' "$WORK/.env")"
    90	
    91	COMPOSE_PROFILE_ARGS=()
    92	if [ "$PLATFORM_TELEMETRY" = "on" ]; then
    93	  COMPOSE_PROFILE_ARGS=(--profile platform-telemetry)
    94	fi
    95	
    96	# --project-directory anchors every relative path in the stack — ./certs, the
    97	# env_file — to /opt/egma, whichever file names it.
    98	compose() {
    99	  docker compose \
   100	    -f "$CODE/docker-compose.yml" \
   101	    -f "$CODE/docker-compose.managed.yml" \
   102	    -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
   103	    --project-directory "$WORK" \
   104	    --project-name egma "${COMPOSE_PROFILE_ARGS[@]}" "$@"
   105	}
   106	
   107	# Activate the collector profile only for this cleanup command. Stop and
   108	# remove it before the rest of the deploy when the flag is off. A failed
   109	# removal stops the deploy; it must not say telemetry is off while an old
   110	# collector still sends data.
   111	if [ "$PLATFORM_TELEMETRY" != "on" ]; then
   112	  compose --profile platform-telemetry rm --stop --force otel-collector
   113	  echo "platform telemetry: off"
   114	fi
   115	
   116	aws ecr get-login-password --region "$REGION" \
   117	  | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin "$REGISTRY"
   118	
   119	# `--no-build` matters: egma's compose file builds all three services from
   120	# source, which is right for a self-hoster and wrong here. CI built these
   121	# already, and this box holds a read-only pull credential on purpose.
   122	compose pull
   123	compose up -d --wait --wait-timeout 300 --no-build
   124	compose ps
   125	if [ "$PLATFORM_TELEMETRY" = "on" ]; then
   126	  echo "platform telemetry: on"
   127	fi
   128	
   129	# ── The images nothing runs anymore ──────────────────────────────────────────
   130	# Every deploy pulls three images tagged with their commit, and the box never
   131	# needs an old set again: the registry keeps every tag, so a rollback re-pulls
   132	# whatever it names. Left alone they only accumulate — 21 GB of them by
   133	# 2026-08-17, 90% of everything docker held — and the only question about an
   134	# unbounded pile is which day it fills the disk. Pruned only here, after the
   135	# new containers are up and healthy, and prune
   136	# never touches an image a container is using — so what is running, including
   137	# everything a `deploy.sh <ref>` rollback would stop, is never the thing
   138	# removed.
   139	docker image prune -af
   140	echo "pruned the images nothing runs"

   171	EGMA_SIMULATOR_CONTROL_PLANE_URL        compose-default
   172	EGMA_SIMULATOR_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS        compose-default
   173	EGMA_SIMULATOR_LOG_LEVEL                compose-default
