item.stdout:
+Grafana is the clearest example of both valid modes.
+
+Server configuration has a documented precedence chain. Grafana starts with defaults, reads a custom INI file, then accepts command-line and `GF_*` environment overrides. Environment variables override known server options; they are not a general product-resource store. File and Vault value providers can inject secret values into a known setting. Source: [Configure Grafana](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/setup-grafana/configure-grafana/).
+
+Data sources are product resources. They have an organization ID, normal `jsonData`, and encrypted `secureJsonData`. Grafana states that its database contains credentials for data sources and alert notifications and encrypts those values before writing them. An external KMS can protect the key that encrypts the database values. Sources: [Grafana provisioning](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/administration/provisioning/) and [database secret encryption](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/setup-grafana/configure-security/configure-database-encryption/).
+
+Grafana also supports GitOps without pretending the database and file are equal writers:
+
+- Startup provisioning creates or updates the database resource to match the file.
+- A numeric resource version prevents an older Grafana node from overwriting newer configuration.
+- `editable: false` blocks UI edits when the file owns the resource.
+- `prune: true` makes file-driven deletion an explicit decision.
+- Secret values can enter `secureJsonData` through environment expansion, but the non-secret resource shape remains in the provisioning file.
+
+Source: [Provision Grafana](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/administration/provisioning/).
+
+**Lesson for Egma:** it is valid to materialize a deployment-owned resource in Postgres. That database row is a projection, not a second owner. It needs provenance, a version, whole-resource reconciliation, and a read-only product surface.
+
+## Airbyte
+
+Airbyte separates a connector resource from its credential payload.
+
+A source is created with a `workspaceId`, name, connector definition, and one configuration object. This makes the source a tenant-scoped domain resource, not a collection of process variables. Source: [Create a source](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/createsource).
+
+Connector schemas identify secret fields. Airbyte does not return those values on reads. A full update replaces the full source configuration, and a masked placeholder tells the API to retain an existing secret. Source: [Full source update](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/putsource).
+
+For OAuth, Airbyte can store the access and refresh tokens in its secret store and return a secret ID. The product later creates the workspace source with that ID. It also supports provider OAuth credentials at workspace or organization scope, instead of one global credential for all customers. Sources: [OAuth source flow](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/creating-oauth-sources), [workspace OAuth override](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/workspaceoauthcredentials), and [organization OAuth override](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/createorupdateorganizationoauthcredentials).
+
+At deployment level, Airbyte's documented configuration selects a secret persistence implementation, including AWS Secrets Manager and Google Secret Manager. `values.yaml` is the operator interface; the secret store holds payloads. Source: [Airbyte deployment configuration](https://github.com/airbytehq/airbyte/blob/master/docs/platform/operator-guides/configuring-airbyte.md#secrets).
+
+**Lesson for Egma:** the organization or project record decides which provider configuration applies. The secret manager stores or resolves its sensitive fields. A secret ID can cross the boundary; the secret value does not have to.
+
+## The repeated mature pattern
+
+Across these products, six rules repeat:
+
+1. **Scope is part of the schema.** A project, organization, workspace, or integration relationship is not inferred from which server read an environment variable.
+2. **Secrets and choices are separate.** A product record says what to use. A protected field or secret reference supplies authority to use it.
+3. **Precedence is declared.** A value is product-owned, inherited, runtime-overridden, or provisioned. It is not whichever row happened to exist first.
+4. **A related bundle moves together.** GitLab inherits a complete integration bundle. Grafana provisions a complete data source. Airbyte updates a complete source configuration.
+5. **Declarative state has a version.** Grafana uses a resource version to reject an older writer. Generated GitLab files are replaced from one canonical deployment input.
+6. **Validation happens before activation.** GitLab validates during reconfigure. Grafana validates provisioned resources and runtime settings. Airbyte validates a source against its connector specification. A process must not report ready only because every individual field is non-empty.
+
+No reviewed product uses this as its durable authority rule:
+
+> Copy each deployment variable into an independent database row only when that row is missing, then combine old and new rows at runtime.
+
+That statement is an inference from the reviewed designs. The products either keep the product database authoritative or use an explicit provisioner that reconciles declared state.
+
+## Consequence for Egma
+
+The current domain decision is sound: a persona version selects its LLM, STT, and TTS provider and model independently; a run pins that persona version; organization-owned provider credentials stay separate. See [ADR-0010 on the managed-model-access branch](https://github.com/egma-ai/egma-planning/blob/codex/managed-model-access/docs/adr/0010-personas-select-models-independently.md).
+
+The safe ownership split is:
+
+| State | Owner | Storage |
+|---|---|---|
+| Persona behavior and LLM/STT/TTS selections | Product domain | Immutable persona version in Postgres |
+| Organization provider access mode | Organization | Postgres |
+| Organization provider credential relationship | Organization | Postgres row with encrypted value or external secret reference |
+| Secret payload | Protected product column or secret manager | Never inside the persona |
+| Simulator implementation choices such as VAD internals | Egma release | Code/default deployment configuration |
+| Database, queues, public origin, signing and encryption roots | Deployment operator | Deployment configuration and secret delivery |
+| Phone carrier resource used by an organization or connection | Product resource with an explicit scope | Postgres relationship plus protected credentials or secret references |
+
+`prepareSimulation` is the boundary that joins these facts. It should:
+
+1. Read the persona version pinned by the run.
+2. Read the organization's current provider access and credential bindings.
+3. Resolve only the secret values required by that persona version.
+4. Validate provider, model job, model, and voice as one compatible structure.
+5. Create one closed work order for the simulator.
+
+The simulator must not add an environment fallback after this boundary. That would create a second runtime answer.
+
+## Architecture C: explicit GitOps-provisioned resources
+
+This architecture is for an operator who wants `egma-cloud` to own selected product resources. It is an alternative authority mode, not another insert-only seed path.
+
+### Resource shape
+
+A versioned manifest contains non-secret product state:
+
+```yaml
+apiVersion: egma.ai/v1alpha1
+kind: Persona
+metadata:
+  externalId: remedy-default
+  organizationId: org_...
+  generation: 7
+spec:
+  llm: { provider: openai, model: gpt-5.6-terra }
+  stt: { provider: openai_realtime, model: gpt-live-transcribe }
+  tts: { provider: cartesia, model: sonic-3.5, voiceId: ... }
+```
+
+A separate organization credential binding contains no plaintext secret:
+
+```yaml
+apiVersion: egma.ai/v1alpha1
+kind: ModelProviderCredentialBinding
+metadata:
+  externalId: production-openai
+  organizationId: org_...
+  generation: 3
+spec:
+  provider: openai
+  secretRef: aws-secrets-manager://egma/providers/openai
+```
+
+AWS Secrets Manager stores only the protected value. The manifest stores the provider relationship and secret reference. Postgres stores the materialized product resource, its tenant, `source=provisioned`, external ID, desired generation, observed generation, and a hash of the normalized specification.
+
+### Reconciliation contract
+
+- The provisioner owns only rows marked `source=provisioned`.
+- The product API refuses edits to those rows and reports that the deployment owns them.
+- The provisioner validates and applies the whole resource in one transaction.
+- An older generation cannot replace a newer generation.
+- Removal does nothing unless the manifest declares deletion or an explicit prune policy.
+- The deployment fails before traffic moves when the resource shape is invalid, a provider/model-job pair is unsupported, or a required secret reference cannot be resolved.
+- A successful deploy records `observedGeneration == generation`. Drift is visible when they differ.
+- A model edit creates a new immutable persona version. It does not rewrite a version used by an earlier run.
+
+The Postgres row is then an active projection of the manifest. It is not an independent source of truth. This follows Grafana's provisioned-resource pattern and GitLab's generated-configuration pattern.
+
+### `prepareSimulation` remains unchanged
+
+The provisioner changes how a persona version and credential binding enter Postgres. It does not create a second simulator path.
+
+`prepareSimulation` still reads the pinned persona version and organization credential binding from the product model, resolves the secret reference just in time, and creates the same closed work order. A product-authored persona and a provisioned persona use the same preparation code.
+
+### Trade-offs
+
+Benefits:
+
+- Non-secret state is reviewed, versioned, diffable, and easy to roll back.
+- AWS contains secrets only.
+- Drift has a visible generation and hash.
+- One controller owns a provisioned resource, so a UI writer cannot conflict with it.
+- Hosted defaults can use the same domain model and execution path as customer-created personas.
+
+Costs:
+
+- The provisioner, status model, and immutable-version creation add real system complexity.
+- A deployment is a slow and unsuitable edit surface for normal customer persona work.
+- Deletion and rollback need deliberate semantics because old runs must keep their pinned persona versions.
+- Secret reference resolution adds an operational dependency at simulation preparation time unless the secret is safely cached.
+
+Use this mode for operator-owned defaults, internal organizations, or customers that explicitly choose GitOps. Keep ordinary hosted customer personas product-owned in Postgres. Do not let the same persona switch silently between UI ownership and deployment ownership.
+
+## Recommended decision test
+
+For each proposed setting, ask these questions in order:
+
+1. Does changing it change how a persona behaves? Put it in a persona version.
+2. Does it authorize an organization to use a provider? Put the relationship in organization state and protect the secret value separately.
+3. Does it define how one connection reaches one agent? Put it on that connection or its scoped carrier resource.
+4. Does it only tell an Egma process how to start or find infrastructure? Put it in deployment configuration.
+5. Must a deployment file own a product resource? Use an explicit provisioned resource with provenance, generation, whole-resource reconciliation, and one writer.
+
+This test prevents a new global key-value table from collecting unrelated domain choices only because each choice is needed during a simulation.

+`prepareSimulation` still reads the pinned persona version and organization credential binding from the product model, resolves the secret reference just in time, and creates the same closed work order. A product-authored persona and a provisioned persona use the same preparation code.
+
+### Trade-offs
+
+Benefits:
+
+- Non-secret state is reviewed, versioned, diffable, and easy to roll back.
+- AWS contains secrets only.
+- Drift has a visible generation and hash.
+- One controller owns a provisioned resource, so a UI writer cannot conflict with it.
+- Hosted defaults can use the same domain model and execution path as customer-created personas.
+
+Costs:
+
+- The provisioner, status model, and immutable-version creation add real system complexity.
+- A deployment is a slow and unsuitable edit surface for normal customer persona work.
+- Deletion and rollback need deliberate semantics because old runs must keep their pinned persona versions.
+- Secret reference resolution adds an operational dependency at simulation preparation time unless the secret is safely cached.
+
+Use this mode for operator-owned defaults, internal organizations, or customers that explicitly choose GitOps. Keep ordinary hosted customer personas product-owned in Postgres. Do not let the same persona switch silently between UI ownership and deployment ownership.
+
+## Recommended decision test
+
+For each proposed setting, ask these questions in order:
+
+1. Does changing it change how a persona behaves? Put it in a persona version.
+2. Does it authorize an organization to use a provider? Put the relationship in organization state and protect the secret value separately.
+3. Does it define how one connection reaches one agent? Put it on that connection or its scoped carrier resource.
+4. Does it only tell an Egma process how to start or find infrastructure? Put it in deployment configuration.
+5. Must a deployment file own a product resource? Use an explicit provisioned resource with provenance, generation, whole-resource reconciliation, and one writer.
+
+This test prevents a new global key-value table from collecting unrelated domain choices only because each choice is needed during a simulation.

+Grafana is the clearest example of both valid modes.
+
+Server configuration has a documented precedence chain. Grafana starts with defaults, reads a custom INI file, then accepts command-line and `GF_*` environment overrides. Environment variables override known server options; they are not a general product-resource store. File and Vault value providers can inject secret values into a known setting. Source: [Configure Grafana](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/setup-grafana/configure-grafana/).
+
+Data sources are product resources. They have an organization ID, normal `jsonData`, and encrypted `secureJsonData`. Grafana states that its database contains credentials for data sources and alert notifications and encrypts those values before writing them. An external KMS can protect the key that encrypts the database values. Sources: [Grafana provisioning](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/administration/provisioning/) and [database secret encryption](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/setup-grafana/configure-security/configure-database-encryption/).
+
+Grafana also supports GitOps without pretending the database and file are equal writers:
+
+- Startup provisioning creates or updates the database resource to match the file.
+- A numeric resource version prevents an older Grafana node from overwriting newer configuration.
+- `editable: false` blocks UI edits when the file owns the resource.
+- `prune: true` makes file-driven deletion an explicit decision.
+- Secret values can enter `secureJsonData` through environment expansion, but the non-secret resource shape remains in the provisioning file.
+
+Source: [Provision Grafana](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/administration/provisioning/).
+
+**Lesson for Egma:** it is valid to materialize a deployment-owned resource in Postgres. That database row is a projection, not a second owner. It needs provenance, a version, whole-resource reconciliation, and a read-only product surface.
+
+## Airbyte
+
+Airbyte separates a connector resource from its credential payload.
+
+A source is created with a `workspaceId`, name, connector definition, and one configuration object. This makes the source a tenant-scoped domain resource, not a collection of process variables. Source: [Create a source](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/createsource).
+
+Connector schemas identify secret fields. Airbyte does not return those values on reads. A full update replaces the full source configuration, and a masked placeholder tells the API to retain an existing secret. Source: [Full source update](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/putsource).
+
+For OAuth, Airbyte can store the access and refresh tokens in its secret store and return a secret ID. The product later creates the workspace source with that ID. It also supports provider OAuth credentials at workspace or organization scope, instead of one global credential for all customers. Sources: [OAuth source flow](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/creating-oauth-sources), [workspace OAuth override](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/workspaceoauthcredentials), and [organization OAuth override](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/createorupdateorganizationoauthcredentials).
+
+At deployment level, Airbyte's documented configuration selects a secret persistence implementation, including AWS Secrets Manager and Google Secret Manager. `values.yaml` is the operator interface; the secret store holds payloads. Source: [Airbyte deployment configuration](https://github.com/airbytehq/airbyte/blob/master/docs/platform/operator-guides/configuring-airbyte.md#secrets).
+
+**Lesson for Egma:** the organization or project record decides which provider configuration applies. The secret manager stores or resolves its sensitive fields. A secret ID can cross the boundary; the secret value does not have to.
+
+## The repeated mature pattern
+
+Across these products, six rules repeat:
+
+1. **Scope is part of the schema.** A project, organization, workspace, or integration relationship is not inferred from which server read an environment variable.
+2. **Secrets and choices are separate.** A product record says what to use. A protected field or secret reference supplies authority to use it.
+3. **Precedence is declared.** A value is product-owned, inherited, runtime-overridden, or provisioned. It is not whichever row happened to exist first.
+4. **A related bundle moves together.** GitLab inherits a complete integration bundle. Grafana provisions a complete data source. Airbyte updates a complete source configuration.
+5. **Declarative state has a version.** Grafana uses a resource version to reject an older writer. Generated GitLab files are replaced from one canonical deployment input.
+6. **Validation happens before activation.** GitLab validates during reconfigure. Grafana validates provisioned resources and runtime settings. Airbyte validates a source against its connector specification. A process must not report ready only because every individual field is non-empty.
+
+No reviewed product uses this as its durable authority rule:
+
+> Copy each deployment variable into an independent database row only when that row is missing, then combine old and new rows at runtime.
+
+That statement is an inference from the reviewed designs. The products either keep the product database authoritative or use an explicit provisioner that reconciles declared state.
+
+## Consequence for Egma
+
+The current domain decision is sound: a persona version selects its LLM, STT, and TTS provider and model independently; a run pins that persona version; organization-owned provider credentials stay separate. See [ADR-0010 on the managed-model-access branch](https://github.com/egma-ai/egma-planning/blob/codex/managed-model-access/docs/adr/0010-personas-select-models-independently.md).
+
+The safe ownership split is:
+
+| State | Owner | Storage |
+|---|---|---|
+| Persona behavior and LLM/STT/TTS selections | Product domain | Immutable persona version in Postgres |
+| Organization provider access mode | Organization | Postgres |
+| Organization provider credential relationship | Organization | Postgres row with encrypted value or external secret reference |
+| Secret payload | Protected product column or secret manager | Never inside the persona |
+| Simulator implementation choices such as VAD internals | Egma release | Code/default deployment configuration |
+| Database, queues, public origin, signing and encryption roots | Deployment operator | Deployment configuration and secret delivery |
+| Phone carrier resource used by an organization or connection | Product resource with an explicit scope | Postgres relationship plus protected credentials or secret references |
+
+`prepareSimulation` is the boundary that joins these facts. It should:
+
+1. Read the persona version pinned by the run.
+2. Read the organization's current provider access and credential bindings.
+3. Resolve only the secret values required by that persona version.
+4. Validate provider, model job, model, and voice as one compatible structure.
+5. Create one closed work order for the simulator.
+
+The simulator must not add an environment fallback after this boundary. That would create a second runtime answer.

+metadata:
+  externalId: remedy-default
+  organizationId: org_...
+  generation: 7
+spec:
+  llm: { provider: openai, model: gpt-5.6-terra }
+  stt: { provider: openai_realtime, model: gpt-live-transcribe }
+  tts: { provider: cartesia, model: sonic-3.5, voiceId: ... }
+```

+A separate organization credential binding contains no plaintext secret:

+```yaml
+apiVersion: egma.ai/v1alpha1
+kind: ModelProviderCredentialBinding
+metadata:
+  externalId: production-openai
+  organizationId: org_...
+  generation: 3
+spec:
+  provider: openai

+# Provider model catalogue: OpenAI, Deepgram, Cartesia
+
+Date: 2026-08-22
+
+## Question
+
+Which models can Egma's persona catalogue offer today for each job in the pipecat pipeline — LLM (OpenAI chat completions), streaming STT (Deepgram `/v1/listen` websocket, OpenAI realtime transcription websocket), and streaming TTS (Cartesia websocket, OpenAI `/v1/audio/speech`)? And are the five IDs currently in the catalogue (`gpt-4o-mini`, `gpt-live-transcribe`, `nova-3-general`, `sonic-3.5`, `gpt-4o-mini-tts`) real, current, or superseded?
+
+## Method
+
+Every claim below was verified on 2026-08-22 against live provider documentation. OpenAI's platform docs now live at `developers.openai.com` (`platform.openai.com/docs/*` 301-redirects there); OpenAI, Deepgram, and Cartesia all serve clean Markdown by appending `.md` to a docs URL, which is what was fetched. Adapter facts come from reading the installed pipecat 1.7.0 sources in `/home/user/egma/apps/simulator/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/pipecat/`. Latency figures marked "TTFS p99" are pipecat's own [stt-benchmark](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/stt-benchmark) constants shipped in `pipecat/services/stt_latency.py` (p99 from end of speech to final transcript).
+
+Headline findings:
+
+- **`gpt-live-transcribe` is real.** It is a GA OpenAI model and the recommended model for realtime transcription sessions. It is *not* in pipecat 1.7.0's docstrings, and it changes the session payload (`languages` array instead of `language`), so it needs a small adapter change before it is safe to list.
+- **OpenAI's current text lineup is the GPT-5.6 family** (`gpt-5.6-sol` / `gpt-5.6-terra` / `gpt-5.6-luna`). The whole gpt-5 (Aug 2025) family is deprecated with a Dec 11, 2026 shutdown. `gpt-4o-mini` still works but is two generations behind and off the current models index.
+- **`gpt-4o-transcribe` and `gpt-4o-mini-transcribe` no longer work over the realtime transcription websocket** — their model pages now mark `v1/realtime/transcription_sessions` as *Not supported*. They only work via the segmented endpoint, which is banned in this codebase.
+- Deepgram and Cartesia offer **no general-purpose LLM** (confirmed below).
+

+
+## 1. LLM — OpenAI chat-completions text models
+
+Only OpenAI qualifies. Confirmation that the other two providers have no general LLM:

The Voice Agent "think" stage explicitly runs *third-party* LLMs (`open_ai`, `anthropic`, `aws_bedrock`, `google`, `groq`, `nvidia`); Deepgram manages hosted proxies of those models but ships no LLM of its own. [Voice Agent LLM models](https://developers.deepgram.com/docs/voice-agent-llm-models), [docs index](https://developers.deepgram.com/llms.txt)
+- **Cartesia**: its API surface is TTS (Sonic), STT (Ink), Voices, pronunciation dictionaries, and the Line/agents telephony platform. No text-generation endpoint exists anywhere in the docs index. [docs index](https://docs.cartesia.ai/llms.txt)

+| `tts-1` | Available, **legac…5282 tokens truncated…tern has three different kinds of state:
+
+1. **Deployment configuration** tells the application how to run. Examples are database addresses, public origins, service topology, encryption roots, and feature enablement. It normally comes from a deployment file, command-line argument, or environment variable.
+2. **Product configuration** tells the application what a customer-created resource means. It belongs to a tenant-scoped database record and changes through the product API or a declared provisioning API.
+3. **Secret material** gives authority to another system. It is encrypted in the product database or stored in an external secret manager. The product record keeps its tenant relationship and either the encrypted value or a secret reference.
+
+Environment variables and a secret manager are delivery mechanisms. They do not decide which model makes up a persona. A secret manager can hold an OpenAI key, but it should not decide that a persona uses OpenAI or select the model ID.
+
+When a deployment file is allowed to manage a product resource, mature systems make that authority explicit. They reconcile the whole resource, record its source, and prevent an older file or a second writer from silently changing part of it.
+
+## Comparison
+
+| Product | Deployment configuration | Product configuration | Secret handling | Authority and drift control |
+|---|---|---|---|---|
+| GitLab | `gitlab.rb` is the canonical installation configuration. `gitlab-ctl reconfigure` turns it into generated service files. | Instance application settings live in the database. Integrations can be configured at instance, group, or project scope. | GitLab distinguishes operational secrets from application secrets. Operational bootstrap secrets stay outside the database. Feature credentials normally use encrypted database columns. | Generated files are overwritten on reconfigure. Integration inheritance applies to the complete integration settings, not selected fields. |
+| Sentry | `config.yml` and `sentry.conf.py` control the installation. A declared value can supply a default or lock a value against UI changes. | Project options and organization integration records are database models with explicit tenant relationships. | Integration metadata that can contain credentials uses an encrypted JSON database field. | A project option write is transactional and invalidates the project configuration cache. Deployment-enforced values and product-editable values have an explicit precedence rule. |
+| Grafana | Defaults, `grafana.ini`, command-line arguments, and `GF_*` environment overrides configure the server. | Data sources and dashboards are organization-scoped product resources stored in the database. | Data-source passwords and tokens use `secureJsonData` and are encrypted before database storage. An external KMS can protect the database encryption keys. | Provisioning files actively update existing database resources. A resource `version` rejects stale writers; `prune` makes deletion explicit. Provisioned resources can be read-only in the UI. |
+| Airbyte | Helm `values.yaml` and deployment variables configure the Airbyte services and the chosen secret persistence backend. | A source is a workspace-scoped resource with one configuration object. OAuth provider overrides can be workspace- or organization-scoped. | Connector schemas mark secret fields. Airbyte can store secret payloads in AWS or Google Secret Manager, and its API can accept a secret ID instead of an OAuth token. | A full source update replaces the complete source configuration. Reads mask secret fields. The connector specification defines the allowed configuration shape. |
+
+## GitLab
+
+GitLab draws a direct line between installation state and application state.
+
+For a Linux package, `gitlab.rb` is the canonical deployment configuration. A reconfigure run parses it, computes defaults, validates input, and creates the service-specific files. GitLab tells operators not to edit the generated `gitlab.yml`, because the next reconfigure run replaces it. This gives deployment state one declared owner instead of two editable copies. Sources: [Omnibus architecture](https://docs.gitlab.com/omnibus/development/architecture/), [changing generated configuration](https://docs.gitlab.com/omnibus/settings/gitlab.yml/), and [reconfigure internals](https://docs.gitlab.com/omnibus/development/reconfigure_in_detail/).
+
+Application settings are separate database-backed state with an administrator API. They are cached, but the database remains the product store. Source: [Application settings API](https://docs.gitlab.com/api/settings/).
+
+GitLab also gives a useful secret split:
+
+- Application secrets, such as feature access tokens, use encrypted database columns.
+- Operational secrets, such as keys required before the database can be opened, remain outside the database in a protected file, Kubernetes Secret, or Vault-backed deployment path.
+- GitLab explicitly advises against putting unrelated feature secrets into one global application-settings record because one decryption problem could affect the full application.
+
+Source: [GitLab application secrets](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/application_secrets/).
+
+GitLab integrations show how tenant configuration can inherit safely. An integration can have instance, group, or project settings. A project can inherit a group bundle or use a custom bundle. A change to group defaults affects only descendants that still declare inherited ownership. GitLab documents that inheritance is for the entire settings bundle, not field by field. Source: [Project integrations and inherited settings](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/integrations/).
+
+**Lesson for Egma:** a provider credential and its ownership can inherit, but one provider bundle must move together. The system must not keep an old provider while adding a new model from another desired bundle.
+
+## Sentry
+
+Sentry uses deployment files for system behavior and database models for tenant behavior.
+
+Self-hosted Sentry has `config.yml` for most installation options and `sentry.conf.py` for advanced process configuration. Its default configuration states that file values can provide defaults or prevent UI changes. This is an explicit authority choice, not an insert-once side effect. Sources: [Sentry self-hosted configuration](https://develop.sentry.dev/self-hosted/) and [the default `config.yml` contract](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/cc46bf5b89b8576b461d223cda2ab765013f98e8/src/sentry/data/config/config.yml.default#L1-L4).
+
+Product choices use tenant-scoped models. `ProjectOption` has a project foreign key and states that the option applies to one project. Its manager writes in a transaction and refreshes the project configuration cache. Source: [`ProjectOption`](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/cc46bf5b89b8576b461d223cda2ab765013f98e8/src/sentry/models/options/project_option.py#L143-L170) and [its tenant scope](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/cc46bf5b89b8576b461d223cda2ab765013f98e8/src/sentry/models/options/project_option.py#L215-L235).
+
+Provider integrations use a separate model. Sentry stores integration metadata, including possible credentials, in an encrypted JSON field. An `OrganizationIntegration` row connects the provider integration to a specific organization and holds organization-specific configuration. Sources: [`Integration`](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/cc46bf5b89b8576b461d223cda2ab765013f98e8/src/sentry/integrations/models/integration.py#L38-L58) and [`OrganizationIntegration`](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/cc46bf5b89b8576b461d223cda2ab765013f98e8/src/sentry/integrations/models/organization_integration.py#L19-L44).
+
+**Lesson for Egma:** installation defaults and tenant records can use the same application, but they need different owners and schemas. A deployment-wide key-value table is not a substitute for an organization or project relationship.
+
+## Grafana
+
+Grafana is the clearest example of both valid modes.
+
+Server configuration has a documented precedence chain. Grafana starts with defaults, reads a custom INI file, then accepts command-line and `GF_*` environment overrides. Environment variables override known server options; they are not a general product-resource store. File and Vault value providers can inject secret values into a known setting. Source: [Configure Grafana](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/setup-grafana/configure-grafana/).
+
+Data sources are product resources. They have an organization ID, normal `jsonData`, and encrypted `secureJsonData`. Grafana states that its database contains credentials for data sources and alert notifications and encrypts those values before writing them. An external KMS can protect the key that encrypts the database values. Sources: [Grafana provisioning](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/administration/provisioning/) and [database secret encryption](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/setup-grafana/configure-security/configure-database-encryption/).
+
+Grafana also supports GitOps without pretending the database and file are equal writers:
+
+- Startup provisioning creates or updates the database resource to match the file.
+- A numeric resource version prevents an older Grafana node from overwriting newer configuration.
+- `editable: false` blocks UI edits when the file owns the resource.
+- `prune: true` makes file-driven deletion an explicit decision.
+- Secret values can enter `secureJsonData` through environment expansion, but the non-secret resource shape remains in the provisioning file.
+
+Source: [Provision Grafana](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/administration/provisioning/).
+
+**Lesson for Egma:** it is valid to materialize a deployment-owned resource in Postgres. That database row is a projection, not a second owner. It needs provenance, a version, whole-resource reconciliation, and a read-only product surface.
+
+## Airbyte
+
+Airbyte separates a connector resource from its credential payload.
+
+A source is created with a `workspaceId`, name, connector definition, and one configuration object. This makes the source a tenant-scoped domain resource, not a collection of process variables. Source: [Create a source](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/createsource).
+
+Connector schemas identify secret fields. Airbyte does not return those values on reads. A full update replaces the full source configuration, and a masked placeholder tells the API to retain an existing secret. Source: [Full source update](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/putsource).
+
+For OAuth, Airbyte can store the access and refresh tokens in its secret store and return a secret ID. The product later creates the workspace source with that ID. It also supports provider OAuth credentials at workspace or organization scope, instead of one global credential for all customers. Sources: [OAuth source flow](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/creating-oauth-sources), [workspace OAuth override](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/workspaceoauthcredentials), and [organization OAuth override](https://reference.airbyte.com/reference/createorupdateorganizationoauthcredentials).
+
+At deployment level, Airbyte's documented configuration selects a secret persistence implementation, including AWS Secrets Manager and Google Secret Manager. `values.yaml` is the operator interface; the secret store holds payloads. Source: [Airbyte deployment configuration](https://github.com/airbytehq/airbyte/blob/master/docs/platform/operator-guides/configuring-airbyte.md#secrets).
+
+**Lesson for Egma:** the organization or project record decides which provider configuration applies. The secret manager stores or resolves its sensitive fields. A secret ID can cross the boundary; the secret value does not have to.
+
+## The repeated mature pattern
+
+Across these products, six rules repeat:
+
+1. **Scope is part of the schema.** A project, organization, workspace, or integration relationship is not inferred from which server read an environment variable.
+2. **Secrets and choices are separate.** A product record says what to use. A protected field or secret reference supplies authority to use it.
+3. **Precedence is declared.** A value is product-owned, inherited, runtime-overridden, or provisioned. It is not whichever row happened to exist first.
+4. **A related bundle moves together.** GitLab inherits a complete integration bundle. Grafana provisions a complete data source. Airbyte updates a complete source configuration.
+5. **Declarative state has a version.** Grafana uses a resource version to reject an older writer. Generated GitLab files are replaced from one canonical deployment input.
+6. **Validation happens before activation.** GitLab validates during reconfigure. Grafana validates provisioned resources and runtime settings. Airbyte validates a source against its connector specification. A process must not report ready only because every individual field is non-empty.
+
+No reviewed product uses this as its durable authority rule:
+
+> Copy each deployment variable into an independent database row only when that row is missing, then combine old and new rows at runtime.
+
+That statement is an inference from the reviewed designs. The products either keep the product database authoritative or use an explicit provisioner that reconciles declared state.
+
+## Consequence for Egma
+
+The current domain decision is sound: a persona version selects its LLM, STT, and TTS provider and model independently; a run pins that persona version; organization-owned provider credentials stay separate. See [ADR-0010 on the managed-model-access branch](https://github.com/egma-ai/egma-planning/blob/codex/managed-model-access/docs/adr/0010-personas-select-models-independently.md).
+
+The safe ownership split is:
+
+| State | Owner | Storage |
+|---|---|---|
+| Persona behavior and LLM/STT/TTS selections | Product domain | Immutable persona version in Postgres |
+| Organization provider access mode | Organization | Postgres |
+| Organization provider credential relationship | Organization | Postgres row with encrypted value or external secret reference |
+| Secret payload | Protected product column or secret manager | Never inside the persona |
+| Simulator implementation choices such as VAD internals | Egma release | Code/default deployment configuration |
+| Database, queues, public origin, signing and encryption roots | Deployment operator | Deployment configuration and secret delivery |
+| Phone carrier resource used by an organization or connection | Product resource with an explicit scope | Postgres relationship plus protected credentials or secret references |
+
+`prepareSimulation` is the boundary that joins these facts. It should:
+
+1. Read the persona version pinned by the run.
+2. Read the organization's current provider access and credential bindings.
+3. Resolve only the secret values required by that persona version.
+4. Validate provider, model job, model, and voice as one compatible structure.
+5. Create one closed work order for the simulator.
+
+The simulator must not add an environment fallback after this boundary. That would create a second runtime answer.
+
+## Architecture C: explicit GitOps-provisioned resources
+
+This architecture is for an operator who wants `egma-cloud` to own selected product resources. It is an alternative authority mode, not another insert-only seed path.
+
+### Resource shape
+
+A versioned manifest contains non-secret product state:
+
+```yaml
+apiVersion: egma.ai/v1alpha1
+kind: Persona
+metadata:
+  externalId: remedy-default
+  organizationId: org_...
+  generation: 7
+spec:
+  llm: { provider: openai, model: gpt-5.6-terra }
+  stt: { provider: openai_realtime, model: gpt-live-transcribe }
+  tts: { provider: cartesia, model: sonic-3.5, voiceId: ... }
+```
+
+A separate organization credential binding contains no plaintext secret:
+
+```yaml
+apiVersion: egma.ai/v1alpha1
+kind: ModelProviderCredentialBinding
+metadata:
+  externalId: production-openai
+  organizationId: org_...
+  generation: 3
+spec:
+  provider: openai
+  secretRef: aws-secrets-manager://egma/providers/openai
+```
+
+AWS Secrets Manager stores only the protected value. The manifest stores the provider relationship and secret reference. Postgres stores the materialized product resource, its tenant, `source=provisioned`, external ID, desired generation, observed generation, and a hash of the normalized specification.
+
+### Reconciliation contract
+
+- The provisioner owns only rows marked `source=provisioned`.
+- The product API refuses edits to those rows and reports that the deployment owns them.
+- The provisioner validates and applies the whole resource in one transaction.
+- An older generation cannot replace a newer generation.
+- Removal does nothing unless the manifest declares deletion or an explicit prune policy.
+- The deployment fails before traffic moves when the resource shape is invalid, a provider/model-job pair is unsupported, or a required secret reference cannot be resolved.
+- A successful deploy records `observedGeneration == generation`. Drift is visible when they differ.
+- A model edit creates a new immutable persona version. It does not rewrite a version used by an earlier run.
+
+The Postgres row is then an active projection of the manifest. It is not an independent source of truth. This follows Grafana's provisioned-resource pattern and GitLab's generated-configuration pattern.
+
+### `prepareSimulation` remains unchanged
+
+The provisioner changes how a persona version and credential binding enter Postgres. It does not create a second simulator path.
+
+`prepareSimulation` still reads the pinned persona version and organization credential binding from the product model, resolves the secret reference just in time, and creates the same closed work order. A product-authored persona and a provisioned persona use the same preparation code.
+
+### Trade-offs
+
+Benefits:
+
+- Non-secret state is reviewed, versioned, diffable, and easy to roll back.
+- AWS contains secrets only.
+- Drift has a visible generation and hash.
+- One controller owns a provisioned resource, so a UI writer cannot conflict with it.
+- Hosted defaults can use the same domain model and execution path as customer-created personas.
+
+Costs:
+
+- The provisioner, status model, and immutable-version creation add real system complexity.
+- A deployment is a slow and unsuitable edit surface for normal customer persona work.
+- Deletion and rollback need deliberate semantics because old runs must keep their pinned persona versions.
+- Secret reference resolution adds an operational dependency at simulation preparation time unless the secret is safely cached.
+
+Use this mode for operator-owned defaults, internal organizations, or customers that explicitly choose GitOps. Keep ordinary hosted customer personas product-owned in Postgres. Do not let the same persona switch silently between UI ownership and deployment ownership.
+
+## Recommended decision test
+
+For each proposed setting, ask these questions in order:
+
+1. Does changing it change how a persona behaves? Put it in a persona version.
+2. Does it authorize an organization to use a provider? Put the relationship in organization state and protect the secret value separately.
+3. Does it define how one connection reaches one agent? Put it on that connection or its scoped carrier resource.
+4. Does it only tell an Egma process how to start or find infrastructure? Put it in deployment configuration.
+5. Must a deployment file own a product resource? Use an explicit provisioned resource with provenance, generation, whole-resource reconciliation, and one writer.
+
+This test prevents a new global key-value table from collecting unrelated domain choices only because each choice is needed during a simulation.

L800: ## Using GPT-5.2
L801: 
L802: Learn best practices, features, and migration guidance for GPT-5.2.
L803: ## Introduction
L804: 
L805: GPT-5.2 was released as a flagship general-purpose model for both general and agentic tasks. Compared with GPT-5.1, it improved:
L806: 
L807:   * General intelligence
L808:   * Instruction following
L809:   * Accuracy and token efficiency
L810:   * Multimodality—especially vision
L811:   * Code generation—especially front-end UI creation
L812:   * Tool calling and context management in the API
L813:   * Spreadsheet understanding and creation
L814: Unlike the previous GPT-5.1 model, GPT-5.2 has new features for managing what the model “knows” and “remembers” to improve accuracy.
L815: 
L816: This guide covers key features of the GPT-5 model family and how to get the most out of GPT-5.2.
L817: ## Explore coding examples
L818: 
L819: Click through a few demo applications generated entirely with a single prompt, without writing any code by hand. Note that these examples were either generated by GPT-5.2 or our previous flagship model, GPT-5.
L820: 
L821: Explore
L822: ## Model, API, and feature updates
L823: 
L824: The GPT-5.2 generation includes `gpt-5.2` for complex tasks that require broad world knowledge, `gpt-5.2-chat-latest` for ChatGPT-aligned behavior, and `gpt-5.2-pro` for problems that benefit from more compute.
L825: 
L826: For a smaller model, use `gpt-5-mini`.
L827: 
L828: To help you pick the model that best fits your use case, consider these tradeoffs:
L829: Variant  | Best for
L830: --- | ---
L831: cite423†`gpt-5.2` | Complex reasoning, broad world knowledge, and code-heavy or multi-step agentic tasks
L832: cite424†`gpt-5.2-pro` | Tough problems that may take longer to solve but require harder thinking
L833: cite425†`gpt-5.2-codex` | Companies building interactive coding products; full spectrum of coding tasks
L834: cite426†`gpt-5-mini` | Cost-optimized reasoning and chat; balances speed, cost, and capability
L836: ### New features in GPT-5.2
L837: 
L838: Just like GPT-5.1, the new GPT-5.2 has API features like custom tools, parameters to control verbosity and reasoning, and an allowed tools list. What’s new in 5.2 is a new `xhigh` reasoning effort level, concise reasoning summaries, and new context management using compaction.
L839: 
L840: This guide walks through some of the key features of the GPT-5 model family and how to get the most out of 5.2 in particular.
L1262: ### Preambles
L1263: 
L1264: Preambles are brief, user-visible explanations that GPT-5.2 generates before invoking any tool or function, outlining its intent or plan—for example, “why I’m calling this tool.” They appear after the chain of thought and before the actual tool call, making the model’s reasoning easier to understand and debug while supporting precise steering.
L1265: By letting GPT-5.2 “think out loud” before each tool call, preambles boost tool-calling accuracy (and overall task success) without bloating reasoning overhead. To enable preambles, add a system or developer instruction—for example: “Before you call a tool, explain why you are calling it.” GPT-5.2 adds a concise rationale to each specified tool call.
L1266: The model may also output multiple messages between tool calls, which can enhance the interaction experience—particularly for minimal reasoning or latency-sensitive use cases.
L1267: For more on using preambles, see the cite429†GPT-5 prompting cookbook .
L1268: ## Migration quickstart
L1269: 
L1270: GPT-5.2 works best with the Responses API, which supports preserving reasoning context between turns. Read below to migrate from your current model or API.
L1271: ### Migrating from other models to GPT-5.2
L1272: 
L1273: While the model should be close to a drop-in replacement for GPT-5.1, there are a few key changes to call out. See the cite428†GPT-5.2 prompting guide for specific updates to make in your prompts.
L1274: Using GPT-5 models with the Responses API provides improved intelligence because of the API design. The Responses API can pass the previous turn’s CoT to the model. This leads to fewer generated reasoning tokens, higher cache hit rates, and less latency. To learn more, see an cite430†in-depth guide on the benefits of the Responses API.
L1275: When migrating to GPT-5.2 from an older OpenAI model, start by experimenting with reasoning levels and prompting strategies. Based on our testing, we recommend using our cite431†prompt optimizer†platform.openai.com —which automatically updates your prompts for GPT-5.2 based on our best practices—and following this model-specific guidance:
L1276:   * `gpt-5.1`: `gpt-5.2` with default settings is meant to be a drop-in replacement.
L1277:   * o3: `gpt-5.2` with `medium` or `high` reasoning. Start with `medium` reasoning with prompt tuning, then increase to `high` if you aren’t getting the results you want.
L1278:   * `gpt-4.1`: `gpt-5.2` with `none` reasoning. Start with `none` and tune your prompts; increase if you need better performance.
L1279:   * `o4-mini` or `gpt-4.1-mini`: `gpt-5-mini` with prompt tuning is a great replacement.
L1280:   * `gpt-4.1-nano`: `gpt-5-nano` with prompt tuning is a great replacement.
L1281: ### GPT-5.2 parameter compatibility
L1282: 
L1283: The following parameters are only supported when using GPT-5.2 with reasoning effort set to `none`:
L1284: 
L1285:   * `temperature`
L1286:   * `top_p`
L1287:   * `logprobs`
L1288: 
L1289: Requests to GPT-5.2 or GPT-5.1 with any other reasoning effort setting, or to older GPT-5 models—for example, `gpt-5`, `gpt-5-mini`, or `gpt-5-nano`—that include these fields will raise an error.
L1290: To achieve similar results with reasoning effort set higher, or with another GPT-5 family model, try these alternative parameters:
L1291: 
L1292:   * Reasoning depth: `reasoning: { effort: "none" | "low" | "medium" | "high" | "xhigh" }`
L1293:   * Output verbosity: `text: { verbosity: "low" | "medium" | "high" }`
L1294:   * Output length: `max_output_tokens`
L1295: ### Migrating from Chat Completions to Responses API
L1296: 
L1297: The biggest difference, and main reason to migrate from Chat Completions to the Responses API for GPT-5.2, is support for passing chain of thought (CoT) between turns. See a full cite432†comparison of the APIs .
L1298: Passing CoT exists only in the Responses API, and we’ve seen improved intelligence, fewer generated reasoning tokens, higher cache hit rates, and lower latency as a result of doing so. Most other parameters remain at parity, though the formatting is different. Here’s how new parameters are handled differently between Chat Completions and the Responses API:

L1490: ### 2. Key behavioral differences
L1491: 
L1492: Compared with previous generation models (e.g. GPT-5 and GPT-5.1), GPT-5.2 delivers:
L1498: This guide focuses on prompting GPT-5.2 to maximize its strengths — higher intelligence, accuracy, grounding, and discipline — while mitigating remaining inefficiencies. Existing GPT-5 / GPT-5.1 prompting guidance largely carries over and remains applicable.
L1844: ### 8. Prompt Migration Guide to GPT-5.2
L1845: 
L1846: This section helps you migrate prompts and model configs to GPT-5.2 while keeping behavior stable and cost/latency predictable. GPT-5-class models support a reasoning_effort knob (e.g., none|minimal|low|medium|high|xhigh) that trades off speed/cost vs. deeper reasoning.
L1847: 
L1848: Migration mapping Use the following default mappings when updating to GPT-5.2
L1849: Current model  | Target model  | Target reasoning_effort  | Notes
L1850: --- | --- | --- | ---
L1851: GPT-4o  | GPT-5.2  | none  | Treat 4o/4.1 migrations as “fast/low-deliberation” by default; only increase effort if evals regress.
L1852: GPT-4.1  | GPT-5.2  | none  | Same mapping as GPT-4o to preserve snappy behavior.
L1853: GPT-5  | GPT-5.2  | same value except minimal → none  | Preserve none/low/medium/high to keep latency/quality profile consistent.
L1854: GPT-5.1  | GPT-5.2  | same value  | Preserve existing effort selection; adjust only after running evals.
L1855: *Note that default reasoning level for GPT-5 is medium, and for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 is none.
L1856: 
L1857: We introduced the cite435†Prompt Optimizer†platform.openai.com in the Playground to help users quickly improve existing prompts and migrate them across GPT-5 and other OpenAI models. General steps to migrate to a new model are as follows:
L1858:   * Step 1: Switch models, don’t change prompts yet. Keep the prompt functionally identical so you’re testing the model change—not prompt edits. Make one change at a time.
L1859:   * Step 2: Pin reasoning_effort. Explicitly set GPT-5.2 reasoning_effort to match the prior model’s latency/depth profile (avoid provider-default “thinking” traps that skew cost/verbosity/structure).

1	#!/bin/bash
     2	# Turn settings.map into the .env the platform runs on.
     3	#
     4	#   ./assemble-env.sh [output-path] [path-to-egma-checkout]
     5	#
     6	# Replaces the hand-written fetch-env.sh that used to live on the box. That file
     7	# was maintained separately from the code, drifted behind a rename, and took the
     8	# platform's persona down with it. Nothing here is maintained separately: the
     9	# list of settings comes from egma's own compose files and the answers come from
    10	# settings.map, which check-settings.sh proves covers them.
    11	#
    12	# **It refuses to write anything if the check fails.** A half-answered .env is
    13	# the failure this whole arrangement exists to prevent, so a gap stops the
    14	# deployment rather than reaching it.
    15	#
    16	# **No secret value is written anywhere but the output file**, which is created
    17	# with mode 600. Nothing is echoed, and a secret is fetched once however many
    18	# settings read from it.
    19	set -euo pipefail
    20	
    21	HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
    22	OUT="${1:-/opt/egma/.env}"
    23	CODE="${2:-$(cd "$HERE/../../.." && pwd)}"
    24	REGION="${AWS_REGION:-us-east-1}"
    25	
    26	bash "$HERE/check-settings.sh" "$CODE" || {
    27	  echo >&2
    28	  echo "Refusing to assemble a .env that does not answer every setting." >&2
    29	  exit 1
    30	}
    31	
    32	umask 077
    33	tmp="$(mktemp)"
    34	trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT
    35	
    36	declare -A cache
    37	
    38	fetch() {
    39	  local id="$1"
    40	  [ -n "${cache[$id]+set}" ] || cache[$id]="$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value \
    41	    --secret-id "$id" --region "$REGION" --query SecretString --output text)"
    42	  printf '%s' "${cache[$id]}"
    43	}
    44	
    45	field() {
    46	  python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.loads(sys.argv[1])[sys.argv[2]])' "$1" "$2"
    47	}
    48	
    49	written=0
    50	while read -r name how a b _rest; do
    51	  case "$how" in
    52	    secret)
    53	      value="$(field "$(fetch "$a")" "$b")"
    54	      printf '%s=%s\n' "$name" "$value" >> "$tmp"
    55	      written=$((written + 1))
    56	      ;;
    57	    literal|inert)
    58	      # inert writes exactly like literal — the difference is what it tells a
    59	      # reader of the map: this value feeds a profiled-out container that never
    60	      # starts, and exists only because compose checks `:?` markers for every
    61	      # service at file load, switched-off ones included.
    62	      printf '%s=%s\n' "$name" "$a" >> "$tmp"
    63	      written=$((written + 1))
    64	      ;;
    65	    deploy-time)
    66	      # deploy.sh appends these after this script runs, because they describe
    67	      # the deployment being made rather than the platform being deployed.
    68	      ;;
    69	    compose-default|unset)
    70	      # Deliberately absent, so egma's own default applies. Writing an empty
    71	      # value here would not be the same thing: compose passes an unset
    72	      # optional through as an empty string, and the API treats "" and "never
    73	      # set" alike only because it filters blanks out again on the way in.
    74	      ;;
    75	    *)
    76	      echo "settings.map: $name has an unknown disposition '$how'" >&2
    77	      exit 1
    78	      ;;
    79	  esac
    80	done < <(grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' "$HERE/settings.map")
    81	
    82	install -m 600 "$tmp" "$OUT"
    83	echo "assembled $written settings into $OUT"
     1	#!/bin/bash
     2	# Does this deployment have an answer for every setting egma asks for?
     3	#
     4	#   ./check-settings.sh [path-to-egma-checkout]
     5	#
     6	# **This is the file that stops a rename reaching production silently.** On
     7	# 2026-08-15 a variable was renamed in the code on 14 August, every test passed,
     8	# and the platform came up with its persona unconfigured — because the box's
     9	# settings were maintained by hand, in a file no test could see.
    10	#
    11	# It needs no AWS credential and reads no secret. It compares two lists:
    12	#
    13	#   what egma asks for   the compose files in the code repository, resolved by
    14	#                        `docker compose config --no-interpolate`, which needs
    15	#                        no values at all
    16	#   what we answer       settings.map beside this script
    17	#
    18	# A variable in the first list and not the second fails. So does a map entry for
    19	# a variable egma no longer has — otherwise the map silently accumulates answers
    20	# to questions nobody asks any more.
    21	#
    22	# Run it before a deployment, and run it after pulling the code repository.
    23	set -euo pipefail
    24	
    25	HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
    26	MAP="$HERE/settings.map"
    27	
    28	# The code repository. Defaults to the standard nesting — this planning
    29	# repository lives inside the code one — so the common case needs no argument.
    30	CODE="${1:-$(cd "$HERE/../../.." && pwd)}"
    31	[ -f "$CODE/docker-compose.yml" ] || {
    32	  echo "No docker-compose.yml under $CODE" >&2
    33	  echo "Pass the egma checkout as the first argument." >&2
    34	  exit 2
    35	}
    36	
    37	[ -f "$MAP" ] || { echo "No settings.map beside this script." >&2; exit 2; }
    38	
    39	# The three services this deployment runs. The managed overlay switches off the
    40	# seven bundled ones, so this is exactly what is left, derived rather than
    41	# listed — a service added to the overlay is picked up here for free.
    42	asks=$(cd "$CODE" && docker compose \
    43	  -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.managed.yml -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
    44	  config --no-interpolate --format json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "
    45	# json rather than yaml on purpose: PyYAML is preinstalled on CI runners and
    46	# absent on the box, and this check must give the same answer in both places.
    47	import sys, json, re
    48	d = json.load(sys.stdin)
    49	found = set()
    50	for name, svc in (d.get('services') or {}).items():
    51	    # The managed overlay marks stock services with the bundled profile, so
    52	    # their settings are not this deployment's to answer. Other profiles still
    53	    # belong to this deployment: the platform-telemetry collector is
    54	    # conditional, but every setting it reads must remain in the map for the
    55	    # day it is enabled.
    56	    if 'bundled' in set(svc.get('profiles') or []):
    57	        continue
    58	    # The whole service definition, not just its environment block. A variable
    59	    # can arrive through image:, command: or volumes: as easily as through
    60	    # environment: — the tunnel takes its token on the command line, and the
    61	    # image pins take the registry — and a check that read one key would have
    62	    # been blind to exactly the settings this file was written to catch.
    63	    found |= set(re.findall(r'\\\$\{([A-Z_0-9]+)', json.dumps(svc)))
    64	print('\n'.join(sorted(found)))
    65	")
    66	
    67	[ -n "$asks" ] || { echo "Could not read the compose files under $CODE" >&2; exit 2; }
    68	
    69	answers=$(grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' "$MAP" | awk '{print $1}' | sort -u)
    70	
    71	missing=$(comm -23 <(echo "$asks") <(echo "$answers"))
    72	extra=$(comm -13 <(echo "$asks") <(echo "$answers"))
    73	
    74	status=0
    75	
    76	if [ -n "$missing" ]; then
    77	  status=1
    78	  echo "egma asks for settings this deployment does not answer:" >&2
    79	  echo "$missing" | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
    80	  echo >&2
    81	  echo "Add each to settings.map with one of: secret, literal, compose-default, unset." >&2
    82	  echo >&2
    83	fi
    84	
    85	if [ -n "$extra" ]; then
    86	  status=1
    87	  echo "settings.map answers settings egma no longer asks for:" >&2
    88	  echo "$extra" | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
    89	  echo >&2
    90	  echo "Remove each, or check whether it was renamed rather than dropped." >&2
    91	  echo >&2
    92	fi
    93	
    94	# ── Phase two: prove the stack actually loads ────────────────────────────────
    95	# The list comparison above cannot see one compose behaviour: `${VAR:?}`
    96	# markers are checked when the file is loaded, for every service in it —
    97	# profiled-out ones included. The first deploy over this road passed the list
    98	# check and then failed exactly there. So this phase synthesizes a placeholder
    99	# value for every answered setting and asks compose to resolve the whole
   100	# stack, which needs no secret and no AWS — only the same files.
   101	if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then
   102	  envfile="$(mktemp)"
   103	  trap 'rm -f "$envfile"' EXIT
   104	  grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' "$MAP" | while read -r n how a _rest; do
   105	    case "$how" in
   106	      literal|inert) printf '%s=%s\n' "$n" "$a" ;;
   107	      secret)        printf '%s=placeholder\n' "$n" ;;
   108	    esac
   109	  done > "$envfile"
   110	  if ! loaderr=$(cd "$CODE" && EGMA_REGISTRY=placeholder EGMA_IMAGE_TAG=placeholder \
   111	      docker compose --env-file "$envfile" \
   112	        -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.managed.yml -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
   113	        config --services 2>&1 >/dev/null); then
   114	    status=1
   115	    echo "every setting is answered, and the stack still refuses to load:" >&2
   116	    echo "$loaderr" | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
   117	    echo >&2
   118	    echo "Usually a \${VAR:?} marker on a profiled-out service — answer it with inert." >&2
   119	  fi
   120	
   121	  # The collector is the deployment half of the one telemetry flag. It must
   122	  # be absent without its profile and present with it. deploy.sh maps
   123	  # EGMA_TELEMETRY=on to this profile and removes an old collector when off.
   124	  if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then
   125	    off_services=$(cd "$CODE" && EGMA_REGISTRY=placeholder EGMA_IMAGE_TAG=placeholder \
   126	      docker compose --env-file "$envfile" \
   127	        -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.managed.yml -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
   128	        config --services)
   129	    on_services=$(cd "$CODE" && EGMA_REGISTRY=placeholder EGMA_IMAGE_TAG=placeholder \
   130	      docker compose --env-file "$envfile" --profile platform-telemetry \
   131	        -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.managed.yml -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
   132	        config --services)
   133	    if echo "$off_services" | grep -qx otel-collector; then
   134	      status=1
   135	      echo "otel-collector starts without the platform-telemetry profile" >&2
   136	    fi
   137	    if ! echo "$on_services" | grep -qx otel-collector; then
   138	      status=1
   139	      echo "otel-collector is absent with the platform-telemetry profile" >&2
   140	    fi
   141	  fi
   142	fi
   143	
   144	if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then
   145	  echo "settings.map answers all $(echo "$asks" | wc -l | tr -d ' ') settings egma asks for, the stack loads, and the telemetry profile is gated."
   146	fi
   147	
   148	exit "$status"

    10	# settings.map, which check-settings.sh proves covers them.

    13	# the failure this whole arrangement exists to prevent, so a gap stops the
    14	# deployment rather than reaching it.

    17	# with mode 600. Nothing is echoed, and a secret is fetched once however many
    18	# settings read from it.

    59	    # can arrive through image:, command: or volumes: as easily as through
    60	    # environment: — the tunnel takes its token on the command line, and the
    61	    # image pins take the registry — and a check that read one key would have
    62	    # been blind to exactly the settings this file was written to catch.
    63	    found |= set(re.findall(r'\\\$\{([A-Z_0-9]+)', json.dumps(svc)))
    64	print('\n'.join(sorted(found)))
    65	")

    67	[ -n "$asks" ] || { echo "Could not read the compose files under $CODE" >&2; exit 2; }
    68	
    69	answers=$(grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' "$MAP" | awk '{print $1}' | sort -u)
    70	
    71	missing=$(comm -23 <(echo "$asks") <(echo "$answers"))
    72	extra=$(comm -13 <(echo "$asks") <(echo "$answers"))
    73	
    74	status=0
    75	
    76	if [ -n "$missing" ]; then
    77	  status=1
    78	  echo "egma asks for settings this deployment does not answer:" >&2
    79	  echo "$missing" | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
    80	  echo >&2
    81	  echo "Add each to settings.map with one of: secret, literal, compose-default, unset." >&2
    82	  echo >&2
    83	fi
    84	
    85	if [ -n "$extra" ]; then
    86	  status=1
    87	  echo "settings.map answers settings egma no longer asks for:" >&2
    88	  echo "$extra" | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
    89	  echo >&2
    90	  echo "Remove each, or check whether it was renamed rather than dropped." >&2
    91	  echo >&2
    92	fi

    94	# ── Phase two: prove the stack actually loads ────────────────────────────────
    95	# The list comparison above cannot see one compose behaviour: `${VAR:?}`
    96	# markers are checked when the file is loaded, for every service in it —
    97	# profiled-out ones included. The first deploy over this road passed the list
    98	# check and then failed exactly there. So this phase synthesizes a placeholder
    99	# value for every answered setting and asks compose to resolve the whole
   100	# stack, which needs no secret and no AWS — only the same files.

   103	  trap 'rm -f "$envfile"' EXIT
   104	  grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' "$MAP" | while read -r n how a _rest; do
   105	    case "$how" in
   106	      literal|inert) printf '%s=%s\n' "$n" "$a" ;;
   107	      secret)        printf '%s=placeholder\n' "$n" ;;
   108	    esac

   111	      docker compose --env-file "$envfile" \
   112	        -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.managed.yml -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
   113	        config --services 2>&1 >/dev/null); then
   114	    status=1
   115	    echo "every setting is answered, and the stack still refuses to load:" >&2
   116	    echo "$loaderr" | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
   117	    echo >&2
   118	    echo "Usually a \${VAR:?} marker on a profiled-out service — answer it with inert." >&2
   119	  fi

   122	  # be absent without its profile and present with it. deploy.sh maps
   123	  # EGMA_TELEMETRY=on to this profile and removes an old collector when off.
   124	  if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then
   125	    off_services=$(cd "$CODE" && EGMA_REGISTRY=placeholder EGMA_IMAGE_TAG=placeholder \
   126	      docker compose --env-file "$envfile" \
   127	        -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.managed.yml -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
   128	        config --services)
   129	    on_services=$(cd "$CODE" && EGMA_REGISTRY=placeholder EGMA_IMAGE_TAG=placeholder \
   130	      docker compose --env-file "$envfile" --profile platform-telemetry \
   131	        -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.managed.yml -f "$HERE/local.yml" \
   132	        config --services)
   133	    if echo "$off_services" | grep -qx otel-collector; then
   134	      status=1
   135	      echo "otel-collector starts without the platform-telemetry profile" >&2
   136	    fi
   137	    if ! echo "$on_services" | grep -qx otel-collector; then
   138	      status=1
   139	      echo "otel-collector is absent with the platform-telemetry profile" >&2
   140	    fi
   141	  fi
   142	fi
   143	
   144	if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then
   145	  echo "settings.map answers all $(echo "$asks" | wc -l | tr -d ' ') settings egma asks for, the stack loads, and the telemetry profile is gated."
   146	fi
   147	
   148	exit "$status"

There were two later attempts that never shipped:

- A complete Terra/reasoning implementation is only in local `stash@{0}`, stash commit `3d1317462c120819b50ae1fe44da043a133b6fdf`. It was mixed with unrelated monitoring work, never committed, never pushed, and never merged.

Current cloud ownership:

- [deployment/settings.map](/tmp/egma-cloud-audit.HKTxdW/deployment/settings.map:133) says persona and grader versions own provider/model/voice choices in Postgres.
- The cloud only names `EGMA_PROVIDER_CREDENTIALS_SECRET_ID` and `EGMA_PROVIDER_CREDENTIALS_REGION`.

- [assemble-env.sh](/tmp/egma-cloud-audit.HKTxdW/deployment/assemble-env.sh:49) writes only declared literals and secret fields. `unset` values are omitted.
- [check-settings.sh](/tmp/egma-cloud-audit.HKTxdW/deployment/check-settings.sh:69) fails if the cloud map contains an obsolete setting. An old `EGMA_PERSONA_MODEL` entry cannot silently return.

- Latest production workflow run `32793517233` completed successfully.
- Its SSM output reported public source at `d1dbbc759adfdc30aa546056a995e40bdd4162eb`.
- API, grader, and simulator all ran ECR images tagged with that exact SHA; the API was healthy.
- Current deployed source still accepts only `openai/gpt-4o-mini` and sends only `model` plus `messages`.

I could not query the live Supabase row directly because this shell has no AWS credentials. `aws sts get-caller-identity` returned `NoCredentials`. The deployed source and image SHA are confirmed from the production SSM log; the live `persona_version` row still needs a direct read-only database query for independent row-level proof.

The correct fix is not another environment variable and not rewriting version 1. Add Default Persona version 2 with `gpt-5.6-terra` plus reasoning `none`, widen the database and simulation contracts, restore the runtime field, and let startup seed version 2 into Postgres and move the shared persona’s current pointer. Old runs must remain pinned to version 1.
